question: How do normality assumptions affect the validity of the paired t-test when comparing machine learning model performances, and what role do non-parametric alternatives such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test play in addressing violations of these assumptions?

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Statistical comparison of machine learning model performances is a fundamental task in model evaluation and selection. When comparing two models on the same dataset, researchers typically use paired statistical tests that account for the dependency between observations from the same data points <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The paired t-test is the most commonly used parametric test for this purpose, but it relies on the critical assumption that the differences between paired observations follow a normal distribution <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. However, in practice, machine learning performance metrics such as accuracy scores, F1-scores, or error rates often violate normality assumptions due to bounded ranges, skewed distributions, or the presence of outliers <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This creates a need for non-parametric alternatives like the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which can provide valid statistical inferences without requiring distributional assumptions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Understanding when and how to use these different statistical approaches is essential for drawing reliable conclusions about model performance differences.

sections.title: Normality Assumptions and Their Violations in ML Model Comparison
sections.text:
The paired t-test, like other parametric statistical tests, relies on three fundamental assumptions that must be satisfied for valid results: normality (samples must originate from populations with normal distributions), independence (samples must be independent of each other), and homoscedasticity (equality of variances across samples) (Rego et al., 2022) (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020). However, these assumptions are frequently violated in machine learning contexts, making parametric tests unreliable for model comparison (Trawinski et al., 2012) (Wu et al., 2020).

The independence assumption is particularly problematic in machine learning evaluations. When researchers use common validation techniques like k-fold cross-validation with multiple runs, the training and test sets inevitably overlap, violating the independence requirement of the t-test and leading to underestimated standard errors (Sarigiannis et al., 2019) (Can et al., 2020) (Spooner et al., 2020). This violation inflates Type I error rates because the lack of independence results in incorrect variance estimation (Spooner et al., 2020).

The normality assumption also poses significant challenges in machine learning model comparison. Performance metrics such as accuracy, F1-scores, and error rates often do not follow normal distributions, especially when sample sizes are small (≤ 30 data points) (Can et al., 2020) (Deng et al., 2022). Empirical studies have demonstrated that the output of machine learning algorithms for regression problems frequently fails to satisfy normality requirements when tested using multiple normality tests (Trawinski et al., 2012). Researchers can assess normality using statistical tests like the Shapiro-Wilk test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, or Anderson-Darling test, as well as graphical methods such as histograms and Q-Q plots (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020) (Rego et al., 2022).

When any of these three conditions are not met, non-parametric tests become more reliable than parametric alternatives (Nasiri et al., 2018). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is widely recommended as the preferred non-parametric alternative because it makes fewer distributional assumptions while still accounting for the relative magnitude of differences between paired observations (Sarigiannis et al., 2019) (Wu et al., 2020).

sections.title: Effects of Normality Violations on Paired T-test Validity
sections.text:
Violations of normality assumptions lead to significant degradation in the paired t-test's statistical validity, manifesting as both increased Type I errors (false positives) and Type II errors (false negatives). The paired t-test is not robust against violations of the normality assumption, and when this assumption fails, it produces untrustworthy results (Ghadhban et al., 2021) (Ghadhban et al._1, 2021). As a likelihood-ratio test, the t-test often shows drastic performance degradation due to deviations from its hard-to-verify distributional assumptions (Alyakin et al., 2019).

The consequences of normality violations are particularly severe when dealing with heavy-tailed distributions or outliers. Research has shown that the t-test has greater than expected Type II error when the normality assumption does not hold, causing it to fail to detect significant improvements and potentially missing good results that could impact users and businesses negatively (Cai et al., 2023). The power of the t-test can break down under the addition of even a single outlier in the worst case (Shamsudheen et al., 2019) (Fay et al., 2010).

Real-world examples demonstrate these validity issues clearly. In machine learning model comparisons, paired t-tests may indicate statistically significant differences (p = 0.0080 and p = 0.0247) while Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the same data show no significant differences (p = 0.1250 and p = 0.2500), highlighting how normality assumptions can lead to false conclusions about model performance (Abdullakutty et al., 2024) (Yan et al., 2021). Similarly, empirical studies have found that t-tests work well enough for most functions but are not ideal on all functions, indicating that the normality assumption is frequently not met in practice (Vermetten et al., 2022).

Importantly, using preliminary normality testing to decide between parametric and non-parametric tests can actually make matters worse. Studies show that conditional testing (using normality tests first, then choosing the statistical test) results in Type I error rates that are further away from the nominal 5% level compared to using tests unconditionally (Shamsudheen et al., 2019). Normality tests tend to have little power for detecting distributions that cause problems for the t-test, making them unreliable gatekeepers for test selection (Shamsudheen et al., 2019) (Fay et al., 2010).

When the paired t-test is applied to paired outcomes that are not bivariate normal, it will generally be biased (Proudfoot et al., 2018). Given these substantial validity concerns, many researchers recommend switching to non-parametric alternatives when normality assumptions are violated to ensure more reliable statistical inference (Rehman et al., 2025).

snippets: In a mathematical approach to hypothesis tests, we start with a clearly defined set of hypotheses and choose the test with the best properties for those hypotheses. In practice, we often start with less precise hypotheses. For example, often a researcher wants to know which of two groups generally has the larger responses, and either a t-test or a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney (WMW) test could be acceptable. Although both t-tests and WMW tests are usually associated with quite different hypotheses, the decision rule and p-value from either test could be associated with many different sets of assumptions, which we call perspectives. It is useful to have many of the different perspectives to which a decision rule may be applied collected in one place, since each perspective allows a different interpretation of the associated p-value. Here we collect many such perspectives for the two-sample t-test, the WMW test and other related tests. We discuss validity and consistency under each perspective and discuss recommendations between the tests in light of these many different perspectives. Finally, we briefly discuss a decision rule for testing genetic neutrality where knowledge of the many perspectives is vital to the proper interpretation of the decision rule.
citations.title: Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney or t-test? On assumptions for hypothesis tests and multiple interpretations of decision rules.

sections.title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test as Non-parametric Alternative
sections.text:
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test serves as the primary non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test for comparing machine learning model performances (Nasiri et al., 2018) (Wu et al., 2020) (Sarigiannis et al., 2019). This test is widely recommended because it makes fewer distributional assumptions while still accounting for the relative magnitude of differences between paired observations (Sarigiannis et al., 2019).

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test operates by comparing the median difference between paired samples rather than means, testing whether this median difference is significantly different from zero (Hasan et al., 2023) . The test works by ranking the absolute differences in magnitude between paired observations, making it a rank-based statistical method (Khiari et al., 2023) (Bargiotas et al., 2023). Importantly, while "ranks" appear in the test name, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks the performance differences pooled across datasets, not the performance rankings of different methods within datasets .

The key advantages of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test in machine learning contexts are substantial. Unlike the paired t-test, it does not assume normal distribution, making it more versatile when the data distribution is unknown or not normally distributed (Picard et al., 2024) (Phalaagae et al., 2025). The test is particularly suitable when sample sizes are small (≤ 30 data points) where normality assumptions frequently fail (Can et al., 2020) (Deng et al., 2022). Additionally, outliers have less effect on the Wilcoxon test compared to the t-test, making it more robust for real-world machine learning evaluations (Duran et al., 2021) (Mohsin et al., 2017).

Despite being non-parametric, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test maintains high statistical efficiency compared to the paired t-test. For normally distributed data, the asymptotic relative efficiency (ARE) is approximately 0.95, meaning it retains 95% of the power of the t-test (Campelo et al., 2018). For non-normal populations, the ARE is at least 0.86 and often exceeds unity, making it more powerful than the t-test in many practical scenarios (Alyakin et al., 2019) (Campelo et al., 2018). This robustness suggests that the Wilcoxon test should be the default choice rather than using it only when there is evidence of non-normality (Alyakin et al., 2019).

However, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test does have some limitations. When data are normally distributed, non-parametric tests may lead to less statistical power, corresponding to a higher chance of Type II errors (failure to detect true effects) (Deng et al., 2022) (Hasan et al., 2023). The test also assumes symmetry about the median, though this assumption is less restrictive than normality (Nourmohammadi-Khiarak et al., 2019) (Campelo et al., 2018). Despite these considerations, empirical evidence from machine learning studies demonstrates that the output of algorithms frequently fails normality requirements, making the Wilcoxon signed-rank test a safer and more rational choice for model comparison (Trawinski et al., 2012) (Mohsin et al., 2017).

sections.title: Practical Guidelines for Test Selection
sections.text:
The selection between parametric and non-parametric tests for machine learning model comparison requires a systematic approach based on statistical assumption testing. The standard protocol involves first checking normality assumptions using statistical tests, then selecting the appropriate test based on the results (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020) (Song et al., 2021) (Alvarez et al., 2024).

The Shapiro-Wilk test serves as the most commonly recommended method for assessing normality in machine learning contexts (Song et al., 2021) (Ding et al., 2023) (Lian et al., 2024) (Alvarez et al., 2024) (Oliver et al., 2025). The test procedure is straightforward: if the p-value is greater than 0.05, the data can be assumed to follow a normal distribution and parametric tests are appropriate; if the p-value is less than 0.05, normality is violated and non-parametric tests should be used (Song et al., 2021) (Alvarez et al., 2024) (Oliver et al., 2025).

Additional normality tests can supplement the Shapiro-Wilk test for more comprehensive assessment. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Anderson-Darling test, and D'Agostino test (which measures sample skewness and kurtosis) provide alternative approaches (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020) (Shan, 2022). Graphical methods including histograms, empirical distribution functions, and quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots offer visual confirmation of distributional properties (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020).

The decision rule is clear: when normality assumptions are satisfied, parametric tests like the paired t-test should be used because they have higher statistical power than non-parametric alternatives (Bartz-Beielstein et al., 2020) (Mancini et al., 2018). However, when normality fails, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test becomes the preferred choice (Song et al., 2021) (Shan, 2022) (Lian et al., 2024) (Oliver et al., 2025).

Practical implementations demonstrate this workflow effectively. Research studies show mixed results within the same experiment, where some data subsets pass normality tests (enabling paired t-tests) while others fail (requiring Wilcoxon tests) (Song et al., 2021) (Ding et al., 2023). Many researchers adopt a dual-testing approach, conducting both parametric and non-parametric tests to ensure robust conclusions, often finding that the Wilcoxon test yields slightly larger p-values but with minimal practical differences (Shan, 2022) (Hu et al., 2024).

question: What are some of the methods of detecting GPS location spoofing attack in Connected and Autonomous Vehicles?

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: GPS location spoofing attacks represent one of the most significant cybersecurity threats facing Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) today <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. These attacks work by transmitting fake GPS signals that are stronger than authentic satellite signals, causing vehicle navigation systems to calculate incorrect position data <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The consequences can be severe, ranging from route deviation and traffic disruption to potential accidents and safety hazards <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. What makes GPS spoofing particularly dangerous is that modern spoofing attacks can be highly sophisticated, using techniques that make fake signals nearly indistinguishable from legitimate GPS transmissions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Traditional GPS receivers in vehicles often cannot detect these attacks because they lack the ability to verify signal authenticity <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This vulnerability has led researchers to develop multiple detection approaches that use different sensors, data sources, and analytical methods to identify when GPS signals may be compromised <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Effective spoofing detection typically requires combining several of these methods rather than relying on any single approach <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Signal-Based Detection Methods
sections.text:
Signal-based detection methods form the foundation of GPS spoofing detection by examining the physical characteristics and patterns of GPS signals themselves. These approaches can be broadly categorized into cryptographic techniques and signal-level anomaly detection (Dasgupta et al., 2020). Cryptographic techniques authenticate satellite signals using additional security keys to make signals undecryptable for unauthorized users, while signal-level detection identifies discrepancies in physical signal waveforms or arrival angles from signal sources (Dasgupta et al., 2020).

Multiple signal characteristics can be analyzed to detect spoofing attacks. Key signal features include GNSS signal frequency drift, signal strength, pseudo-range measurements, Doppler shift, and signal-to-noise ratio (Dasgupta et al., 2020) (Dang et al., 2022) (Manesh et al., 2019). Direction-of-arrival (DOA) analysis and GPS signal distortion patterns also serve as effective detection mechanisms (Abrar et al., 2024). Some methods use correlation between free-running crystal oscillator signals and GNSS signals to identify anomalies (Dasgupta et al., 2020).

Advanced signal processing techniques include cross-correlation analysis among GPS signals from multiple receivers and codeless-cross-correlation measures (Dasgupta et al., 2021) (Semanjski et al., 2019). However, sophisticated spoofers can generate synchronized signals for multiple satellites to overcome multi-receiver verification systems (Dasgupta et al., 2020). Some detection methods treat GPS spoofing as an outlier detection problem, analyzing time-series position estimates and identifying outlier values through statistical tests like the Grubbs outlier test (Burbank et al., 2024) (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022).

For connected and autonomous vehicles specifically, researchers have developed collaborative detection schemes where vehicles exchange GPS code pseudo-range values with neighboring vehicles using short-range communications to detect high correlations during spoofed GPS signal arrival (Milaat et al., 2018) (Abrar et al., 2024). Additional approaches include Data Bit Latency Defense and Vestigial Signal Defense methods, as well as entropy-based detection using Kullback-Leibler divergence measures to search for anomalies in GPS data (Dasgupta et al., 2020) (Basan et al., 2021).

snippets: Typically, existing countermeasures against spoofing attacks can be generally be categorized into two classes: cryptographic techniques and anomaly detection at the signal level. In general, satellite signals are authenticated using additional signals using cryptographic techniques to make the signal undecryptable for the users who do not have the security key (19). Signal level detection is performed by identifying discrepancies in the physical signal waveform or arrival angle from the source of the signal. Another detection approach is to verify the signal using multiple receivers of GNSS signals to detect any anomaly (20) (21). However, spoofers can spoof such receivers by generating synced signals for multiple satellites. GNSS signal frequency drift, signal strength, and the correlation between free-running crystal oscillator and GNSS signals can also be used to detect spoofing attacks (22). Humphreys et al. developed a software-defined civil GPS receiver-spoofer, which can generate an attack. They also developed two software-defined user-equipment based spoofing defense methods: (i) Data Bit Latency Defense and (ii) Vestigial Signal Defense (23)
Panice et al. developed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) based spoofing detection method by comparing the estimating the current state and actual location of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (24)

Wang et al. developed an approach to reconstruct a lost GPS where authors used real-time driving data and GPS coordinates. Their approach reconstructs the driving route using the driving data and flag an attack if the input GPS coordinates deviate more than an error threshold from the predicted GPS coordinates (25).
citations.title: Prediction-Based GNSS Spoofing Attack Detection for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: Manesh et al. (Manesh et al., 2019) exploited the received GPS signal characteristics, such as pseudo range, Doppler shift and signalto-noise ratio, to build a supervised neural network model for detecting GPS spoofing against unmanned aerial systems. Similarly, the spoofing detection approach in (Shafiee et al., 2017) used a neural network to analyze the differences between the spoofing and authentic signal patterns. The neural network takes as inputs the delta criterion, coefficient of early and late phase criterion, and total levels of signal. The authors in (Semanjski et al., 2019) proposed a GPS spoofing detection approach that leverages a supervised ML algorithm, specifically Support Vector Machine (SVM), to analyze the cross-correlation among the GPS signals of multiple GPS receivers. The work in (Gallardo et al., 2020) introduced RBF SVM, Ada Boost, Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forests methods for GPS signal's radio frequency interference analysis under the assumption that the attacker was not able to null the satellite signal

To overcome the weakness of GPS signal analyses based spoofing detection methods, the external positioning techniques, such as INS and MPS, are also used to not only provide location services for UAVs when the GPS is unavailable but also to cross-validate the authenticity of GPS information.
citations.title: Deep-Ensemble-Learning-Based GPS Spoofing Detection for Cellular-Connected UAVs

snippets: Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) have received a huge interest in military and civil applications. Applications of UAS are dependent on successful communications of these systems with different entities in their networks. A UAS network can include the UAS, ground control station, navigation satellite system, and automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) receiver. Through these entities, a UAS is vulnerable to different cyber-attacks such as GPS spoofing. In this attack, a malicious user transmits fake signals to the GPS receiver on the UAS. The fake signals can mislead not only the aircraft but also air traffic controllers, leading to serious problems. These problems range from aircraft hijacking to collisions and human casualties. This paper proposes a supervised machine learning method based on the artificial neural network to detect GPS spoofing signals. Different features such as pseudo range, Doppler shift, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are used to perform the classification of GPS signals. We examine and compare the efficiency of one-and two-hidden-layer neural networks with various numbers of hidden neurons. The results show that our proposed method provides a high probability of detection and a low probability of false alarm.
citations.title: Detection of GPS Spoofing Attacks on Unmanned Aerial Systems

snippets: GPS signal characteristics-based approaches rely on signal processing techniques to detect attacks. For instance, in (Psiaki et al., 2016), Psiaki and Humphreys proposed a GPS spoofing attack detection scheme based on the direction-of-arrival (DOA) induction. He et al. (He et al., 2014) proposed the use of GPS signal distortion to detect GPS spoofing attacks. For connected and autonomous vehicles, an anomaly detection model is proposed by Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2023) to detect GPS spoofing on the localization system using the "Learning From Demonstration" technique. Milaat and Liu (Milaat et al., 2018) proposed a decentralized technique where vehicles exchange GPS code pseudo-range values with neighbors using short-range communications to detect high correlations during spoofed GPS signal arrival. On the other hand, machine learning-based approaches rely on machine learning and data analytics techniques to detect attacks. Researchers have used one-class classifiers (Whelan et al., 2020), Artificial Neural Networks (Manesh et al., 2019), Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks [71], (Agyapong et al., 2021) to detect GPS attacks.
citations.title: GPS-IDS: An Anomaly-based GPS Spoofing Attack Detection Framework for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: Many methods exist to detect a sophisticated GNSS spoofing attack by analyzing GNSS signals (5)-(9). Encryption mechanisms, codeless-cross-correlation measures, signal statistics analysis, and antenna-based approaches are common techniques for detecting spoofing attacks. In addition, researchers also use in-vehicle inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensors, such as gyroscope and accelerometer, to calculate a vehicle's position and acceleration to flag a spoofing attack by comparing with GNSS-based position and acceleration information

several studies presented inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensor-based spoofing attack detection strategies as these sensors are resilient against signal spoofing attacks and provide a low-cost solution. Gyroscope and accelerometer are two examples of INS and IMU sensors. A spoofing attack can be detected by comparing IMU-based acceleration and GNSS-based acceleration (Neish et al., 2018)

Manickam and O'Keefe have compared position information from the accelerometer and gyroscope with the position information from GNSS to flag a spoofing attack (Manickam et al., 2016). They also analyzed different types of IMU combining with different GNSS receiver grades to evaluate their performance for attack detection. Researchers also used INS to keep track of the position of a vehicle, and eventually, it helps to detect GNSS spoofing attacks (11), (12)

They have selected three features from the GPS signal pattern-i.e., early-late phase criterion, delta criterion, and total levels of signal-to train and test the performance of their MLP-NN approach.

snippets: Spoofing of the GNSS signals presents continuous threat to the users of safety of life applications due to unaware use of false signals in generating position and timing solution. Among numerous anti-spoofing techniques applied at different stages of the signal processing, we present approach of monitoring the cross-correlation of multiple GNSS observables and measurements as an input for supervised machine learning based approach to detect potentially spoofed GNSS signals. snippets: Several papers exist in the literature that analyze various aspects of signal statistics, of both the authentic signal and the spoofed signal, in detecting the presence of a spoofing threat. As an example, the authors of (Wei et al., 2024) considered the use of Doppler frequency and carrier-to-noise (C/N) density ratio as the primary metrics to discern a spoofed signal from an authentic signal. The authors then used numerous types of ML and analytical models to analyze performance utilizing these metrics, including SVM, KNN, RF, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), DT, and XGBoost

Many other existing approaches do not cleanly fit into a taxonomy. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022) proposed an approach to GPS spoofing detection that treats GPS spoofing detection as an outlier detection problem, analyzing the time-series history of the position estimates and identifying outlier values through the Grubbs outlier test. Any outlier is a spoofed position estimation in this approach. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2021) also treated GPS spoofing as an outlier problem. They implemented a navigation filter based on a constant velocity model. This model employed a 3D Kalman filter to identify and remove outlier values, which were presumed to be spoofed locations. The authors of (Basan et al., 2021) also viewed GPS spoofing detection (in part) as an outlier detection problem, employing a Kullback-Leibler divergence measure to search for anomalies in data. The authors coupled this anomaly detection approach with an entropy-based method for spoofing detection
Other proposed approaches utilize ADS-B broadcasts from aircraft and UASs to detect GPS spoofing attacks. Ground sensors monitor ADS-B broadcasts while geolocating the corresponding aircraft.
citations.title: Detecting and Mitigating Attacks on GPS Devices

snippets: Global positioning system (GPS) is favored to provide the position, velocity, and time (PVT) details across the globe. This paper proposes an epoch-by-epoch robust positioning algorithm followed by the Grubbs outlier test to address the GPS spoofing problem. We propose to accept both authentic and spoofed GPS signals to compute the robust positions. The robust positioning considers all possible combinations of measurements and generates several position estimates, which contain actual position, spoof position, and biased positions. In this case, the positions evolved due to spoof pseudorange measurements must be removed. Hence, we model eliminating spoof locations as an outlier problem and is addressed using Grubbs outlier test. The median of the processed data after the Grubbs test is the positional information at that epoch. Moreover, this problem is also extended to the Kalman filter’s (KF) framework to address the time-varying kinematics of the target. Simulations are carried out for various numbers of actual and spoofed pseudorange measurements. In order to illustrate the robustness of the proposed technique, position root mean square error (PRMSE) is taken as a metric.
citations.title: Robust Positioning and Grubbs Outlier Test for Navigation in GPS Spoofing Environment

snippets: This letter proposes a decentralized scheme for the detection of global positioning system (GPS) spoofing in vehicular ad hoc networks. In this scheme, vehicles exchange their measured GPS code pseudo-ranges with neighboring vehicles using dedicated short-range communications. The vehicles then perform linear operations on the exchanged GPS data and derive independent statistics that are related to the measurements of each neighbor. Using these statistics, a vehicle implements a cumulative sum procedure to locally detect high correlations in the time of arrival of spoofed GPS signals. The vehicles report their local detection values to an elected head vehicle, which employs a min–max change-detection procedure to optimize the global-spoofing detection. Our experimental results show that: 1) the average detection delay decreases as the number of vehicles increase and 2) the proposed scheme converges to optimal as the probability of false-alarm reduces to zero.
citations.title: Decentralized Detection of GPS Spoofing in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks

snippets: Here, we developed a method for detecting cyber security attacks aimed at spoofing the Global Positioning System (GPS) signal of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). Most methods for detecting UAV anomalies indicative of an attack use machine learning or other such methods that compare normal behavior with abnormal behavior. Such approaches require large amounts of data and significant "training" time to prepare and implement the system. Instead, we consider a new approach based on other mathematical methods for detecting UAV anomalies without the need to first collect a large amount of data and describe normal behavior patterns. Doing so can simplify the process of creating an anomaly detection system, which can further facilitate easier implementation of intrusion detection systems in UAVs. This article presents issues related to ensuring the information security of UAVs. Development of the GPS spoofing detection method for UAVs is then described, based on a preliminary study that made it possible to form a mathematical apparatus for solving the problem. We then explain the necessary analysis of parameters and methods of data normalization, and the analysis of the Kullback—Leibler divergence measure needed to detect anomalies in UAV systems.
citations.title: GPS-Spoofing Attack Detection Technology for UAVs Based on Kullback–Leibler Divergence

sections.title: Sensor Fusion and IMU-Based Methods
sections.text:
Sensor fusion and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) based approaches represent a robust class of GPS spoofing detection methods that leverage the fact that IMU sensors are resilient against signal spoofing attacks and provide a low-cost solution (Dasgupta et al., 2021). These methods work by using in-vehicle inertial navigation system (INS) and IMU sensors, such as gyroscopes and accelerometers, to calculate a vehicle's position and acceleration independently, then comparing these measurements with GNSS-based position and acceleration information to flag potential spoofing attacks (Dasgupta et al., 2021).

The fundamental approach involves analyzing acceleration discrepancies between GPS receivers and IMU measurements. A spoofing attack can be detected by comparing IMU-based acceleration with GNSS-based acceleration, where mismatches beyond certain thresholds signify potential attacks (Dasgupta et al., 2021) (Kamal et al., 2021) (Kwon et al., 2020). Researchers have found that both the magnitude of acceleration error and the magnitude of north or east components of acceleration error can serve as effective decision variables for spoofing detection (Kwon et al., 2020).

Advanced sensor fusion frameworks have been developed that integrate multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors including accelerometers, steering angle sensors, speed sensors, and GNSS data (Dasgupta et al._1, 2021). These systems employ three concurrent strategies: predicting location shift between timestamps, detecting vehicle turns, and recognizing motion states including standstill conditions (Dasgupta et al._1, 2021). The data is processed through machine learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for location shift prediction and Random Forest models for turn detection and classification (Dasgupta et al._1, 2021) (Dasgupta et al., 2024).

More sophisticated approaches use multi-phase detection systems that combine prediction, update, and attack detection phases. In the prediction phase, readings from on-board sensors collected through the On-Board Unit (OBU) and Controller Area Network (CAN) bus are used to predict the vehicle's location using GPS-free methods based on Bayesian filtering (Kamal et al., 2021) (Vitale et al., 2021). The attack detection phase then compares GPS location measurements with refined location estimates, triggering alarms when deviations exceed predetermined thresholds (Kamal et al., 2021).

Recent developments have incorporated artificial intelligence algorithms to correct INS sensor errors that accumulate over time. LSTM algorithms are used to correct accelerations and angular rates, which are then compared to accelerations and angular rates estimated from GPS data using modified M-of-N detection methods (Aftatah et al., 2024). Other approaches combine speedometer and gyroscope data processed through Deep Neural Networks to predict vehicle displacement, continuously comparing these predictions with GPS-provided displacement and velocity to detect various types of spoofing attacks (Mohammadi et al., 2025).

The consistency check approach represents another effective strategy, where spoofing detection analyzes GNSS and IMU/odometer measurements independently during pre-selected observation windows and cross-checks the solutions provided by GNSS with inertial navigation solutions (Broumandan et al., 2018). These methods can detect sophisticated spoofing attacks including turn-by-turn, stop, and overshoot attacks by establishing thresholds based on clean datasets and monitoring deviations in real-time (Mohammadi et al., 2025).

several studies presented inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensor-based spoofing attack detection strategies as these sensors are resilient against signal spoofing attacks and provide a low-cost solution. Gyroscope and accelerometer are two examples of INS and IMU sensors. A spoofing attack can be detected by comparing IMU-based acceleration and GNSS-based acceleration (Neish et al., 2018)

Manickam and O'Keefe have compared position information from the accelerometer and gyroscope with the position information from GNSS to flag a spoofing attack (Manickam et al., 2016). They also analyzed different types of IMU combining with different GNSS receiver grades to evaluate their performance for attack detection. Researchers also used INS to keep track of the position of a vehicle, and eventually, it helps to detect GNSS spoofing attacks (11), (12)

Shafiee et al. presented a new MLP-NN approach for GPS spoofing attack detection (Shafiee et al., 2017). They have selected three features from the GPS signal pattern-i.e., early-late phase criterion, delta criterion, and total levels of signal-to train and test the performance of their MLP-NN approach.
citations.title: A Reinforcement Learning Approach for Global Navigation Satellite System Spoofing Attack Detection in Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: Based on the multi-source data readily available from the CAV's On-Board Unit (OBU) or the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus
the proposed solution is based on an in-vehicle GPS location integrity check
In the Prediction phase, the readings from the on-board sensors collected through the OBU and/or the CAN bus are used to predict the CAV's location
In the Update phase, the GPS-free CAV location measurements provided by the LA are used to update the prediction by means of Bayesian filtering and produce the refined location estimate

Finally, in the Attack Detection phase, the GPS location measurements provided by the vehicle's GPS receiver are compared with [the refined location estimate]. In case the deviation exceeds a pre-determined threshold, an alarm is triggered that signifies an attack detection

.One of the developed solutions in the literature leverages in-vehicle multi-sensory data (e.g., accelerometer, gyroscope, compass, etc.) to compute a parallel GPS-free stream of estimated vehicles' locations using a fallback localization method based on Bayesian filtering [12]. This enables the detection of potential location spoofing attacks by comparing the estimated vehicle position with the GPS location reading. A second solution is essentially a collaborative GPS spoofing defense mechanism that relies on multi-modal sensor fusion among the vehicles within a VANET, that includes such measurements as the relative distances, the relative angles, and the relative azimuth angles among the vehicles, as well as the absolute position measurements (i.e., GPS positions) of all vehicles [13]

accelerometer readings of the vehicle are used to compare with the estimated acceleration measurements of the GPS device, with the mismatch beyond a certain threshold signifying a GPS spoofing attack [14].
citations.title: GPS Location Spoofing Attack Detection for Enhancing the Security of Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: The global positioning system (GPS) is an essential technology that provides positioning capabilities and is used in various applications such as navigation, surveying, mapping, robot simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), location-based service (LBS), etc. However, the GPS is known to be vulnerable to intentional attacks such as spoofing because of its simple signal structure. In this study, a direct method is proposed for GPS spoofing detection, using Attitude and Heading Reference System (AHRS) accelerometer and analyzing the detection performance with corresponding probability density functions (PDFs). The difference in the acceleration between the GPS receiver and the accelerometer is used to detect spoofing. The magnitude of the acceleration error may be used as a decision variable. Additionally, using the magnitude of the north (or east) component of the acceleration error as another decision variable is proposed, which shows better performance in some conditions. The performance of the two decision variables is compared by calculating the probability of spoofing detection and the detectable minimum spoofing acceleration (DMSA), given a pre-defined false alarm probability and a pre-defined detection probability. It turns out that both decision variables need to be used together to obtain the best spoofing detection performance.
citations.title: Performance Analysis of Direct GPS Spoofing Detection Method with AHRS/Accelerometer

snippets: a sensor fusion based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework is presented that consists of three concurrent strategies for an autonomous vehicle (AV): (i) prediction of location shift, (ii) detection of turns (left or right), and (iii) recognition of motion state (including standstill state). Data from multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors (i.e., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, speed sensor, and GNSS) are fused and fed into a recurrent neural network model, which is a long short-term memory (LSTM) network for predicting the location shift

We have then combined k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms to detect turns using data from the steering angle sensor. In addition, data from an AV's speed sensor is used to recognize the AV's motion state including the standstill state
the use of low-cost invehicle sensors (e.g., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, and speed sensor) could provide effective strategies for detecting sophisticated spoofing attacks

we have developed a framework for detecting spoofing attacks on GNSS services by identifying and predicting AV states, which include location shift, turning direction, and motion state using data from low-cost in-vehicle sensors.
citations.title: Sensor Fusion-based GNSS Spoofing Attack Detection Framework for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: The detection framework employs two strategies: First, it compares the predicted location shift (distance between consecutive timestamps) with the inertial sensor-based location shift, monitoring vehicle motion states. Data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors are fused into an LSTM neural network to predict AV travel distance. Second, a Random-Forest model detects and classifies turns based on the steering angle sensor. Both strategies compare GNSS-derived speed with vehicle velocity

The detection framework combines RTK GNSS receiver and high-performing IMU data to enhance AV navigation accuracy and reliability. The framework employs two distinct strategies: a LSTM neural network for predicting AV distance between timestamps, comparing it with inertial sensorbased location shifts and monitoring motion states; and an RF-supervised machine learning model for detecting and classifying turns using the steering angle sensor's output. GNSS-derived speed is compared with the actual vehicle velocity output in both strategies.
citations.title: Experimental Validation of Sensor Fusion-based GNSS Spoofing Attack Detection Framework for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: CARAMEL is able to detect the location spoofing attack thanks to a parallel stream of vehicle locations that relies on GPS-free signals, e.g., in-vehicle sensor measurements, or thanks to a collaborative approach enabled by the support of the infrastructure. This secondary location stream is compared with the GPS locations and in case their difference exceeds a predefined threshold, an alarm is raised to signify a GPS spoofing attack
Adopted attack detection techniques exploit robust in-vehicle and cooperative approaches that do not rely on encrypted GPS signals, but only on measurements available in the CARAMEL architecture.
citations.title: CARAMEL: results on a secure architecture for connected and autonomous vehicles detecting GPS spoofing attacks

snippets: This paper proposes a method for GPS spoofing detection that utilizes artificial intelligence algorithms in combination with raw data from an inertial navigation system (INS). Since INS sensors are prone to accumulating errors over time, these inaccuracies are corrected via a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithm. The corrected accelerations and angular rates are then compared to the accelerations and angular rates estimated from the GPS data to detect GPS spoofing signals. This comparison uses the modified M-of-N method, demonstrating its effectiveness by a detection rate reaching 80% of the spoofing zones.
citations.title: Detecting GPS Spoofing Attacks Using Corrected Low-Cost INS Data with an LSTM Network

snippets: The algorithm combines data from in-vehicle sensors, including the speedometer and gyroscope. This data is then fed into a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to predict the vehicle's displacement between timestamps. These predictions are continuously compared with GPS-provided displacement and velocity to detect the turn-by-turn, stop, and overshoot GPS spoofing attacks. Also, the same data is processed through an analytical model that uses the vehicle's dynamic movement equations to compute its position and velocity and to juxtapose them with GPS-provided position and velocity to detect the aforementioned spoofing attacks. A threshold is predetermined by using clean datasets to calculate the maximum possible deviation between in-vehicle sensor and GPS provided position/displacement and speed. Subsequently, spoofing attack detection uses this threshold for its continuous, real time comparison. Additionally, the proposed algorithm is able to detect a sequence of multiple biased attacks that fall below the mentioned threshold but can create a large deviation between the position/displacement and speed provided by GPS and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).
citations.title: Detection of Multiple Small Biased GPS Spoofing Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: A spoofing detection approach based on a consistency check between GNSS and IMU/odometer mechanization is proposed. To detect a spoofing attack, the method analyses GNSS and IMU/odometer measurements independently during a pre-selected observation window and cross checks the solutions provided by GNSS and inertial navigation solution (INS)/odometer mechanization.
citations.title: Spoofing Detection Using GNSS/INS/Odometer Coupling for Vehicular Navigation

sections.title: Machine Learning and AI-Based Approaches
sections.text:
Machine learning and artificial intelligence have emerged as powerful tools for GPS spoofing detection, offering automated approaches that can learn patterns and identify anomalies in GPS data and related sensor measurements. These methods can be broadly categorized into supervised learning techniques that use labeled training data and unsupervised approaches that detect anomalies without prior knowledge of attack patterns (Wang et al., 2022).

Supervised machine learning approaches have shown notable success in GPS spoofing detection. Support Vector Machine (SVM) based methods have been developed that compare estimated current state with actual location of vehicles to detect spoofing attacks (Dasgupta et al., 2020). Artificial neural networks represent another widely used approach, with researchers developing supervised neural network models that analyze GPS signal characteristics such as pseudo-range, Doppler shift, and signal-to-noise ratio to classify GPS signals as authentic or spoofed (Manesh et al., 2019) (Dang et al., 2022) (Filippou et al., 2023). These neural network approaches have demonstrated high probability of detection with low false alarm rates across various vehicle platforms (Manesh et al., 2019).

Deep learning techniques have gained particular attention for their ability to process complex temporal and spatial patterns in vehicle data. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are commonly used for location shift prediction and trajectory analysis, processing data from multiple in-vehicle sensors to detect discrepancies with GPS-reported positions (Dasgupta et al._1, 2021). Advanced deep learning frameworks combine multiple neural network architectures, with Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) being employed to analyze received signal strength values and theoretical radio map data for spoofing detection (Dang et al., 2023).

Ensemble learning and multi-algorithm approaches have also been developed to improve detection accuracy. Researchers have combined k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms for turn detection using steering angle sensor data (Dasgupta et al._1, 2021). Other studies have compared various machine learning models including Random Forest, SVM, Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, and XGBoost for GPS signal analysis and spoofing detection (Dang et al., 2022) (Gallardo et al., 2020).

One-class classification methods have emerged as particularly useful for spoofing detection since they can be trained using only benign data, making them practical for real-world deployment where spoofed data may be limited (Wang et al., 2022) (Whelan et al., 2020). These approaches include One-Class Support Vector Machines, Autoencoder Neural Networks, and Local Outlier Factor methods that can achieve detection accuracies exceeding 99% for both benign and malicious sensor readings (Whelan et al., 2020) (Agyapong et al., 2021).

Recent developments have focused on real-time detection capabilities using AI algorithms to correct sensor errors and improve detection accuracy. LSTM algorithms are used to correct accelerations and angular rates from inertial navigation systems, with the corrected values compared to GPS-estimated values using modified M-of-N detection methods (Aftatah et al., 2024). Deep Neural Networks have also been employed to process speedometer and gyroscope data for predicting vehicle displacement, enabling continuous comparison with GPS-provided displacement and velocity to detect various types of spoofing attacks including turn-by-turn, stop, and overshoot attacks (Mohammadi et al., 2025).

Advanced ML approaches treat GPS spoofing as an outlier detection problem, using statistical tests like the Grubbs outlier test to identify anomalous position estimates in time-series data (Burbank et al., 2024) (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022). Some methods employ entropy-based detection using Kullback-Leibler divergence measures to search for anomalies in GPS data streams (Burbank et al., 2024) (Basan et al., 2021).

snippets: Classical GPS spoofing detection methods focus on collecting and processing rich information in GPS signals, such as accurate clock information, signal power and arrival angle (Shen et al., 2020), (Ceccato et al., 2021), (Liu et al., 2021)

With various sensors increasingly prevalent in vehicles, detecting sensor (e.g., GPS) attacks via cross-comparing multiple data sources has attracted considerable attention in recent years (Huang et al., 2021)- (Wyk et al., 2020). One typical approach is to detect anomalies in received real-time measurements by comparing them with patterns in previously recorded data. This is often done by a supervised machine learning model or a statistical model corresponding to specific attacks from these records and applying the learned model to real-time anomaly detection (Luo et al., 2020)
some studies have developed methods based on one-class classification where anomaly detection models are trained using only benign data (Wang et al., 2021)

Another type of approaches to detect attacks is to integrate other real-time data sources (e.g., IMU data) with the vehicle's (mathematical) motion model (Min et al., 2019). An anomaly/attack is detected if data from the subject sensor deviate too much from the predicted output (e.g., vehicle's position) from the motion model (Liu et al., 2019)
We propose an infrastructure-enabled framework using roadside units as an independent, secured data source. A real-time detector, based on the Isolation Forest, is constructed to detect GPS spoofing.
citations.title: Infrastructure-Enabled GPS Spoofing Detection and Correction

snippets: Typically, existing countermeasures against spoofing attacks can be generally be categorized into two classes: cryptographic techniques and anomaly detection at the signal level. In general, satellite signals are authenticated using additional signals using cryptographic techniques to make the signal undecryptable for the users who do not have the security key (19). Signal level detection is performed by identifying discrepancies in the physical signal waveform or arrival angle from the source of the signal. Another detection approach is to verify the signal using multiple receivers of GNSS signals to detect any anomaly (20) (21). However, spoofers can spoof such receivers by generating synced signals for multiple satellites. GNSS signal frequency drift, signal strength, and the correlation between free-running crystal oscillator and GNSS signals can also be used to detect spoofing attacks (22). Humphreys et al. developed a software-defined civil GPS receiver-spoofer, which can generate an attack. They also developed two software-defined user-equipment based spoofing defense methods: (i) Data Bit Latency Defense and (ii) Vestigial Signal Defense (23)
Panice et al. developed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) based spoofing detection method by comparing the estimating the current state and actual location of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (24)

Wang et al. developed an approach to reconstruct a lost GPS where authors used real-time driving data and GPS coordinates. Their approach reconstructs the driving route using the driving data and flag an attack if the input GPS coordinates deviate more than an error threshold from the predicted GPS coordinates (25).
citations.title: Prediction-Based GNSS Spoofing Attack Detection for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) have received a huge interest in military and civil applications. Applications of UAS are dependent on successful communications of these systems with different entities in their networks. A UAS network can include the UAS, ground control station, navigation satellite system, and automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) receiver. Through these entities, a UAS is vulnerable to different cyber-attacks such as GPS spoofing. In this attack, a malicious user transmits fake signals to the GPS receiver on the UAS. The fake signals can mislead not only the aircraft but also air traffic controllers, leading to serious problems. These problems range from aircraft hijacking to collisions and human casualties. This paper proposes a supervised machine learning method based on the artificial neural network to detect GPS spoofing signals. Different features such as pseudo range, Doppler shift, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are used to perform the classification of GPS signals. We examine and compare the efficiency of one-and two-hidden-layer neural networks with various numbers of hidden neurons. The results show that our proposed method provides a high probability of detection and a low probability of false alarm.
citations.title: Detection of GPS Spoofing Attacks on Unmanned Aerial Systems

snippets: Manesh et al. (Manesh et al., 2019) exploited the received GPS signal characteristics, such as pseudo range, Doppler shift and signalto-noise ratio, to build a supervised neural network model for detecting GPS spoofing against unmanned aerial systems. Similarly, the spoofing detection approach in (Shafiee et al., 2017) used a neural network to analyze the differences between the spoofing and authentic signal patterns. The neural network takes as inputs the delta criterion, coefficient of early and late phase criterion, and total levels of signal. The authors in (Semanjski et al., 2019) proposed a GPS spoofing detection approach that leverages a supervised ML algorithm, specifically Support Vector Machine (SVM), to analyze the cross-correlation among the GPS signals of multiple GPS receivers. The work in (Gallardo et al., 2020) introduced RBF SVM, Ada Boost, Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forests methods for GPS signal's radio frequency interference analysis under the assumption that the attacker was not able to null the satellite signal

To overcome the weakness of GPS signal analyses based spoofing detection methods, the external positioning techniques, such as INS and MPS, are also used to not only provide location services for UAVs when the GPS is unavailable but also to cross-validate the authenticity of GPS information.
citations.title: Deep-Ensemble-Learning-Based GPS Spoofing Detection for Cellular-Connected UAVs

snippets: In order to detect GPS spoofing attacks, existing works either apply signal processing techniques (Friedt et al., 2021), (Milaat et al., 2018) that require additional hardware or follow data-driven approaches (Kwon et al., 2020)- (Kamal et al., 2021) that depend on the availability of GPS data

in (Friedt et al., 2021), real-time attack detection is implemented using Software-Defined Radios (SDR) by analyzing the phase difference of the GPS signals collected by different antennas. In (Milaat et al., 2018), the vehicles use dedicated shortrange communication to exchange the GPS pseudo-range measurements with other vehicles in the vicinity. Each vehicle uses these measurements to compute statistics that enable the local detection of possibly spoofed GPS signals on the high correlation of their arrival times
data-driven attack detection solutions process data that are readily available by COTS GPS receivers and try to learn the attack behavior

authors in (Kwon et al., 2020) compare the vehicle's accelerometer readings against the estimated acceleration measurements of the GPS device, with the mismatch beyond a certain threshold signifying a GPS spoofing attack. In (Shen et al., 2020), Multi-Sensor Fusion (MSF) algorithms are employed to estimate the vehicle's location by partially relying on the GPS readings. Leveraging measurements from neighboring vehicles, collaborative mechanisms are able to detect GPS location spoofing attacks within Vehicular Adhoc NETworks (VANET) by means of MSF (Kamal et al., 2022)

In our previous works [10] we employed in-vehicle multisensory data (e.g., accelerometer, gyroscope, steering angle, etc.) to estimate the GPS-free locations of the vehicle and compared them with the corresponding locations reported by the vehicle's GPS receiver
With the increasing volume of sensory data produced by vehicles, ML methods have also been applied for detecting location spoofing attacks

authors in (So et al., 2018) utilize k-Nearest Neighbor, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) for the detection and classification of location spoofing misbehavior based on features such as location and movement plausibility check. In (Manesh et al., 2019), an artificial Neural Network (NN) is used to detect GPS spoofing signals on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)

In (Arjoune et al., 2020), the authors compared various ML methods for detecting jamming attacks in wireless networks. Specifically, they investigated different signal features to recognize jamming signals and applied the Random Forest, SVM, and NN models
In (Shafiee et al., 2017), a method for detecting spoofing of the GPS signals is presented that employs a multilayer NN
some works have explored unsupervised ML methods and have approached the intended task through anomaly detection.
citations.title: A Machine Learning Approach for Detecting GPS Location Spoofing Attacks in Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: a sensor fusion based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework is presented that consists of three concurrent strategies for an autonomous vehicle (AV): (i) prediction of location shift, (ii) detection of turns (left or right), and (iii) recognition of motion state (including standstill state). Data from multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors (i.e., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, speed sensor, and GNSS) are fused and fed into a recurrent neural network model, which is a long short-term memory (LSTM) network for predicting the location shift

We have then combined k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms to detect turns using data from the steering angle sensor. In addition, data from an AV's speed sensor is used to recognize the AV's motion state including the standstill state
the use of low-cost invehicle sensors (e.g., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, and speed sensor) could provide effective strategies for detecting sophisticated spoofing attacks

we have developed a framework for detecting spoofing attacks on GNSS services by identifying and predicting AV states, which include location shift, turning direction, and motion state using data from low-cost in-vehicle sensors.
citations.title: Sensor Fusion-based GNSS Spoofing Attack Detection Framework for Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: 3D radio map and machine learning methods to detect and mitigate GPS spoofing attacks for cellular-connected UAVs. Precisely, the edge UAV flight controller uses ray tracing tools deterministic channel models, and Kriging methods to construct a theoretical 3D radio map. Then the machine learning methods, such as Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), are employed to detect GPS spoofing by analyzing the UAV/base station reported Received Signal Strength (RSS) values and the theoretical radio map RSS values
deep ensemble learning on edge servers to detect GPS spoofing with only a single base station
3D Angle of Arrival (AOA) of cellular signals can assist UAV self-localization and help UAV to detect and mitigate GPS spoofing attacks
artificial neural networks such as MLP, CNN, and RNN, are implemented on the edge server.
citations.title: 3D Radio Map-Based GPS Spoofing Detection and Mitigation for Cellular-Connected UAVs

snippets: Spoofing attacks pose a clear cybersecurity risk for all systems relying on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for time synchronization or positioning. Secure Code Estimation and Replay (SCER) spoofing attacks are the most challenging type of spoofing attacks, as these may be problematic even for future GNSS protection systems, like Navigation Message Authentication (NMA) or Spreading Code Authentication (SCA). This is one of the reasons that make the development of complementary protection techniques, like the one proposed in this work, necessary. In the first part of the paper, the spoofing SCER attacks are analyzed in detail for GPS and, particularly, for Galileo. The role of the Galileo Pseudorandom Noise (PRN) intra-satellite non-orthogonality distortion term in hindering the attacks is discussed and a detailed comparison between GPS and Galileo expected quality curves for the SCER attack is provided. A complementary detection method for end-user receivers (assuming NMA is used) against SCER attacks is proposed, based on the application of machine learning and a proposed set of features extracted from the receiver search space, assuming the attacker was not able to null the satellite signal.
citations.title: SCER Spoofing Attacks on the Galileo Open Service and Machine Learning Techniques for End-User Protection

snippets: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have proven to be a useful technology in numerous industries including industrial control systems surveillance, law enforcement, and military operations. Due to their heavy reliance on wireless protocols and hostile operating environments, UAVs face a large threat landscape. As attacks against UAVs increase, an intelligent intrusion detection system (IDS) is needed to aid the UAV in identifying attacks. The UAV domain presents unique challenges for intelligent IDS development, such as the variety of sensors, communication protocols, UAV platforms, control configurations, and dataset availability. In this paper, we propose a novelty-based approach to intrusion detection in UAVs by using one-class classifiers. One-class classifiers require only non-anomalous data to exist in the training set. This allows for the use of flight logs as training data, which are created by most UAVs during flight by default. Principal Component Analysis is applied to sensor logs for dimensionality reduction, and one-class classifier models are generated per sensor. A number of one-class classifiers are selected: One-Class Support Vector Machine, Autoencoder Neural Network, and Local Outlier Factor. The pre-processing, feature selection, training, and tuning of the selected algorithms is discussed. GPS spoofing is used throughout the paper as a common example of an external sensor-based attack. This approach shows to be effective across multiple UAV platforms with platform-specific F1 scores up to 99.56% and 99.73% for benign and malicious sensor readings respectively.
citations.title: Novelty-based Intrusion Detection of Sensor Attacks on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles

snippets: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) have gained major attention in recent years due to its numerous benefits. The navigation of UAVs is heavily reliant on sensors such as the Global Positioning System (GPS). However, sensor attacks that specifically target the GPS are a major concern. Equipment such as the software-defined radio can be used to launch GPS spoofing attacks. Existing techniques used to monitor the GPS and channel characteristics as a way to detect these attacks are insufficient due to the clear knowledge of the structure of GPS and channel characteristics which gives adversaries a blueprint to launch stealthy attacks. In this work, we developed various deep learning models that rely on UAV flight logs and telemetry data to detect GPS spoofing attacks in real time. We generate UAV data for different UAV models and use the data to train the models to detect the GPS spoofing attacks through classification. We developed two types of detectors: a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) binary classifier and an LSTM autoencoder-based one-class classifier (OCC). For each type, we compared two variations namely a UAV-specific detector that is customized for different UAV types and a UAV-generalized detector that can work with any model of UAV. We test and compare the efficiency of detection models in simulation. Hardware validation experiments were also performed using Intel® NCS2. For the binary classifier, we get a detection accuracy of 97.79% for the UAV-generalized detector and up to 99.56% for the UAV-model-specific detector. While for the OCC, we get 94.98% for the UAV-generalized detector and up to 99.24% for the UAV-model-specific detector.
citations.title: Efficient Detection of GPS Spoofing Attacks on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Using Deep Learning

snippets: This paper proposes a method for GPS spoofing detection that utilizes artificial intelligence algorithms in combination with raw data from an inertial navigation system (INS). Since INS sensors are prone to accumulating errors over time, these inaccuracies are corrected via a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithm. The corrected accelerations and angular rates are then compared to the accelerations and angular rates estimated from the GPS data to detect GPS spoofing signals. This comparison uses the modified M-of-N method, demonstrating its effectiveness by a detection rate reaching 80% of the spoofing zones.
citations.title: Detecting GPS Spoofing Attacks Using Corrected Low-Cost INS Data with an LSTM Network

snippets: The algorithm combines data from in-vehicle sensors, including the speedometer and gyroscope. This data is then fed into a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to predict the vehicle's displacement between timestamps. These predictions are continuously compared with GPS-provided displacement and velocity to detect the turn-by-turn, stop, and overshoot GPS spoofing attacks. Also, the same data is processed through an analytical model that uses the vehicle's dynamic movement equations to compute its position and velocity and to juxtapose them with GPS-provided position and velocity to detect the aforementioned spoofing attacks. A threshold is predetermined by using clean datasets to calculate the maximum possible deviation between in-vehicle sensor and GPS provided position/displacement and speed. Subsequently, spoofing attack detection uses this threshold for its continuous, real time comparison. Additionally, the proposed algorithm is able to detect a sequence of multiple biased attacks that fall below the mentioned threshold but can create a large deviation between the position/displacement and speed provided by GPS and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).
citations.title: Detection of Multiple Small Biased GPS Spoofing Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles

snippets: Several papers exist in the literature that analyze various aspects of signal statistics, of both the authentic signal and the spoofed signal, in detecting the presence of a spoofing threat. As an example, the authors of (Wei et al., 2024) considered the use of Doppler frequency and carrier-to-noise (C/N) density ratio as the primary metrics to discern a spoofed signal from an authentic signal. The authors then used numerous types of ML and analytical models to analyze performance utilizing these metrics, including SVM, KNN, RF, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), DT, and XGBoost

Many other existing approaches do not cleanly fit into a taxonomy. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022) proposed an approach to GPS spoofing detection that treats GPS spoofing detection as an outlier detection problem, analyzing the time-series history of the position estimates and identifying outlier values through the Grubbs outlier test. Any outlier is a spoofed position estimation in this approach. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2021) also treated GPS spoofing as an outlier problem. They implemented a navigation filter based on a constant velocity model. This model employed a 3D Kalman filter to identify and remove outlier values, which were presumed to be spoofed locations. The authors of (Basan et al., 2021) also viewed GPS spoofing detection (in part) as an outlier detection problem, employing a Kullback-Leibler divergence measure to search for anomalies in data. The authors coupled this anomaly detection approach with an entropy-based method for spoofing detection
Other proposed approaches utilize ADS-B broadcasts from aircraft and UASs to detect GPS spoofing attacks. Ground sensors monitor ADS-B broadcasts while geolocating the corresponding aircraft.
citations.title: Detecting and Mitigating Attacks on GPS Devices

snippets: Global positioning system (GPS) is favored to provide the position, velocity, and time (PVT) details across the globe. This paper proposes an epoch-by-epoch robust positioning algorithm followed by the Grubbs outlier test to address the GPS spoofing problem. We propose to accept both authentic and spoofed GPS signals to compute the robust positions. The robust positioning considers all possible combinations of measurements and generates several position estimates, which contain actual position, spoof position, and biased positions. In this case, the positions evolved due to spoof pseudorange measurements must be removed. Hence, we model eliminating spoof locations as an outlier problem and is addressed using Grubbs outlier test. The median of the processed data after the Grubbs test is the positional information at that epoch. Moreover, this problem is also extended to the Kalman filter’s (KF) framework to address the time-varying kinematics of the target. Simulations are carried out for various numbers of actual and spoofed pseudorange measurements. In order to illustrate the robustness of the proposed technique, position root mean square error (PRMSE) is taken as a metric.
citations.title: Robust Positioning and Grubbs Outlier Test for Navigation in GPS Spoofing Environment

snippets: Here, we developed a method for detecting cyber security attacks aimed at spoofing the Global Positioning System (GPS) signal of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). Most methods for detecting UAV anomalies indicative of an attack use machine learning or other such methods that compare normal behavior with abnormal behavior. Such approaches require large amounts of data and significant "training" time to prepare and implement the system. Instead, we consider a new approach based on other mathematical methods for detecting UAV anomalies without the need to first collect a large amount of data and describe normal behavior patterns. Doing so can simplify the process of creating an anomaly detection system, which can further facilitate easier implementation of intrusion detection systems in UAVs. This article presents issues related to ensuring the information security of UAVs. Development of the GPS spoofing detection method for UAVs is then described, based on a preliminary study that made it possible to form a mathematical apparatus for solving the problem. We then explain the necessary analysis of parameters and methods of data normalization, and the analysis of the Kullback—Leibler divergence measure needed to detect anomalies in UAV systems.
citations.title: GPS-Spoofing Attack Detection Technology for UAVs Based on Kullback–Leibler Divergence

sections.title: Collaborative and Infrastructure-Based Methods
sections.text:
Collaborative and infrastructure-based detection methods represent a significant advancement in GPS spoofing detection by leveraging the connectivity capabilities of modern transportation systems to provide independent verification of location data. These approaches recognize that sophisticated spoofing attacks may be difficult to detect using individual vehicle sensors alone, and instead rely on distributed detection across multiple vehicles and infrastructure components.

Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) collaborative approaches have emerged as particularly effective detection mechanisms. In these systems, vehicles exchange GPS code pseudo-range measurements with neighboring vehicles using dedicated short-range communications, then perform linear operations on the exchanged GPS data to derive independent statistics related to each neighbor's measurements (Milaat et al., 2018). Vehicles implement cumulative sum procedures to locally detect high correlations in the time of arrival of spoofed GPS signals, with local detection values reported to an elected head vehicle that employs min-max change-detection procedures to optimize global spoofing detection (Milaat et al., 2018). Recent developments have extended this approach using density clustering algorithms and cooperative localization with multi-information fusion from neighboring vehicles to defend against GPS attacks (Wang et al., 2025).

Infrastructure-enabled frameworks represent another major category of collaborative detection methods. These systems utilize roadside units (RSUs) as independent, secured data sources, with real-time detectors based on algorithms like Isolation Forest constructed to detect GPS spoofing (Wang et al., 2022). Advanced infrastructure approaches employ coupled generalized dynamic Bayesian networks to learn interactions between RF signals received by RSUs from multiple vehicles and their corresponding trajectories, integrating vehicles' positional information with vehicle-to-infrastructure communications for semantic learning (Krayani et al., 2023).

The CARAMEL project has developed comprehensive collaborative detection architectures that utilize both in-vehicle sensor measurements and collaborative approaches enabled by infrastructure support (Vitale et al., 2020) (Vitale et al., 2021). These systems create parallel streams of vehicle locations that rely on GPS-free signals, comparing secondary location streams with GPS locations and raising alarms when differences exceed predefined thresholds (Vitale et al., 2021). The collaborative method involves vehicles sharing measurements with Intelligent Transportation System applications in Multi-access Edge Computing platforms, which then employ robust localization algorithms to identify inconsistencies (Tariq, 2024).

Cellular network-assisted detection has also gained attention, particularly for connected vehicles and UAVs. These methods use cellular towers and cellular network infrastructure to aid the detection process, with some approaches achieving detection rates above 95% by leveraging uplink received signal strength measurements to cross-check position validity (Mykytyn et al., 2023) (Dang et al., 2020). Deep ensemble learning methods deployed on edge cloud servers analyze path loss statistical features between base stations and vehicles to detect trajectory deviations caused by GPS spoofing, achieving above 97% accuracy with two base stations and at least 83% accuracy with only one base station (Dang et al., 2022).

Learning from demonstration approaches have been developed for implementation in both vehicles and transportation infrastructure, using computational-efficient driving models learned from historical vehicle trajectories to predict normal driving behaviors and employing statistical methods to measure dissimilarities between observed and predicted trajectories for anomaly detection (Yang et al., 2023). These collaborative methods offer significant advantages over individual vehicle-based detection by providing redundancy, reducing false positives through consensus mechanisms, and enabling detection of coordinated spoofing attacks that might fool individual vehicle sensors.

snippets: This letter proposes a decentralized scheme for the detection of global positioning system (GPS) spoofing in vehicular ad hoc networks. In this scheme, vehicles exchange their measured GPS code pseudo-ranges with neighboring vehicles using dedicated short-range communications. The vehicles then perform linear operations on the exchanged GPS data and derive independent statistics that are related to the measurements of each neighbor. Using these statistics, a vehicle implements a cumulative sum procedure to locally detect high correlations in the time of arrival of spoofed GPS signals. The vehicles report their local detection values to an elected head vehicle, which employs a min–max change-detection procedure to optimize the global-spoofing detection. Our experimental results show that: 1) the average detection delay decreases as the number of vehicles increase and 2) the proposed scheme converges to optimal as the probability of false-alarm reduces to zero.
citations.title: Decentralized Detection of GPS Spoofing in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks

snippets: Classical GPS spoofing detection methods focus on collecting and processing rich information in GPS signals, such as accurate clock information, signal power and arrival angle (Shen et al., 2020), (Ceccato et al., 2021), (Liu et al., 2021)

With various sensors increasingly prevalent in vehicles, detecting sensor (e.g., GPS) attacks via cross-comparing multiple data sources has attracted considerable attention in recent years (Huang et al., 2021)- (Wyk et al., 2020). One typical approach is to detect anomalies in received real-time measurements by comparing them with patterns in previously recorded data. This is often done by a supervised machine learning model or a statistical model corresponding to specific attacks from these records and applying the learned model to real-time anomaly detection (Luo et al., 2020)
some studies have developed methods based on one-class classification where anomaly detection models are trained using only benign data (Wang et al., 2021)

Another type of approaches to detect attacks is to integrate other real-time data sources (e.g., IMU data) with the vehicle's (mathematical) motion model (Min et al., 2019). An anomaly/attack is detected if data from the subject sensor deviate too much from the predicted output (e.g., vehicle's position) from the motion model (Liu et al., 2019)
We propose an infrastructure-enabled framework using roadside units as an independent, secured data source. A real-time detector, based on the Isolation Forest, is constructed to detect GPS spoofing.
