snippets: The envisioned key role of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in assisting the upcoming mobile networks calls for addressing the challenge of their secure and safe integration in the airspace. The GPS spoofing is a prominent security threat of UAVs. In this paper, we propose a 5G-assisted UAV position monitoring and anti-GPS spoofing system that allows live detection of GPS spoofing by leveraging Uplink received signal strength (RSS) measurements to cross-check the position validity. We introduce the Adaptive Trustable Residence Area (ATRA); a novel strategy to determine the trust area within which the UAV's GPS position should be located in order to be considered as non-spoofed. The performance evaluation shows that the proposed solution can successfully detect spoofed GPS positions with a rate of above 95%.

sections.title: Vision-Based and Multi-Modal Approaches
sections.text:
Vision-based detection methods represent an innovative approach to GPS spoofing detection by leveraging onboard cameras and visual processing capabilities that are increasingly common in connected and autonomous vehicles. These approaches work on the principle that while GPS signals can be spoofed, the visual environment captured by cameras remains unaffected by fake GPS transmissions, providing an independent reference for location verification.

Visual Odometry (VO) techniques form the foundation of many vision-based detection systems. These methods extract relative trajectory information from sequential camera images and compare this visual trajectory with the absolute trajectory derived from GPS coordinates (Varshosaz et al., 2019). The comparison employs multiple dissimilarity measures including Sum of Euclidean Distances between Corresponding Points (SEDCP), angle distance, and taxicab distance between Histogram of Oriented Displacements of sub-trajectories (Varshosaz et al., 2019) (Eshmawi et al., 2024). Research has shown that SEDCP is particularly effective for detecting spoofing attacks even when there is no redirection and only vehicle velocity is changed (Varshosaz et al., 2019).

Real-time video stream analysis represents another significant vision-based approach. These systems collect frames from onboard cameras along with their GPS coordinates, then calculate correlations between vehicle movements derived from GPS data and those observed in real-time video streams (Mykytyn et al., 2023) (Davidovich et al., 2022). Advanced implementations can detect GPS spoofing attacks where spoofed locations differ from real locations by as little as 1-4 meters, with an average detection capability of 2.5 meters for vehicles operating in urban environments (Davidovich et al., 2022).

Multi-modal fusion approaches combine vision sensors with other onboard systems to create robust detection frameworks. These methods integrate monocular cameras with IMU sensors to detect GPS spoofing through sensor fusion techniques (Khoei et al., 2022) (Eshmawi et al., 2024). Advanced multi-source fusion systems use Unscented Kalman filters to integrate camera data with high-precision maps, creating comprehensive anomaly detection and mitigation methods that ensure accurate vehicle localization even during GPS attacks (Chen et al., 2023).

The effectiveness of vision-based methods has been demonstrated across various attack scenarios, including sophisticated receiver-based GPS spoofing, long-range flight spoofing with direction changes larger than 3 degrees, and incremental spoofing with redirection rates of 1 degree (Varshosaz et al., 2019). These approaches offer the significant advantage of being independent of complementary sensors and requiring no prior knowledge or archived map datasets, making them suitable for real-time implementation in diverse operating environments (Varshosaz et al., 2019).

snippets: Spoofing of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) is generally carried out through spoofing of the UAV’s Global Positioning System (GPS) receiver. This paper presents a vision-based UAV spoofing detection method that utilizes Visual Odometry (VO). This method is independent of the other complementary sensors and any knowledge or archived map and datasets. The proposed method is based on the comparison of relative sub-trajectory of the UAV from VO, with its absolute replica from GPS within a moving window along the flight path. The comparison is done using three dissimilarity measures including (1) Sum of Euclidian Distances between Corresponding Points (SEDCP), (2) angle distance and (3) taxicab distance between the Histogram of Oriented Displacements (HOD) of these sub-trajectories. This method can determine the time and location of UAV spoofing and bounds the drift error of VO. It can be used without any restriction in the usage environment and can be implemented in real-time applications. This method is evaluated on four UAV spoofing scenarios. The results indicate that this method is effective in the detection of UAV spoofing due to the Sophisticated Receiver-Based (SRB) GPS spoofing. This method can detect UAV spoofing in the long-range UAV flights when the changes in UAV flight direction is larger than 3° and in the incremental UAV spoofing with the redirection rate of 1°. Additionally, using SEDCP, the spoofing of the UAV, when there is no redirection and only the velocity of the UAV is changed, can be detected. The results show that SEDCP is more effective in the detection of UAV spoofing and fake GPS positions.
citations.title: Spoofing Detection of Civilian UAVs Using Visual Odometry

snippets: A Global Positioning System (GPS) spoofing attack can be launched against any commercial GPS sensor in order to interfere with its navigation capabilities. These sensors are installed in a variety of devices and vehicles (e.g., cars, planes, cell phones, ships, UAVs, and more). In this study, we focus on micro UAVs (drones) for several reasons: (1) they are small and inexpensive, (2) they rely on a built-in camera, (3) they use GPS sensors, and (4) it is difficult to add external components to micro UAVs. We propose an innovative method, based on the video stream captured by a drone’s camera, for the real-time detection of GPS spoofing attacks targeting drones. The proposed method collects frames from the video stream and their location (GPS coordinates); by calculating the correlation between each frame, our method can detect GPS spoofing attacks on drones. We first analyze the performance of the suggested method in a controlled environment by conducting experiments on a flight simulator that we developed. Then, we analyze its performance in the real world using a DJI drone. Our method can provide different levels of security against GPS spoofing attacks, depending on the detection interval required; for example, it can provide a high level of security to a drone flying at altitudes of 50–100 m over an urban area at an average speed of 4 km/h in conditions of low ambient light; in this scenario, the proposed method can provide a level of security that detects any GPS spoofing attack in which the spoofed location is a distance of 1–4 m (an average of 2.5 m) from the real location.
citations.title: Towards the Detection of GPS Spoofing Attacks against Drones by Analyzing Camera’s Video Stream

question: Compare algorithms for finding a minimum weight spanning tree in a weighted graph.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
The minimum spanning tree problem is a fundamental challenge in graph theory that involves finding a subtree spanning all nodes in a weighted graph while minimizing the total weight of the selected edges (Nabi et al., 2017) (Naukowe et al., 2018). In a weighted graph, each edge has an associated real number representing its weight or cost, and the goal is to find a spanning tree whose total edge weight is no greater than any other possible spanning tree (Naukowe et al., 2018). This problem, also known as finding the minimum connector or economy tree, has significant importance across many practical applications (Nabi et al., 2017).

Two well-established algorithms dominate the solution space for this problem: Kruskal's algorithm and Prim's algorithm (Nabi et al., 2017) (Naukowe et al., 2018) (Honma et al., 2009). Kruskal's approach works by sorting all edges by weight and then adding edges to the spanning tree in order of increasing weight, provided they don't create a cycle (Nabi et al., 2017). Both classical algorithms are sequential in nature and typically require O(n²) time complexity (Honma et al., 2009). Beyond these traditional approaches, parallel algorithms like Sollin's algorithm have been developed to address the problem using multiple processors (Honma et al., 2009).

sections.title: Main Algorithms
sections.text:
The most widely used algorithms for finding minimum spanning trees are **Kruskal's algorithm** and **Prim's algorithm**, both of which employ greedy strategies to achieve optimal solutions (Biswas et al., 2012) (Munier et al., 2017). These algorithms differ fundamentally in their approach to constructing the MST (Sorensen et al., 2005).

**Kruskal's algorithm** operates by first sorting all edges in the graph from minimum to maximum weight, then iteratively adding edges to the spanning tree in order of increasing weight, provided they do not create a cycle with previously selected edges (Levi et al., 2015). This approach starts with a forest consisting of all vertices and no edges, then incrementally adds minimal edges unless a cycle would result (Fichera, 2007). The algorithm essentially grows a forest of trees until this forest reduces to a single tree representing the MST (Sorensen et al., 2005).

**Prim's algorithm** takes a different approach by starting with an arbitrary vertex and progressively growing a single tree until it spans all vertices (Babaee et al., 2013) (McDonald, 2021). At each iteration, the algorithm chooses a minimum-weight edge connecting a vertex already in the tree to a vertex outside the tree, then adds that new vertex to the growing tree (Goldberger et al., 2010). This process continues until all vertices are included, with the algorithm maintaining the property that edges always form a single connected tree throughout execution (Planeta, 2006).

**Borůvka's algorithm** represents a third classical approach that works by examining each vertex simultaneously and adding the edge with the smallest weight from each vertex to the spanning tree, then merging these selections until they form a complete spanning tree (Marpaung et al., 2020). This algorithm, originally developed in 1926, was historically the first algorithm designed for finding minimum spanning trees (Jahan et al., 2020). All three algorithms - Borůvka's, Prim's, and Kruskal's - can solve the MST problem with a time complexity of O(e(G) log v(G)) (Shi et al., 2022) (Kapanowski et al., 2015).

snippets:
There are several greedy algorithms for finding a minimal spanning tree M of a graph. The algorithms of Kruskal and Prim are well known.

Kruskal's algorithm. Repeat the following step until the set M has n-1 edges (initially M is empty). Add to M the shortest edge that does not form a circuit with edges already in M.

Prim's algorithm. Repeat the following step until the set M has n-1 edges (initially M is empty): Add to M the shortest edge between a vertex in M and a vertex not in M (initially pick any edge of shortest length).

Although both are greedy algorithms, they are different in the sense that Prim's algorithm grows a tree until it becomes the MST, whereas Kruskal's algorithm grows a forest of trees until this forest reduces to a single tree, the MST.

sections.title: Time Complexity Analysis
sections.text:
The time complexity of minimum spanning tree algorithms depends heavily on their implementation details and the characteristics of the input graph. **Prim's algorithm** demonstrates varying performance based on the underlying data structures used. With a basic implementation, Prim's algorithm achieves O(n²) complexity where n represents the number of vertices (Goldberger et al., 2010) (Paryati et al., 2022). More sophisticated implementations can achieve better performance: using a d-heap results in O(m log₂₊ₘ/ₙ n) time complexity, which becomes O(m) for dense graphs and O(m log n) for very sparse graphs (Turner, 2016). The most efficient implementation uses Fibonacci heaps, achieving O(m + n log n) worst-case running time, which is particularly beneficial for sparse graphs (Turner, 2016). Some sources report Prim's algorithm running time as O((V + E) · log V) (Dimitriadis et al., 2017).

**Kruskal's algorithm** exhibits O(m log n) time complexity, with performance primarily determined by the initial edge sorting step (Turner, 2016). The algorithm's complexity is characterized as polynomial O(|E| ln |E|) in the number of edges (Fichera, 2007). **Borůvka's algorithm** achieves the same O(e(G) log v(G)) time complexity as the other classical approaches (Shi et al., 2022).

The choice between algorithms often depends on graph density characteristics. Kruskal's algorithm, with its edge-focused complexity, performs better on sparse graphs, while Prim's algorithm, with its vertex-oriented complexity, excels on dense graphs (Yu, 2023) (Zhang, 2023). For parallel processing scenarios, specialized algorithms like Sollin's algorithm can achieve O(log² n) time using O(n²/log² n) processors on CREW PRAM architectures, though parallel implementations of Prim's algorithm tend to be significantly slower due to its inherently sequential vertex addition process (Honma et al., 2009) (Javadi et al., 2017).

Grafalgo contains several algorithms that solve the minimum spanning tree problem (mst). All have two arguments, a weighted graph (Graph w) and a list in which the result is returned. Specifically, on return, the list contains the edge numbers of the edges in the minimum spanning tree.

Prim's algorithm (mst p) sovles the minimum spanning tree problem in O(m log 2+ m/n n) time. For dense graphs, this is O(m), which is optimal. For very sparse graphs (m = Θ(n)), the running time is O(m log n), which falls a little short of optimal. Prim's algorithm uses a d-heap to guide the selection of edges to be included in the tree

A second version of Prim's algorithm (mst pf) that uses a Fibonacci heap in place of the d-heap is also provided. This leads to a worst-case running time of O(m+n log n) which is better for sparse graphs. However, in practice, the relative simplicity of the d-heap data structure makes the first version faster under most conditions.

Kruskal's algorithm (mst k) finds a minimum spanning tree in O(m log n) time. Its running time is determined by an initial step which sorts the edges by weight.

There are two basics strategies for the search of the MST, one consists on the progressive increase of a minimum tree until it is spanning, the other one consists on the progressive coalescence of the trees in a spanning forest (collection of trees) until a single tree is obtained.

In the first one (Prim's algorithm) one starts with a given vertex i ∈ V ′ and progressively increases this set with the minimal edge in B V ′ until every vertex is in V ′ . sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.text:
The selection of an appropriate MST algorithm depends heavily on the characteristics of the input graph, particularly its density. **Kruskal's algorithm** is most suitable for sparse graphs because its complexity is related to the number of edges (Yu, 2023) (Zhang, 2023). Since sparse graphs have relatively few edges, Kruskal's O(m log n) complexity becomes advantageous in these scenarios (Turner, 2016).

**Prim's algorithm** demonstrates superior performance on dense graphs where its vertex-oriented complexity provides benefits (Yu, 2023) (Zhang, 2023). For dense graphs, Prim's algorithm can achieve O(m) optimal time complexity when implemented with appropriate data structures (Turner, 2016). **Borůvka's algorithm** also performs well on dense graphs, making it suitable for the same scenarios as Prim's algorithm (Zhang, 2023).

Implementation choices significantly affect practical performance. While Prim's algorithm using Fibonacci heaps achieves better theoretical complexity for sparse graphs with O(m + n log n) worst-case running time, the simpler d-heap implementation often proves faster in practice due to its reduced overhead (Turner, 2016). For parallel processing applications, Prim's algorithm becomes much less attractive because vertices must be added sequentially, making parallel implementations significantly slower compared to other parallel MST algorithms (Javadi et al., 2017).

Special considerations arise in memory-constrained environments or applications requiring multiple MST computations. Some algorithms are optimal in terms of write operations, requiring only O(n) writes, which becomes valuable when computing multiple MSTs on the same graph structure with varying edge weights, such as in road map applications or time-varying network scenarios (Blelloch et al., 2015).

sections.title: Variants and Advanced Algorithms
sections.text:
### Dynamic MST Algorithms
For graphs where edges are frequently added or removed, **dynamic MST algorithms** maintain the minimum spanning tree efficiently without recomputing from scratch. Early work by Frederickson uses partitions and topology trees with update times ranging from O(n^(2/3)) to O(n^(1/2)) (Hanauer et al., 2021). More advanced approaches achieve polylogarithmic time per operation, with the algorithm by Holm et al. providing O(log^4 n/log log n) expected amortized time per operation (Hanauer et al., 2021) (Holm et al., 2014). Interestingly, experimental studies show that simple adaptations of static algorithms often outperform theoretically superior dynamic algorithms on random inputs (Hanauer et al., 2021).

### Distributed and Parallel Algorithms
Several algorithms are specifically designed for distributed computing environments. The **GHS (Gallager, Humblet, Spira) algorithm** and **Awerbuch's algorithm** are purpose-built for distributed systems (Mazeev et al., 2016). Many classical algorithms have been adapted for both shared memory and distributed memory parallelization (Mazeev et al., 2016). **Sollin's parallel algorithm** runs in O(log^2 n) time using O(n^2/log^2 n) processors on CREW PRAM architectures (Honma et al., 2009).

### Approximation and Sublinear Algorithms
For very large datasets, **approximation algorithms** provide near-optimal solutions with reduced computational cost. The **LipMST algorithm** achieves a (1+ε)-approximation by sampling edge weights uniformly within a range, maintaining Lipschitz continuity (Kumabe et al., 2022). **Sublinear algorithms** estimate MST weights without examining the entire graph, with some achieving (1+ε)-approximation in time Õ(n•poly(1/ε)) or Õ(deg•W•1/ε^2) depending on graph characteristics (Gouleakis et al., 2016).

### Memory-Efficient Variants
**Write-efficient algorithms** are designed for emerging memory technologies where write operations are significantly more expensive than reads. Variants of Borůvka's algorithm can be implemented with O(n) writes across all rounds, while adapted versions of Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms also minimize write operations (Blelloch et al., 2015) (Blelloch et al._1, 2015). These algorithms prove particularly valuable for applications computing multiple MSTs on the same graph structure with time-varying edge weights (Blelloch et al., 2015).

### Algorithmic Relationships
The **Jarník-Dijkstra-Prim (JDP) algorithm** represents a unified view showing the structural similarity between Prim's algorithm and Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, enabling similar parallelization techniques (Badyn et al., 2020) (Tadonki, 2020). This relationship highlights how MST algorithms can benefit from optimizations developed for related graph problems.

snippets: The lower bound of Ω(log ) (Patrascu et al., 2005) on the time per operation for connectivity trivially extends to maintaining the weight of a minimum spanning tree. Holm et al. (Holm et al., 2001) gave the first fully dynamic algorithm with polylogarithmic time per operation for this problem. It was later slightly improved to O (log 4 /log log ) time per operation (Holm et al., 2014)

Amato et al. (Amato et al., 1997) presented the first experimental study of dynamic minimum spanning tree algorithms. In particular, the authors implemented different versions of Frederickson's algorithm (Frederickson, 1985) which uses partitions and topology trees. The algorithms have been adapted with sparsification techniques to improve their performance. The update running times of these algorithms range from O ( 2/3 ) to O ( 1/2 ). The authors further presented a variant of Frederickson's algorithm that is significantly faster than all other implementations of this algorithm. However, the authors also proposed a simple adaption of a partially dynamic data structure of Kruskal's algorithm that was the fastest implementation on random inputs. Later, Cattaneo et al. (Cattaneo et al., 2002)(Cattaneo et al., 2002) presented an experimental study on several algorithms for the problem. The authors presented an efficient implementation of the algorithm of Holm et al. (Holm et al., 2001), proposed new simple algorithms for dynamic MST that are not as asymptotically efficient as the algorithm by Holm et al. but seem to be fast in practice, and lastly compared their algorithms with the results of Amato et al. The algorithm by Holm et al. uses a clever refinement of a technique by Henzinger and King (Henzinger et al., 1997) for developing fully dynamic algorithms starting from the deletions-only case. One outcome of their experiments is that simple algorithms outperform the theoretically more refined algorithms on random and worst-case networks.

snippets: Emerging memory technologies have a significant gap between the cost, both in time and in energy, of writing to memory versus reading from memory. In this paper we present models and algorithms that account for this difference, with a focus on write-efficient sorting algorithms. First, we consider the PRAM model with asymmetric write cost, and show that sorting can be performed in O(n) writes, O(n log n) reads, and logarithmic depth (parallel time). Next, we consider a variant of the External Memory (EM) model that charges k > 1 for writing a block of size B to the secondary memory, and present variants of three EM sorting algorithms (multi-way merge sort, sample sort, and heap sort using buffer trees) that asymptotically reduce the number of writes over the original algorithms, and perform roughly k block reads for every block write. Finally, we define a variant of the Ideal-Cache model with asymmetric write costs, and present write-efficient,cache-oblivious parallel algorithms for sorting, FFTs, and matrix multiplication. Adapting prior bounds for work-stealing and parallel-depth-first schedulers to the asymmetric setting, these yield provably good bounds for parallel machines with private caches or with a shared cache, respectively.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: The maximum matching problem in bipartite graphs asks us to find the largest set of edges where no two edges share a vertex. This problem appears often in practice - from matching workers to jobs, to pairing kidney donors with recipients, to optimizing network flows <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. A bipartite graph has two distinct sets of vertices where edges only connect vertices from different sets, making it easier to work with than general graphs <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The algorithms for solving this problem range from classical approaches that use augmenting paths to modern methods that leverage matrix operations and randomization <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Each algorithm offers different benefits in terms of time complexity, ease of implementation, and performance on specific types of inputs, making the choice of algorithm dependent on the particular application and constraints <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Classical Deterministic Algorithms
sections.text:
The earliest polynomial-time approaches include the Ford-Fulkerson method and the Hungarian algorithm, which provided the first systematic solutions to bipartite matching (Li et al., 2022) (Wu et al., 2022). The Hungarian algorithm, developed by Kuhn and later refined by Munkres, runs in O(n³) time and can handle weighted matching problems by transforming unequal bipartite sets into perfect matching problems by adding zero-weight edges (Das, 2020) (Tu et al., 2023).

The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm represents a major breakthrough in bipartite matching, achieving O(√nm) or O(n^2.5) time complexity and remaining the most efficient known algorithm for many years (Das, 2020) (Mansour et al., 2013) (Xie, 2018) (Turner, 2016) (Das et al., 2016). The algorithm works by finding augmenting paths through breadth-first search followed by depth-first search, processing multiple augmenting paths in each phase (Xie, 2018).

For dense graphs, the Alt-Blum-Mehlhorn-Paul algorithm offers a slight improvement over Hopcroft-Karp, running faster by a factor of (log n)^1/2 (Das et al., 2016) (Tassa, 2011). More recent theoretical advances have pushed beyond these classical bounds, with Madry's O(m^10/7) algorithm in 2013 and Liu and Sidford's O(m^4/3) algorithm, culminating in the near-linear O(m^1+o(1)) time algorithm by Chen et al. in 2022 (Farago, 2023) (Madry, 2013) (Chen et al., 2022).

snippets: We present an Õ(m10/7) = Õ(m1.43)-time1 algorithm for the maximum s-t flow and the minimum s-t cut problems in directed graphs with unit capacities. snippets: We give an algorithm that computes exact maximum flows and minimum-cost flows on directed graphs with m edges and polynomially bounded integral demands, costs, and capacities in $m^{1+o(1)}$ time. sections.title: Modern Algorithmic Advances
sections.text:
The first major departure from classical augmenting path methods came through randomized algorithms that leverage matrix multiplication. The randomized O(n^ω) algorithm, where ω ≈ 2.373 is the matrix multiplication exponent, offers significant improvements over Hopcroft-Karp for dense graphs (Nisan, 2019) (Booth et al., 2021) . This approach represents a fundamental shift from combinatorial to algebraic methods.

A breakthrough came in 2013 when Madry's work broke the decades-old O(m√n) barrier that had stood since Hopcroft-Karp (Annamalai, 2015) (Madry, 2013). Madry's O(m^10/7) algorithm uses interior-point methods and establishes a deeper understanding of convex optimization in flow problems, providing the first improvement for sparse graphs (Farago, 2023) (Madry, 2013).

The most recent and notable advance is the Õ(m + n^1.5) algorithm by Brand et al., which provides near-linear time complexity for moderately dense graphs and represents the first significant improvement over Hopcroft-Karp in many practical cases (Booth et al., 2021) (Brand et al., 2020). This work combines interior-point methods with dynamic graph algorithms and fast linear system solvers.

The field has culminated in Chen et al.'s m^1+o(1) near-linear time algorithm in 2022, which solves not just bipartite matching but general minimum-cost flows (Farago, 2023) (Chen et al., 2022). Meanwhile, purely combinatorial approaches continue to advance, with new algorithms like the Õ(m^1/3 n^5/3) algorithm that outperforms both Hopcroft-Karp and matrix multiplication methods on moderately dense graphs (Chuzhoy et al., 2023).

snippets: The fastest known deterministic algorithm for the problem (Hopcroft et al., 1971) is close to half a century old and runs in time O(n 5/2 ). It is a long standing open problem whether this running time may be improved, but a faster randomized algorithm whose running time is n ω (where ω = 2.3

is the matrix multiplication exponent) was given in (Mucha et al., 2004). Another long standing open problem is whether there exists a deterministic NC algorithm (a parallel algorithm running in poly-logarithmic time using a polynomial number of processors) for finding a maximum matching. Randomized such algorithms were given in (Karp et al., 1985)(Mulmuley et al., 1987)

There exists an algorithm for maximum matching in a bipartite graph that uses O(n 3/2 ) demand queries. This is obtained by first running the ascending auction algorithm with = 1/ √ n. This requires O(n 3/2 ) demand queries and produces a matching whose size is at least (1 − 1/ √ n) times the maximum size. We then run a sequence of augmenting path steps, each of which requires O(n) additional demand queries.
citations.title: The Demand Query Model for Bipartite Matching

snippets:
Long-standing previously state-of-the-art classical algorithms for finding maximum matchings run in O(m √ n) time; the algorithm of Hopcroft and Karp (HK) is for bipartite graphs (Hopcroft et al., 1971), while the algorithm of Micali and Vazirani (MV) applies to general graphs (Micali et al., 1980)[58]. Given any initial matching, these algorithms operate in phases, where each phase of the algorithm looks to find a matching of greater size. The runtime of each phase is O(m), and O( |M |) = O( √ n) phases are required (Hopcroft et al., 1971), where |M | is the size of the maximum matching. In terms of the variable-value graph properties, since |M | is bounded by |X|, these algorithms take O(|E| |X|) time.

Following the algorithms of HK and MV, a randomized O(n ω )-time algorithm (Mucha et al., 2004)(Ibarra et al., 1981) was proposed for bipartite graphs, where ω corresponds to the classical asymptotic cost of matrix multiplication; the best upper bound known on ω is approximately 2.373 (Alman et al., 2020). In terms of the variable-value graph properties, this algorithm takes O(|X| ω−1 |V |) time (Ibarra et al., 1981). Alt et al. then proposed an O(n 3/2 m/log n) algorithm (Alt et al., 1991). Each of these algorithms offer modest improvements over HK for dense graphs.

Finally, very recent work using interior-point methods and dynamic graph algorithms have led to anÕ(m + n 3/2 )-time classical algorithm (Brand et al., 2020) for finding maximum matchings in bipartite graphs, offering the first significant improvement over HK. The algorithm leverages fast linear system solvers to provide near-linear asymptotic complexity for moderately dense graphs. In terms of the variable-value graph properties, with n = O(|V |), their algorithm runs inÕ(|E| + |V | 3/2 ) time.

snippets: We present an $\tilde{O}(m+n^{1.5})$-time randomized algorithm for maximum cardinality bipartite matching and related problems (e.g. transshipment, negative-weight shortest paths, and optimal transport) on m-edge, n-node graphs. For maximum cardinality bipartite matching on moderately dense graphs, i.e. $m=\Omega(n^{1.5})$, our algorithm runs in time nearly linear in the input size and constitutes the first improvement over the classic $O(m\sqrt{n})$-time [Dinic 1970; Hopcroft-Karp 1971; Karzanov 1973] and $\widetilde{O}(n^{\omega})$-time algorithms [Ibarra-Moran 1981] (where currently $\omega\approx 2.373$). On sparser graphs, i.e. when $m=n^{9/8+\delta}$ for any constant $\delta > 0$, our result improves upon the recent advances of [Madry 2013] and [Liu-Sidford 2020b, 2020a] which achieve an $\widetilde{O}(m^{4/3+o(1)})$ runtime. We obtain these results by combining and advancing recent lines of research in interior point methods (IPMs) and dynamic graph algorithms. First, we simplify and improve the IPM of [v.d.Brand-Lee-Sidford-Song 2020], providing a general primal-dual IPM framework and new sampling-based techniques for handling infeasibility induced by approximate linear system solvers. Second, we provide a simple sublinear-time algorithm for detecting and sampling high-energy edges in electric flows on expanders and show that when combined with recent advances in dynamic expander decompositions, this yields efficient data structures for maintaining the iterates of both [v.d.Brand et al.] and our new IPMs. Combining this general machinery yields a simpler $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{m})$ time algorithm for matching based on the logarithmic barrier function, and our state-of-the-art $\widetilde{O}(m+n^{1.5})$ time algorithm for matching based on the [Lee-Sidford 2014] barrier (as regularized in [v.d.Brand et al.]).
citations.title: Bipartite Matching in Nearly-linear Time on Moderately Dense Graphs

Our algorithm builds the flow through a sequence of $m^{1+o(1)}$ approximate undirected minimum-ratio cycles, each of which is computed and processed in amortized $m^{o(1)}$ time using a new dynamic graph data structure. Our framework extends to algorithms running in $m^{1+o(1)}$ time for computing flows that minimize general edge-separable convex functions to high accuracy. This gives almost-linear time algorithms for several problems including entropy-regularized optimal transport, matrix scaling, p-norm flows, and p-norm isotonic regression on arbitrary directed acyclic graphs.

snippets: The maximum bipartite matching problem is among the most fundamental and well-studied problems in combinatorial optimization. A beautiful and celebrated combinatorial algorithm of Hopcroft and Karp (1973) shows that maximum bipartite matching can be solved in $O(m \sqrt{n})$ time on a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. For the case of very dense graphs, a fast matrix multiplication based approach gives a running time of $O(n^{2.371})$. These results represented the fastest known algorithms for the problem until 2013, when Madry introduced a new approach based on continuous techniques achieving much faster runtime in sparse graphs. This line of research has culminated in a spectacular recent breakthrough due to Chen et al. (2022) that gives an $m^{1+o(1)}$ time algorithm for maximum bipartite matching (and more generally, for min cost flows)

Our work makes progress on this question by presenting a new, purely combinatorial algorithm for bipartite matching, that runs in $\tilde{O}(m^{1/3}n^{5/3})$ time, and hence outperforms both Hopcroft-Karp and the fast matrix multiplication based algorithms on moderately dense graphs.
citations.title: A Faster Combinatorial Algorithm for Maximum Bipartite Matching

sections.title: Specialized Algorithm Categories
sections.text:
Several distinct algorithmic approaches have emerged to address specific computational constraints and graph structures. **Parallel and distributed algorithms** form one major category, with randomized NC algorithms using algebraic methods like the Isolation Lemma for certain graph classes (Anari et al., 2019). Recent work has developed efficient parallel algorithms for specific graph families, including deterministic logspace algorithms for K₃,₃-free and K₅-free bipartite graphs (Datta et al., 2021) (Arora et al., 2014), and NC algorithms for perfect matching in minor-closed graph families (Eppstein et al., 2018). For distributed settings, recent algorithms achieve sublinear round complexity, with randomized algorithms for exact bipartite matching running in Õ(τ⁴D + τ⁷) rounds (Izumi et al., 2022).

**Three main algorithmic paradigms** dominate practical implementations: augmenting path algorithms (including Hopcroft-Karp), push-relabel algorithms, and pseudoflow algorithms (Deveci et al., 2013). Experimental studies show that the first two classes perform comparably and outperform pseudoflow methods in practice.

**Streaming algorithms** address memory-constrained environments where the graph cannot be stored entirely. These algorithms typically use one or two passes over the edge stream, with notable approaches including greedy methods achieving 2-√2 ≈ 0.5857 approximation and degree-bounded semi-matching techniques achieving 1/2 + 1/12 ≈ 0.5833 approximation (Konrad et al., 2021) (Besta et al., 2020) (Konrad et al., 2011).

**Dynamic algorithms** maintain matchings as graphs change over time, with deterministic algorithms achieving (2+ε)-approximation in general graphs and αₖ-approximation in bipartite graphs with various update time guarantees (Bhattacharya et al., 2016). **Specialized variants** include priority matching algorithms that optimize based on vertex priorities, running in O(km^(1/2)n) time for k priority classes (Turner, 2015) (Duan et al., 2011), and randomized MCMC-based approaches for regular bipartite graphs achieving O(m log²n) time (Jindal et al., 2011).

snippets: The most efficient known algorithm for maximum matching in bipartite graphs (Hopcroft et al., 1971)Kar[73] obtained via an alternating breadth first search, extends via a much more elaborate algorithm with the same running time via the graph search procedure of double depth first search (Micali et al., 1980) and blossoms defined from the perspective of minimum length alternating paths (Vazirani, 1990). The RNC matching algorithms [KUW86; MVV[87] use Tutte's theorem to extend to general graphs. The randomized matching algorithm of Rabin and Vazirani [RV[89] uses Tutte's theorem and a theorem of Frobenius on ranks of sub-matrices of skew-symmetric matrices
The quasi-NC algorithm of Fenner, Gurjar, and Thierauf [FGT[16] for bipartite graphs extends by handling tight odd cuts appropriately [ST[17].
citations.title: Matching Is as Easy as the Decision Problem, in the NC Model

snippets: Recently Datta et al. (Datta et al., 2018) have shown that the bipartite maximum matching can be solved in SPL in the planar, bounded genus, K 3,3 -free and K 5 -free graphs. Their techniques can be extended to any graph class where nonzero circulation weights can be assigned in logspace. For constructing a maximum matching in K 3,3 -free and K 5 -free bipartite graphs, they use the logspace algorithm of (Arora et al., 2014) as a black box

In a related work recently, Eppstein and Vazirani (Eppstein et al., 2018) have shown an NC algorithm for the case when the graph is not necessarily bipartite. However, the result holds only for constructing perfect matchings. In non-bipartite graphs, there is no known parallel (e.g., NC) or space-efficient algorithm for deterministically constructing a maximum matching even in the case of planar graphs (Sankowski, 2017)(Datta et al., 2018). Datta et al. (Datta et al., 2018) givelo an approach to design a pseudo-deterministic NC algorithm for this problem

Using the Gallai-Edmonds decomposition theorem, (Datta et al., 2018) shows that the search version of the maximum matching problem reduces to determining the size of the maximum matching in the presence of algorithms to (a) find a perfect matching and to (b) solve the bipartite version of the maximum matching, all in the same class of graphs. This reduction implies a pseudo-deterministic NC algorithm as we only need to use randomization for determining the size of the matching, which always returns the same result.
citations.title: Reachability and Matching in Single Crossing Minor Free Graphs

snippets:
The perfect matching problem has a randomized NC algorithm, using the celebrated Isolation Lemma of Mulmuley, Vazirani and Vazirani. The Isolation Lemma states that giving a random weight assignment to the edges of a graph, ensures that it has a unique minimum weight perfect matching, with a good probability. We derandomize this lemma for $K_{3,3}$-free and $K_5$-free bipartite graphs, i.e. we give a deterministic log-space construction of such a weight assignment for these graphs. Such a construction was known previously for planar bipartite graphs. Our result implies that the perfect matching problem for $K_{3,3}$-free and $K_5$-free bipartite graphs is in SPL. 
It also gives an alternate proof for an already known result -- reachability for $K_{3,3}$-free and $K_5$-free graphs is in UL.
citations.title: Derandomizing Isolation Lemma for $K_{3, 3}$-free and $K_5$-free Bipartite Graphs

snippets:
In 1988, Vazirani gave an NC algorithm for computing the number of perfect matchings in $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs by building on Kasteleyn's scheme for planar graphs, and stated that this "opens up the possibility of obtaining an NC algorithm for finding a perfect matching in $K_{3,3}$-free graphs." In this paper, we finally settle this 30-year-old open problem. Building on recent NC algorithms for planar and bounded-genus perfect matching by Anari and Vazirani and later by Sankowski, we obtain NC algorithms for perfect matching in any minor-closed graph family that forbids a one-crossing graph. This family includes several well-studied graph families including the $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs and $K_5$-minor-free graphs. Graphs in these families not only have unbounded genus, but can have genus as high as $O(n)$. Our method applies as well to several other problems related to perfect matching. In particular, we obtain NC algorithms for the following problems in any family of graphs (or networks) with a one-crossing forbidden minor: 
$\bullet$ Determining whether a given graph has a perfect matching and if so, finding one. 
$\bullet$ Finding a minimum weight perfect matching in the graph, assuming that the edge weights are polynomially bounded. 
$\bullet$ Finding a maximum $st$-flow in the network, with arbitrary capacities. 
The main new idea enabling our results is the definition and use of matching-mimicking networks, small replacement networks that behave the same, with respect to matching problems involving a fixed set of terminals, as the larger network they replace.
citations.title: NC Algorithms for Computing a Perfect Matching and a Maximum Flow in One-Crossing-Minor-Free Graphs

snippets: We present a randomized algorithm that computes exact unweighted maximum matching in bipartite graphs running in Õ(τ 4 D + τ 7 ) rounds. While the maximum matching problem has received much attention in the context of distributed approximation [KMW06, AKO18, LPSP15, BYCHGS[17], the complexity of finding an exact solution is yet unknown. For general graphs, (Ben-Basat et al., 2018) were the first to present a non-trivial algorithm with a running time of O(s 2 max ) rounds, where s max is the size of the maximum matching. This was recently improved to O(s 3/2 max ) (Kitamura et al., 2021). For the case of bipartite graphs, an algorithm by Ahmadi et al. (Ahmadi et al., 2018) is the only result for exact maximum matching. It achieves a running time of Õ(s max ) rounds (and thus the worst-case bound is Õ(n), even in low-treewidth graphs). We present the first algorithm for a non-trivial graph class which achieves a running time sublinear in n.
citations.title: Fully Polynomial-Time Distributed Computation in Low-Treewidth Graphs

snippets: There are three main classes of algorithms for finding the maximum cardinality matchings in bipartite graphs. The first class of algorithms is based on augmenting paths (see a detailed summary by Duff et al. (Duff et al., 2011)). Pushrelabel-based algorithms form a second class (Goldberg et al., 1986). A third class, pseudoflow algorithms, is based on a more recent work (Hochbaum, 1998). There are O( √ nτ ) algorithms in the first two classes (e.g., Hopcroft-Karp algorithm (Hopcroft et al., 1971) and a variant of the push relabel algorithm (Goldberg et al., 1997)), where n is the number of vertices and τ is the number of edges in the given bipartite graph. This is asymptotically best bound for practical algorithms. Most of the other known algorithms in the first two classes and in the third class have the running time complexity of O(nτ ). These three classes of algorithms are described and compared in a recent study (Kaya et al., 2013). It has been demonstrated experimentally that the champions of the first two families are comparable in performance and better than that of the third family.
citations.title: GPU Accelerated Maximum Cardinality Matching Algorithms for Bipartite Graphs

snippets: We study two-pass streaming algorithms for Maximum Bipartite Matching (MBM). All known two-pass streaming algorithms for MBM operate in a similar fashion: They compute a maximal matching in the first pass and find 3-augmenting paths in the second in order to augment the matching found in the first pass

we combine the two main techniques, i.e., subsampling followed by the Greedy matching algorithm [Konrad, MFCS'[18] which gives a $2-\sqrt{2} \approx 0.5857$-approximation, and the computation of \emph{degree-bounded semi-matchings} [EHM, ICDMW'[16][KT, APPROX'[17] which gives a $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{12} \approx 0.5833$-approximation, and obtain a meta-algorithm that yields Konrad's and Esfandiari et al.'s algorithms as special cases
By optimizing parameters, we discover that Konrad's algorithm is optimal for the implied class of algorithms and, perhaps surprisingly, that there is a second optimal algorithm.
citations.title: On Two-Pass Streaming Algorithms for Maximum Bipartite Matching

snippets: A simple maximal matching can be obtained by iterating over edges in some arbitrary order and greedily adding an edge only if both its endpoints are not used yet; this scheme requires  () space (Kemper, 2003). Since every maximal matching is a 1/2-approximation to a maximum matching, this scheme leads to a 1/2-approximation for the maximum cardinality matching

Konrad et al. (Konrad et al., 2011) present a variety of algorithms, taking either one or two passes over the input stream of edges. The general idea is to simulate a three pass algorithm. The original three pass algorithm relies on the refinement of a maximum matching in a bipartite graph using -augmenting paths, as already used by Feigenbaum et al. (Kemper, 2003)Theorem 1]

Kapralov et al. (Kapralov et al., 2014) simulate a local distributed algorithm in the semi-streaming model. The local algorithm is able to distinguish graphs with an Ω() size matching from the graphs having no /polylog() size matching. This approach is transformed into a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm, requiring only  (polylog()) space.  (log()) many instances of this algorithm are executed in parallel, resulting in an  (polylog())-approximation

For bipartite graphs, (1 − 1/)-approximations are possible in both the online (Karp et al., 1990) and vertex model (Goel et al., 2012). Both assume that both vertex classes belonging to sets  , of the bipartite graph  = ( , , ) have the same size, and that one set of the vertices is known beforehand (say  ). The other set (say  ) is then streamed in and at the same time the edges are revealed to the other set. However, the two approaches differ by the fact that one is online, so must make a decision as soon as the edges arrive, and the other can defer the decision to a later point in time. Additionally, the algorithm of Goel et al. [64] is deterministic.
citations.title: Substream-Centric Maximum Matchings on FPGA

snippets: We present three semi-streaming algorithms for Maximum Bipartite Matching with one and two passes. Our one-pass semi-streaming algorithm is deterministic and returns a matching of size at least 1/2 + 0.005 times the optimal matching size in expectation, assuming that edges arrive one by one in (uniform) random order. Our first two-pass algorithm is randomized and returns a matching of size at least 1/2 + 0.019 times the optimal matching size in expectation (over its internal random coin flips) for any arrival order. These two algorithms apply the simple Greedy matching algorithm several times on carefully chosen subgraphs as a subroutine. Furthermore, we present a two-pass deterministic algorithm for any arrival order returning a matching of size at least 1/2 + 0.019 times the optimal matching size. This algorithm is built on ideas from the computation of semi-matchings.
citations.title: Maximum Matching in Semi-streaming with Few Passes

snippets: This paper focuses on dynamic matching algorithms rather than static algorithms for finding maximum matchings in bipartite graphs. The paper presents two deterministic dynamic algorithms for the maximum matching problem. (1) An algorithm that maintains a (2+є)-approximate maximum matching in general graphs with O(poly(logn, 1/є)) update time. (2) An algorithm that maintains an αK approximation of the value of the maximum matching with O(n2/K) update time in bipartite graphs, for every sufficiently large constant positive integer K. Here, 1≤ αK < 2 is a constant determined by the value of K.
citations.title: New deterministic approximation algorithms for fully dynamic matching

snippets: The maximum priority matching problem was introduced in [9]. In this problem, each vertex has an integer-valued priority and the objective is to find a matching that maximizes a priority score defined with respect to these values. The priority score is defined as the n-ary number in which the i-th most-significant digit is the number of matched vertices with priority i. The earlier paper described an algorithm for finding maximum priority matchings in O(mn) time that is based on Edmonds' algorithm for the maximum size matching problem (Edmonds, 1965)(Gabow, 1976)[6]

In a private communication, Tarjan observed that the 2-priority case for bipartite graphs could be solved in O(mn 1/2 ) time using a recent algorithm for weighted matchings in bipartite graphs (Duan et al., 2011)(Goldberg et al., 2015)(Ramshaw et al., 2012). One assigns a weight of 0, 1 or 2 to each edge based on the number of high priority vertices it is incident to. A maximum weight matching of this graph matches the largest possible number of high priority vertices. It can then be extended to a maximum priority matching using an algorithm by Hopcroft and Karp [5]. Tarjan speculated that this approach might be extended to handle multiple priority classes. The {\em maximum cardinality} and {\em maximum weight matching} problems can be solved in time $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{n})$, a bound that has resisted improvement despite decades of research. (Here $m$ and $n$ are the number of edges and vertices.) In this article we demonstrate that this "$m\sqrt{n}$ barrier" is extremely fragile, in the following sense. For any $\epsilon>0$, we give an algorithm that computes a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximate maximum weight matching in $O(m\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1})$ time, that is, optimal {\em linear time} for any fixed $\epsilon$. Our algorithm is dramatically simpler than the best exact maximum weight matching algorithms on general graphs and should be appealing in all applications that can tolerate a negligible relative error. 
Our second contribution is a new {\em exact} maximum weight matching algorithm for integer-weighted bipartite graphs that runs in time $O(m\sqrt{n}\log N)$. This improves on the $O(Nm\sqrt{n})$-time and $O(m\sqrt{n}\log(nN))$-time algorithms known since the mid 1980s, for $1\ll \log N \ll \log n$. Here $N$ is the maximum integer edge weight.

question: Summarize the history of Ramsey theory and explain the recent breakthroughs in the area.

sections.title: Introduction/Background
sections.text:
Ramsey theory is founded on the principle that in any sufficiently large structure, there must exist a relatively large uniform substructure (Mattheus et al., 2023) (Hons, 2025). The field originated from Frank Ramsey's 1930 work on formal logic, where he established what would become known as Ramsey's theorem (Carmesin, 2022) (Bartosova et al., 2022) (Fioravanti et al., 2024). In its most well-known graph-theoretic form, Ramsey's theorem states that for every natural number r, there exists a number n such that every graph with at least n vertices either contains the complete graph Kr or its complement (Carmesin, 2022).

While Ramsey's original work was motivated by problems in formal logic, it was only after Erdős and Szekeres' contributions in 1935 that the theorem gained broader mathematical attention, marking the beginning of what is now a well-established branch of research (Fioravanti et al., 2024) (Erdos, 1947). The seeds of Ramsey theory were actually planted even before Ramsey's work, with connections to earlier results in various mathematical areas (Low et al., 2022).

The scope of Ramsey theory extends far beyond its graph-theoretic origins. Applications can be found in number theory, algebra, geometry, topology, set theory, logic, ergodic theory, information theory, and computer science (Low et al., 2022) (Bartosova et al., 2022). Notable connections include van der Waerden's theorem on arithmetic progressions and Szemerédi's theorem (Kral et al., 2022) (Szemeredi, 1975). The field has grown substantially, with over 2900 entries appearing under "Ramsey" searches in mathematical databases as of recent counts (Low et al., 2022).

Central to Ramsey theory are the Ramsey numbers, which quantify exactly how large a structure must be to guarantee the existence of desired substructures (Mattheus et al., 2023). While the existence of these numbers is guaranteed by Ramsey's theorem, determining their exact values or even good bounds remains extraordinarily difficult. The quantitative behavior of Ramsey numbers represents one of the most challenging problems in the field, with known upper bounds being exponential and the best lower bounds coming from probabilistic constructions pioneered by Erdős (Carmesin, 2022) (Kral et al., 2022).

snippets: Ramsey Theory is an area of mathematics underpinned by the philosophy that in any large enough structure, there exists a relative large uniform substructure. The area is named after F. P. Ramsey [46], but has roots in a variety of branches of mathematics, including logic, set theory, topology, geometry and number theory. Celebrated results include Schur's Theorem [49] leading to Fermat's Last Theorem modulo primes, Rado's partition regularity [45], van der Waerden's Theorem [57] on arithmetic progressions and Shelah's Theorem [51], and Bourgain's Theorem [9] on Euclidean distortion in metric Ramsey Theory, to mention a few. The area has grown into a cornerstone of modern combinatorics research, and the central quantities of study are known as Ramsey Numbers

The quantities r(s, t) are the cornerstone of Ramsey Theory, and have been studied for many decades; their existence is proved by Ramsey's Theorem [46] -see also the book by Graham, Rothschild, Solymosi and Spencer [23]. The quantities r(t, t) are sometimes referred to as diagonal Ramsey Numbers -see Campos, Griffiths, Morris, Sahasrabudhe [12] for a recent major breakthrough -whereas r(s, t) for fixed s and t → ∞ are referred to as off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
The original upper bounds on off-diagonal Ramsey numbers were given by Erdős and Szekeres [20] in 1935. They showed that for all fixed s ≥ 3 and t → ∞ we have r(s, t) = O(t s−1 ).

snippets: Ramsey theory is an area of mathematics asserting that each sufficiently large object contains a still large well-structured subobject. The foundational theorem, proved by Frank Ramsey in 1930, states that every sufficiently large graph contains a still large homogeneous subgraph, i.e. a clique or an independent set (Ramsey, 0). It is well known by a theorem of Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) and a probabilistic construction by Erdős (Erdös, 1947) that there is always a logarithmically large homogeneous set, but we cannot hope to find a larger one in general. Finding the exact base of the logarithm is one of the most difficult and important problems in Ramsey theory, which have recently witnessed a major breakthrough by the work of Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [8], which was subsequently optimized by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [20]

The celebrated Erdős-Hajnal conjecture states that for each graph H the class of H-free graphs admits the Erdős-Hajnal property (Hajnal, 1977). The conjecture is widely open in full, and was only recently resolved for all graphs on 5 vertices [25] (Chudnovsky, 2014)
Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour recently proved that graphs of bounded VC-dimensions admit the Erdős-Hajnal property [24].

snippets: In 1930, Ramsey proved that for every natural number r there is a number nmuch larger than r -such that every graph with at least n vertices either contains the complete graph K r or its complement, which consists of r vertices with no edges in between [72]. Ramsey's theorem is the first of its kind, in fact it finds certain pre-determined substructures in all large-enough graphs. In addition to numerous applications within combinatorics, extensions of Ramsey's theorem to infinite sets provide tools in set theory, and there is a close connection between Ramsey's theorem and Van der Waerden numbers for arithmetic progressions in number theory. Natural variants of Ramsey's Theorem suggest themselves and have been studied a lot in the past century, and are usually subsumed to form the field of 'Ramsey Theory'. While Ramsey's theorem as such is not too difficult to prove, the quantitative behaviour of this phenomenon seems to be particularly difficult to handle
Given r, the Ramsey number is the smallest number n such that every graph on n vertices contains a K r or its complement

The observation that Ramsey numbers, even for pretty small values of r, are difficult to compute was popularised by Paul Erdős [87]. While determining particular Ramsey numbers for r ≥ 6 exactly is certainly not an easy task, the real challenge here is to understand their asymptotic behaviour. The known proofs give an exponential upper bound of the order 2 2r . The best known lower bounds are based on randomly constructed graphs, and are of the order of magnitude 2 r/2 .

Ramsey theory started with the celebrated work of Ramsey [33], in particular the Finite Ramsey Theorem, which states that for any natural numbers r, s, k, there exists a number R(r, s, k), called the Ramsey number, such that for any coloring of r-tuples of a finite set with at least R(r, s, k) elements into s colors, there is a monochromatic subset of size k.This theorem follows from the Infinite Ramsey Theorem, which states that for any coloring of r-tuples of an infinite set into s colors, there is an infinite monochromatic subset. Ramifications of this theorem in various directions have been overwhelmingly present in all areas of discrete mathematics (see for example the books [7], [38] and a survey article [13]), so much so that it would be an injustice to attempt to give a historical overview in this limited space.Suffices to say that Ramsey theory is now in the very core of discrete mathematics, combinatorial set theory and theoretical computer sciences, with important applications to other fields of mathematics, such as topology, Banach spaces, or operator algebras.

Much research has been done into possible generalizations of Ramsey's Theorem, be it to larger infinities such as in the book [7], or with strengthenings of the conclusion to preserve not just the prescribed size of a set, but also some structure on it.We shall be interested in the latter direction, which is called structural Ramsey theory.

snippets: Frank P. Ramsey clearly set the primary goal of his seminal work [48] to be a problem of formal logic and described his fundamental theorem in the abstract as a result of "independent interest" useful in that specific setting. It was only a few years later, thanks to Erdős and Szekeres [26], that Ramsey's theorem, in its most well-known graph-theoretic variant, got the attention of the mathematical community, marking the beginning of what is now a wellestablished branch of mathematical research: Ramsey theory. In a broad sense, Ramsey theory refers to a growing literature of results showing that, given a partition of a mathematical structure into classes, if it is large enough, then it will admit a sub-structure that is regular in some sense. The problem of quantifying what "large enough" means is usually greatly challenging, and many existence results are not accompanied by quantitative bounds on the so-called Ramsey numbers

Applications of Ramsey theory, however, are not limited to combinatorics and formal logic but extend to many areas of both mathematics and theoretical computer science: to name but a few, number theory (Szemerédi, 1975), convex geometry (Bárány et al., 2000), ergodic theory [31], and lower bounds for computing boolean functions (Alon et al., 1986). A special mention goes to the quest for finding explicit constructions for graphs witnessing the tightness of Ramsey theorems: these results raise great interest in theoretical computer science because of their link with the theory of pseudorandomness.

sections.title: Historical Foundations (1920s-1970s)
sections.text:
The historical development of Ramsey theory actually predates Ramsey's famous 1930 theorem, with the earliest substantial contribution coming from I. Schur in 1916 (Goswami, 2024) (Berikkyzy et al., 2023). Schur proved that in any finite coloring of the natural numbers, there must always be a monochromatic solution to the equation x + y = z, establishing what would later be recognized as one of the first theorems in arithmetic Ramsey theory (Nasso et al., 2022) (Nasso et al., 2025).

The next major milestone came in 1927 with van der Waerden's theorem, which demonstrated that for any finite coloring of the natural numbers, one can always find arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions (Berikkyzy et al., 2023) (Nasso et al., 2022). This result was particularly startling because while infinite arithmetic progressions need not be preserved under arbitrary partitions, finite ones of any prescribed length must always exist in at least one color class (Kral et al., 2022) (Szemeredi, 1975).

Following Ramsey's 1930 theorem establishing the existence of Ramsey numbers for complete graphs, the field began to develop more systematically (Bartosova et al., 2022). A significant theoretical advance came through Rado's 1933 work, which generalized Schur's theorem to general linear equations in his doctoral thesis (Li et al., 2023). This established a complete characterization of which linear Diophantine equations are partition regular, providing the foundation for arithmetic Ramsey theory (Nasso et al., 2025).

The period from 1965 to 1974 saw remarkable progress in infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory through topological methods. Nash-Williams proved in 1965 that clopen sets are Ramsey, followed by Galvin and Prikry's 1973 result that Borel sets are Ramsey, and Silver's extension to analytic sets (Dobrinen, 2022) (Dobrinen et al., 2023). This progression culminated in Ellentuck's 1974 topological characterization of Ramsey sets, which provided a complete understanding of which subsets of infinite sequences admit the Ramsey property (Dobrinen, 2022) (Dobrinen et al., 2023).

Throughout this foundational period, the quantitative aspects of Ramsey numbers remained extremely challenging. Even by the 1970s, known upper bounds were exponential while the best lower bounds came from probabilistic constructions, establishing a gap that would persist as one of the field's central problems (Carmesin, 2022) (Kral et al., 2022).

snippets: Ramsey Theory is the study of choosing a set of mathematical elements S, then coloring each element via a surjective coloring function c : S → {1, 2, . . . , r} and determining if there are substructures that are monochromatic. Despite the name, Ramsey Theory was first studied by (Schur, 0) when he showed that we can always find an N such that if n ≥ N and we color [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} with r colors, there must always be a monochromatic solution to x + y = z (see (Schur, 0)). Van der Waerden, in 1927, proved that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N such that if n ≥ N and you color [n] with r-colors, there must a monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression (see [19]). Finally, Ramsey, in 1928, showed that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N so that if n ≥ N, then no matter how you color the edges of the complete graph K n using r many colors, there must be a monochromatic complete subgraph K k (see (Ramsey, 0)). It was not until 1973, in [8], when Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós introduced the idea of looking for polychromatic or rainbow structures. The latter is a branch of combinatorics concerned with the "abundance" of certain arithmetic patterns in the natural numbers. A typical problem in this area is to determine whether a given configuration is ubiquitous enough that one is forced to find instances of it in each piece of every finite partition of N.

In this area, it is customary to call partitions colourings. For instance, a classical theorem by I. Such a triple is called a monochromatic solution of the equation x + y = z, and the existence of monochromatic solutions in all colourings is the statement that the aforementioned equation is partition regular.

It is natural to ask which other equations have the same property. Albeit the linear case is well-understood by a classical result of R. Rado [Rad[33], the polynomial one is still very far from being settled; for instance, whether the Pythagorean equation x 2 + y 2 = z 2 is partition regular is still unknown, and one of the long-standing open problems in the area.

Ramsey theory started with the celebrated work of Ramsey [33], in particular the Finite Ramsey Theorem, which states that for any natural numbers r, s, k, there exists a number R(r, s, k), called the Ramsey number, such that for any coloring of r-tuples of a finite set with at least R(r, s, k) elements into s colors, there is a monochromatic subset of size k.This theorem follows from the Infinite Ramsey Theorem, which states that for any coloring of r-tuples of an infinite set into s colors, there is an infinite monochromatic subset. Ramifications of this theorem in various directions have been overwhelmingly present in all areas of discrete mathematics (see for example the books [7], [38] and a survey article [13]), so much so that it would be an injustice to attempt to give a historical overview in this limited space.Suffices to say that Ramsey theory is now in the very core of discrete mathematics, combinatorial set theory and theoretical computer sciences, with important applications to other fields of mathematics, such as topology, Banach spaces, or operator algebras.

Much research has been done into possible generalizations of Ramsey's Theorem, be it to larger infinities such as in the book [7], or with strengthenings of the conclusion to preserve not just the prescribed size of a set, but also some structure on it.We shall be interested in the latter direction, which is called structural Ramsey theory.

snippets: Ramsey theory was initiated by the following celebrated result. Theorem 1.1 (Ramsey (Ramsey, 0)). Given a positive integer k, suppose that [N] k , the collection of all k-element subsets of the natural numbers, is partitioned into finitely many pieces. Then there is an infinite subset N ⊆ N such that [N ] k is contained in one piece of the partition

Extensions of Ramsey's Theorem to colorings of infinite subsets of N have been proved, subject to constraints necessitated by the Axiom of Choice. Considering the set of all infinite subsets of the natural numbers, denoted by [N] N , as the Baire space with its metric topology, a set X ⊆ [N] N is called Ramsey if for each M ∈ [N] N , there is an N ∈ [M ] N such that either [N ] N ⊆ X or else [N ] N ∩X = ∅. From 1965 through 1974, a beautiful progression of results was obtained using topological properties to guarantee that certain subsets of the Baire space are Ramsey. Nash-Williams proved that clopen sets are Ramsey in (Nash-Williams, 1965); Galvin and Prikry proved that Borel sets are Ramsey in (Galvin et al., 1973); and Silver extended this to analytic sets in (Silver, 1966). This line of work culminated in the topological characterization of Ramsey sets found by Ellentuck in (Ellentuck, 1974) in terms of a topology refining the metric topology on [N] N , now referred to as the Ellentuck topology.

Ramsey theory was initiated by the following celebrated result: Given positive integers m, r and a coloring of [N] m = {F ⊆ N : |F | = m} into r colors, there is an infinite subset M ⊆ N such that [M ] m is monochromatic [32]. Ramsey's theorem is considered "finite-dimensional" as the subsets of N being colored are of the fixed finite size m.

Infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory is concerned with coloring the infinite subsets of N

Using the axiom of choice, Erdős and Rado produced a coloring χ : [N] ∞ → 2 with the property that no set of the form [M ] ∞ is monochromatic (Erdös et al., 1952); however, restrictions to 'definable' colorings have yielded the desired infinite-dimensional Ramsey theorems

An intermediate step in the progression from finitedimensional to infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory was the Nash-Williams Theorem [28], which implies that clopen subsets of the Baire space are Ramsey. In unpublished work, Galvin showed that open sets are Ramsey. Galvin and Prikry [19] substantially advanced the theory by showing that Borel sets are Ramsey, and soon after, Silver [35] extended their result to all analytic sets. This line of work culminated in the Ellentuck Theorem [15], which characterises those sets which are (completely) Ramsey as exactly those with the property of Baire in the Ellentuck topology.

snippets: In 1930, Ramsey proved that for every natural number r there is a number nmuch larger than r -such that every graph with at least n vertices either contains the complete graph K r or its complement, which consists of r vertices with no edges in between [72]. Ramsey's theorem is the first of its kind, in fact it finds certain pre-determined substructures in all large-enough graphs. In addition to numerous applications within combinatorics, extensions of Ramsey's theorem to infinite sets provide tools in set theory, and there is a close connection between Ramsey's theorem and Van der Waerden numbers for arithmetic progressions in number theory. Natural variants of Ramsey's Theorem suggest themselves and have been studied a lot in the past century, and are usually subsumed to form the field of 'Ramsey Theory'. While Ramsey's theorem as such is not too difficult to prove, the quantitative behaviour of this phenomenon seems to be particularly difficult to handle
Given r, the Ramsey number is the smallest number n such that every graph on n vertices contains a K r or its complement

The observation that Ramsey numbers, even for pretty small values of r, are difficult to compute was popularised by Paul Erdős [87]. While determining particular Ramsey numbers for r ≥ 6 exactly is certainly not an easy task, the real challenge here is to understand their asymptotic behaviour. The known proofs give an exponential upper bound of the order 2 2r . The best known lower bounds are based on randomly constructed graphs, and are of the order of magnitude 2 r/2 .

sections.title: Development of Structural Ramsey Theory (1970s-1980s)
sections.text:
The early 1970s marked a pivotal transformation in Ramsey theory with the emergence of structural Ramsey theory, which generalized Ramsey's theorem from sets (unstructured objects) to arbitrary first-order structures (Mavsulovi'c, 2022) (Mavsulovi'c_1, 2022). This successful generalization was motivated by earlier extensions from sets to cardinals (special well-ordered chains), prompting mathematicians to explore whether similar principles could apply to more complex mathematical structures (Mavsulovi'c, 2022).

One of the most significant early developments was the creation of categorical frameworks for structural Ramsey theory. Leeb developed a comprehensive category-theoretic approach in 1973, which was used by Graham, Rothschild, and Leeb to prove a Ramsey theorem for finite vector spaces (Junge, 2022). This categorical perspective provided powerful tools for understanding and proving Ramsey statements in structured settings (Dvzuklevski et al., 2024).

The period's most influential achievement was the Nešetřil-Rödl theorem, developed throughout the 1970s and 1980s, which became fundamental to structural Ramsey theory (Junge, 2022) (Hubivcka et al., 2025). This work was initiated by Abramson and Harrington in 1978, with Nešetřil and Rödl expanding upon their results in subsequent papers from 1977, 1983, and 1989 (Junge, 2022). The theorem established that every class of structures with the Ramsey property has the amalgamation property, revealing a fundamental connection between these two concepts (Mavsulovi'c et al., 2022).

A crucial insight that emerged during this period was that adding carefully chosen linear orders to structures often yields classes with the Ramsey property (Mavsulovi'c, 2022). For example, adding all possible linear orders to finite graphs produces a class of finite ordered graphs that forms a Ramsey class, and similarly, adding linear extensions to finite partial orders creates another Ramsey class (Mavsulovi'c, 2022).

The late 1990s saw the recognition of finite Ramsey degrees as an important weaker property for classes where full Ramsey expansions had been identified (Mavsulovi'c et al., 2022). This observation would later prove significant when the connection between classes with Ramsey expansions and finite Ramsey degrees was formally established by Kechris, Pestov and Todorcevic in 2003, and proven in the reverse direction by Zucker in 2015 (Mavsulovi'c et al., 2022) (Kechris et al., 2003).

By the 1980s, Nešetřil had discovered a crucial connection between Ramsey classes and Fraïssé classes, inspired by Lachlan's seminars, and by 1989 had connected the classification program of homogeneous structures to structural Ramsey theory (Hubivcka et al., 2025). This established structural Ramsey theory as a central area bridging combinatorics, model theory, and later topological dynamics (Russo, 2025).

snippets: This successful generalization of Ramsey's theorem from sets (unstructured objects) to cardinals (special well-ordered chains) prompted in the early 1970's the idea of generalizing the setup to arbitrary first-order structures, giving birth to structural Ramsey theory

Already in the 1970's it was observed that in combinatorially interesting cases adding carefully chosen linear orders yields classes with the Ramsey property. For example, by adding all possible linear orders to finite graphs we get a class of finite ordered graphs which is a Ramsey class; similarly, by adding all possible linear extensions to finite partial orders we get another Ramsey class. On the other hand, if for some reason we do not wish to modify the language, we can prove that almost all combinatorially interesting classes of finite structures enjoy the weaker property of having finite Ramsey degrees. This phenomenon was observed already in the analysis of the Ramsey property for infinite cardinals, and the first Ramsey degrees for combinatorially interesting classes of structures were computed in [3,4](Fouché, 1999)]
(The equivalence of the two approaches was observed and proved only a few years ago, in 2016 in (Zucker, 2015).)

snippets: Ramsey theory is one of only a few mathematical theories whose reach goes from elementary problems that can be demonstrated to undergraduates, to a variety of surprisingly subtle applications in mathematical logic, set theory, finite combinatorics and topological dynamics. The successful generalization of Ramsey's theorem from sets (unstructured objects) to cardinals (special well-ordered chains) lead in the early 1970's to generalizing this setup to arbitrary first-order structures, giving birth to structural Ramsey theory. Interestingly, one of the first comprehensive texts published already in 1973 was Leeb's book [16] where structural Ramsey theory was presented using the language of category theory. Unfortunately, this point of view was relatively quickly pushed out of the focus of the research community and was replaced by the model-theoretic approach that is even today a dominant point of view

As the structural Ramsey theory evolved, it has become evident that the Ramsey phenomena depend not only on the choice of objects but also on the choice of morphisms prompting, thus, the shift of the attention back to categorical interpretations of the Ramsey phenomena

In this paper we provide purely categorical proofs of two important results of structural Ramsey theory: the result of M. Sokić that the free product of Ramsey classes is a Ramsey class (Sokic, 2012), and the result of M. Bodirsky, M. Pinsker and T. Tsankov that adding constants to the language of a Ramsey class preserves the Ramsey property [4] (Bodirsky, 2015).

snippets: Category theory has long been used in Ramsey theory. Leeb created a category theoretic framework for proving Ramsey statements in lecture notes that were recorded in [7] in 1973. In [3] Graham, Rothschild, and Leeb proved a Ramsey theorem for finite vector spaces with this framework. The influential Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem proved in [13], [11], [12] in the 1970's and 1980's was expressed in the language of category theory. After these results there was a shift back to the language of classes, though categorical ideas were implicit in Solecki's papers [19], [17], and [18]. In 2015 Gromov advocated for a deeper use of category theory in Ramsey theory in [5]. More recently the work of Masulovic has created more general categorical techniques to prove Ramsey statements, such as in [9]

Structural Ramsey theory was initiated by the work of Abramason-Harrington in (Abramson et al., 1978) and Nešetřil-Rödl in (Nešetřil et al., 1977), (Nešetřil et al., 1983), and (Nešetřil et al., 1989) expanded upon the Abramson and Harrington result. Recently Nešetřil and Hubička proved a version of the Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem for classes of structures with certain closure properties in (Hubička et al., 2016). This group of theorems is fundamental to structural Ramsey theory, which has seen a revival in the recent years [8], (Fox et al., 2019), (Nguyen et al., 2008), (Nešetřil, 2007), (Sokic, 2015).

snippets: Classical Ramsey theory has successfully extended to relational structures, yielding a wealth of results that have profoundly influenced other areas of mathematics. Interestingly, the same development has not occurred in the case of dual Ramsey theory

One of the first successful applications of category theory in combinatorics was Graham, Leeb and Rothschild's 1972 proof of the Rota Conjecture (Graham et al., 1972) (which can be seen as a vector-space analogue of the Finite Ramsey Theorem from the 1930s (Ramsey, 0)). Around the same time, the first results in the area of structural Ramsey theory were obtained (see (Barton, 2020) for references)

Unlike "direct" Ramsey theory which had successfully evolved to relational structures and supplied us with a plethora of results which have profoundly influenced other ares of mathematics (see for example (Kechris et al., 2003)), the same has not happened with the dual Ramsey theory. A notable exception is Solecki's paper (Solecki, 2010) where a finite dual Ramsey theorem is proved for finite structures over first-order signatures where functional symbols are interpreted as usual finitary operations, and relational symbols are interpreted as dual relations (see (Solecki, 2010) for details). Using a different set of strategies, an attempt was made in (Mavsulovi'c, 2017) to understand the dual Ramsey property for classes of finite relational structures where relational symbols are interpreted as usual relations.
