snippets: In the 1970s, structural Ramsey theory emerged as a new branch of combinatorics. This development came with the isolation of the concepts of the $\mathbf{A}$-Ramsey property and Ramsey class. Following the influential Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il-R\"odl theorem, several Ramsey classes have been identified. In the 1980s, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il, inspired by a seminar of Lachlan, discovered a crucial connection between Ramsey classes and Fra\"iss\'e classes, and, in his 1989 paper, connected the classification programme of homogeneous structures to structural Ramsey theory. In 2005, Kechris, Pestov, and Todor\v{c}evi\'c revitalized the field by connecting Ramsey classes to topological dynamics. This breakthrough motivated Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il to propose a program for classifying Ramsey classes.

snippets: The intimate connection between the amalgamation property and the Ramsey property has been evident from the very beginnings of Structural Ramsey Theory in early 1970's: amalgamation lies at the heart of the partite method, one of the most powerful tools for proving the Ramsey property for a class of finite structures (see, e.g. the proof of the famous Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem (Nešetřil et al., 1977)(Nešetřil et al., 1989)). On the other hand, it is an easy by fundamental result of Nešetřil and Rödl from 1977 that every class of structures with the Ramsey property has the amalgamation property (Nešetřil et al., 1977)

In the late 1990s it was observed that many concrete classes of finite structures where a Ramsey expansion had been identified also enjoyed a weaker property of having finite Ramsey degrees [2,3,(Fouché, 1999). For Fraïssé classes, that this is not a mere coincidence was proven in one direction in (Kechris et al., 2003), who prove that classes with a Ramsey expansion have finite Ramsey degrees, and in the other by the second author in (Zucker, 2015), showing that small Ramsey degrees suffice for the existence of a Ramsey expansion. A more combinatorial proof of the same fact can be found in [11], and a reinterpretation of the latter proof in the language of category theory in (Mašulović, 2020)

In this paper we show that the assumption about the ambient class in which an ultrahomogeneous object oversees the construction is unnecessary. Imposing no additional assumptions, for each category of finite objects with finite small Ramsey degrees (the definitions are given below) we construct a Ramsey expansion.

sections.title: Modern Extensions and Generalizations
sections.text:
The late 20th and early 21st centuries have witnessed remarkable extensions of Ramsey theory into new mathematical territories. One of the most significant developments has been in arithmetic Ramsey theory, which now encompasses patterns far more complex than the classical addition-based results. Recent breakthroughs include Sahasrabudhe's 2016 proof of the existence of monochromatic patterns involving multiplication and exponentiation, demonstrating that for every finite coloring of natural numbers, there exists a monochromatic triple {a, b, a^b} where a, b > 1 (Nasso et al., 2022) (Sahasrabudhe, 2016). This extends to much richer patterns, including monochromatic quadruples of the form {a, b, ab, a^b} (Sahasrabudhe, 2016).

A parallel development has been the study of generalized Ramsey numbers, first proposed by Erdős and Shelah in 1975 but systematically developed by Erdős and Gyárfás beginning in 1997. These generalized Ramsey numbers f(n, p, q) represent the minimum number of colors needed for a (p, q)-coloring of the complete graph K_n, where every p-clique must receive at least q colors (Bennett et al., 2022) (Bennett et al._1, 2022). Recent work has established precise thresholds for when these numbers exhibit linear, quadratic, or sublinear behavior, with significant contributions using the Lovász Local Lemma and color energy techniques (Bennett et al._1, 2022) (Balogh et al., 2021) (Conlon et al., 2014) (Joos et al., 2022).

The emergence of Euclidean Ramsey theory represents another major extension, initiated by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus in 1975. This field explores geometric patterns in continuous domains and has evolved to include the Gallai-Ramsey problem, which combines classical Ramsey theory with the constraint that colorings contain no rainbow triangles (Cheng et al., 2023) (Balogh et al., 2018) (Conlon et al., 2017) (Liu et al., 2020). Recent developments include the Euclidean Gallai-Ramsey problem, which seeks monochromatic or rainbow configurations in colored n-dimensional Euclidean spaces (Cheng et al., 2023).

Perhaps one of the most fascinating modern developments is the birth of anti-Ramsey theory in 1973 with work by Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós, which seeks rainbow (polychromatic) rather than monochromatic structures (Zheng, 2024) (Berikkyzy et al., 2025). This field has produced notable results such as the complete determination of anti-van der Waerden numbers for three-term arithmetic progressions, with exact formulas established for all values of n (Berikkyzy et al., 2016) (Zheng, 2024).

The field has also seen significant developments in computational and logical aspects through reverse mathematics, where variants such as the Free Set Theorem, Thin Set Theorem, and Rainbow Ramsey Theorem have revealed surprising computational properties that differ markedly from classical Ramsey's theorem (Carlucci et al., 2024) (Cholak et al., 2018) (Liu et al., 2021) (Patey, 2015). Additionally, infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory has continued to evolve with advances in topological Ramsey spaces, providing general frameworks for studying combinatorial properties with topological counterparts (Cano et al., 2023).

These extensions demonstrate how Ramsey theory has matured from its classical graph-theoretic origins into a diverse field spanning arithmetic, geometry, topology, logic, and computer science, with each area contributing unique perspectives and techniques to the broader understanding of order within seemingly chaotic structures.

snippets: The Euclidean Ramsey theory, as an important branch of Ramsey theory, was proposed by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus [4] in 1975. Originating from graph theory and Ramsey theory, it aims to explore the presence of geometric patterns in continuous domains and investigates the intricate relationship between combinatorial and geometric structures within Euclidean space. Over the past fifty years, a multitude of profound results have been presented in Euclidean Ramsey theory, exemplified by notable works [2,3,5,6,10,13,22] and the references therein, we also refer the readers to the great textbooks [11]. In 1967, Gallai [8] proposed the Gallai-Ramsey problem, representing an intriguing branch of graph theory that investigates inherent order and structure within graph coloring. By building upon Ramsey theory and combinatorial principles, it seeks to ascertain the existence of monochromatic and rainbow structures within edge-colored complete graphs. The extremal problem associated with the Gallai-Ramsey problem has garnered significant attention, particularly in recent years, see [1,7,12,16,17,23]. Recently, Mao, Ozeki, and Wang [19] combined the concepts of Euclidean Ramsey theory and the Gallai-Ramsey problem, and introduced the Euclidean Gallai-Ramsey problem, which aims to determine the existence of some monochromatic or rainbow configuration in a colored n-dimensional Euclidean space E n.
citations.title: Euclidean Gallai-Ramsey for Various Configurations

snippets: An edge coloring of a graph $G$ is a Gallai coloring if it contains no rainbow triangle. We show that the number of Gallai $r$-colorings of $K_n$ is $\left(\binom{r}{2}+o(1)\right)2^{\binom{n}{2}}$. This result indicates that almost all Gallai $r$-colorings of $K_n$ use only 2 colors. We also study the extremal behavior of Gallai $r$-colorings among all $n$-vertex graphs. We prove that the complete graph $K_n$ admits the largest number of Gallai $3$-colorings among all $n$-vertex graphs when $n$ is sufficiently large, while for $r\geq 4$, it is the complete bipartite graph $K_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor, \lceil n/2 \rceil}$. Our main approach is based on the hypergraph container method, developed independently by Balogh, Morris, and Samotij as well as by Saxton and Thomason, together with some stability results for containers.
citations.title: The Typical Structure of Gallai Colorings and Their Extremal Graphs

snippets: In 1963, A. W. Hales and R. I. Jewett published the eponymous "Hales-Jewett Theorem" which has since become a hallmark of Ramsey Theory [4]. As the study of Ramsey Theory progressed, mathematicians like P. Erdös, M. Simonovits, and V. T. Sós questioned whether there were rainbow duals of Ramsey Theory, which began the branch of Anti-Ramsey Theory. Since their paper in 1975, mathematicians have made many discoveries in Anti-Ramsey Theory; for example, Young et al found a formula for anti-van der Waerden numbers (the rainbow analogue of van der Waerden numbers) of three term arithmetic progressions in (Berikkyzy et al., 2016).

snippets: Ramsey Theory is a branch of mathematics that assigns colors to elements of a set and then determines if monochromatic substructures exist within the set, whereas Anti-Ramsey Theory determines if rainbow (polychromatic) substructures exist within the set. Ramsey Theory has a long history dating back to around 1920 with Schur, Ramsey and van der Waerden making the earliest contributions (see (Ramsey, 0)(Schur, 0)[16]) where the sets considered were integers or graph edges. It was not until 1973 when when Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós, in [8], introduced the idea of Anti-Ramsey Theory. Thirty years later, Jungić et al started investigating anti-van der Waerden problems where the sets being colored were {1, 2, . . . , n} = [n] and Z n and the rainbow substructures were 3-term arithmetic progressions (see (Jungić et al., 2003)(Jungić et al., 2003)). These papers focused on the conditions on the sizes of the color classes that guarantee rainbow arithmetic progressions. The anti-van der Waerden number was first defined in [15] by Uherka in 2013.

snippets:
The \emph{anti-van der Waerden number}, denoted by $aw([n],k)$, is the smallest $r$ such that every exact $r$-coloring of $[n]$ contains a rainbow $k$-term arithmetic progression. Butler et. al. showed that $\lceil \log_3 n \rceil + 2 \le aw([n],3) \le \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$, and conjectured that there exists a constant $C$ such that $aw([n],3) \le \lceil \log_3 n \rceil + C$. In this paper, we show this conjecture is true by determining $aw([n],3)$ for all $n$. We prove that for $7\cdot 3^{m-2}+1 \leq n \leq 21 \cdot 3^{m-2}$, \[ aw([n],3)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} m+2, & \mbox{if $n=3^m$}\\ m+3, & \mbox{otherwise}. 
\end{array}\right.\]

snippets: Ramsey's theorems have been widely investigated from the point of view of Computability Theory, Proof Theory and Reverse Mathematics (see [17] for details and references). In his seminal paper, Jockusch (Jockusch, 1972) gave a deep analysis of Ramsey's theorem using tools from Computability Theory, which established this theorem as an important bridge between Combinatorics and Computability. The effective and logical strength of many consequences and variants of Ramsey's theorem have since been investigated. Among those, the Free Set, Thin Set and Rainbow Ramsey theorems have attracted significant interest in recent decades (see, e.g., (Cholak, 2003)(Wang, 2013)(Patey, 2015)(Cholak et al., 2018)(Liu et al., 2021)), due to the peculiar behavior of these theorems when compared to Ramsey's theorem

The Free Set Theorem (denoted FS n ), introduced in the context of Reverse Mathematics by Harvey Friedman (Friedman et al., 2000), states that for every coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers in unboundedly many colors, there exists an infinite set H of natural numbers such that for all n-subsets s of H, the color of s is either not in H or else is in s itself

The Thin Set Theorem (denoted TS n ω or TS n ) is a weak variant of the Free Set Theorem asserting that for any coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers there is an infinite set H of natural numbers such that the n-subsets of H avoid at least one color. The Rainbow Ramsey Theorem (denoted RRT n k ) asserts that for every coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers in which each color is used at most k times, there is an infinite set H of natural numbers such that the coloring assigns different colors to different n-subsets of H. While Ramsey's theorem for colorings of 3-subsets already codes the halting set (meaning there exists a computable coloring of 3-subsets of N such that any of its solutions computes the halting set), none of these principles does the same for any dimension n ≥ 3. This surprising result is due to Wang [35].
citations.title: Ramsey-like theorems for the Schreier barrier

snippets: Informally, a mathematical statement is robust if its strength is left unchanged under variations of the statement. In this paper, we investigate the lack of robustness of Ramsey’s theorem and its consequence under the frameworks of reverse mathematics and computable reducibility. To this end, we study the degrees of unsolvability of cohesive sets for different uniformly computable sequence of sets and identify different layers of unsolvability. This analysis enables us to answer some questions of Wang about how typical sets help computing cohesive sets.We also study the impact of the number of colors in the computable reducibility between coloring statements. In particular, we strengthen the proof by Dzhafarov that cohesiveness does not strongly reduce to stable Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, revealing the combinatorial nature of this nonreducibility and prove that whenever k is greater than l, stable Ramsey’s theorem for n-tuples and k colors is not computably reducible to Ramsey’s theorem for n-tuples and l colors. In this sense, Ramsey’s theorem is not robust with respect to his number of colors over computable reducibility. Finally, we separate the thin set and free set theorem from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs and identify an infinite decreasing hierarchy of thin set theorems in reverse mathematics. This shows that in reverse mathematics, the strength of Ramsey’s theorem is very sensitive to the number of colors in the output set. In particular, it enables us to answer several related questions asked by Cholak, Giusto, Hirst and Jockusch.
citations.title: The weakness of being cohesive, thin or free in reverse mathematics

snippets: Infinite dimensional Ramsey theory has developed in different directions since its beginning in the 1960's. For instance, topological Ramsey spaces, first introduced by Carlson and Simpson in [4], and later reformulated and extended by Todorčević in [31], provide a general framework to study a wide variety of combinatorial properties that have topological counterparts. The prototype example of the topological characterization of an infinite dimensional combinatorial property is Ellentuck's result in [13], which establishes an infinite dimensional version of Ramsey's theorem restricted to Baire measurable partitions of [N] ω . On the Ramsey property of subsets of [N] ω , Erdős and Rado proved in [14], using the axiom of choice, that there exist subsets of [N] ω which are not Ramsey. Later, Galvin and Prikry showed in [16] that Borel subsets of [N] ω in the metrizable topology are Ramsey, and Silver in [29] extended this fact to analytic subsets. Finally, Ellentuck in [13] characterized topologically Ramsey subsets of [N] ω as those having the Baire property with respect to the exponential topology.
citations.title: Topological games in Ramsey spaces

sections.title: Recent Major Breakthroughs
sections.text:
The period from 2020 to 2024 has witnessed unprecedented progress in Ramsey theory, culminating in what many consider the most significant breakthrough since the field's founding. The journey began with incremental improvements to the classic bounds: Conlon's 2006 work achieved a super-polynomial improvement over the Erdős-Szekeres bound, followed by Sah's 2020 optimization showing R(k+1,k+1) ≤ exp(-c(log k)²)(2k choose k) (Sah, 2020) (Conlon, 2006). However, Sah's result represented what appeared to be a natural barrier for the quasirandomness-based approach that had dominated the field (Sah, 2020).

The transformative moment came in March 2023 with the work of Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe, who proved that R(k) ≤ (4-ε)^k for some constant ε > 0 (Campos et al., 2023). This achievement marked the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres from 1935, ending nearly 90 years of stagnation (Campos et al., 2023) (Gupta et al., 2024) (Wigderson, 2024). Remarkably, their approach completely departed from previous quasirandomness methods, instead centering on a novel "book algorithm" that works with pairs of disjoint vertex sets with high density of red edges between them (Gupta et al., 2024).

The breakthrough was quickly refined and extended. Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin and Wei optimized the original result, improving the constant ε to 2^(-7) (Gupta et al., 2024). Subsequently, Balister, Bollobás, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba provided an alternative and more conceptual proof of the result (Wigderson, 2024) (Balister et al., 2024).

The impact extended beyond diagonal Ramsey numbers. Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe also established exponential improvements for off-diagonal Ramsey numbers, surpassing the best previously known bounds by exponential factors (Gupta et al., 2024). For multicolor Ramsey numbers with three or more colors, Balister and colleagues achieved the first exponential improvement over the Erdős-Szekeres bound from 1935 (Balister et al., 2024). Recent work has also made progress on the famous problem of multicolor triangles, where the gap between lower and upper bounds remains enormous, with the best lower bound of (321-o(1))^(r/5) and upper bound of er! (Boyadzhiyska et al., 2024).

Parallel advances occurred in canonical Ramsey theory. Girão, Hurley, Pehova and Pokrovskiy made substantial progress on the Lefmann-Rödl-Thomas conjecture from 1992, proving it for l ≥ k³(log k)^(1+o(1)) and reducing the gap between lower and upper bounds from exponential to polynomial in k (Girao et al., 2023).

Additional breakthroughs resolved long-standing conjectures in related areas. Lee's 2017 proof of the Burr-Erdős conjecture established that graphs with bounded degeneracy have linear Ramsey numbers, solving a problem that had remained open since 1973 (Bradavc et al., 2024) (Lee, 2015). Progress on the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture included its resolution for all graphs on 5 vertices and the recent proof by Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour that graphs of bounded VC-dimension admit the Erdős-Hajnal property (Hons, 2025) (Chudnovsky, 2014).

These breakthroughs represent a fundamental shift in Ramsey theory methodology and have opened new avenues for research that had seemed impossible under the previous quasirandomness paradigm. The field has moved from decades of incremental progress to exponential improvements, suggesting that even more dramatic advances may be possible in the coming years.

snippets: The Ramsey number R(k) is the minimum n ∈ N such that every red-blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains a monochromatic clique on k vertices. Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) proved in 1930 that R(k) is finite for every k ∈ N, and a few years later Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) gave the first reasonable upper bound on the Ramsey numbers, showing that R(k) 4 k . An exponential lower bound on R(k) was obtained by Erdős (Erdös, 1947) in 1947, whose beautiful non-constructive proof of the bound R(k) 2 k/2 initiated the development of the probabilistic method (see [2])

Over the 75 years since Erdős' proof, the problem of improving either bound has attracted an enormous amount of attention. Despite this, however, progress has been extremely slow, and it was not until 1988 that the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres was improved by a polynomial factor, by Thomason [21]. About 20 years later, an important breakthrough was made by Conlon (Conlon, 2006), who improved the upper bound by a super-polynomial factor, in the process significantly extending the method of Thomason. More recently, Sah (Sah, 2020) optimised Conlon's technique, obtaining the bound R(k) 4 k−c(log k) 2 for some constant c > 0. This represents a natural barrier for the approach of Thomason and Conlon, which exploits quasirandom properties of colourings of E(K n ) with no monochromatic K k that hold when n is close to the Erdős-Szekeres bound. For the lower bound, even less progress has been made: the bound proved by Erdős in 1947 has only been improved by a factor of 2, by Spencer (Spencer, 1977) in 1977, using the Lovász Local Lemma
R(k) ⩽ (4 − ε)^k for some constant ε>0. This is the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres, proved in 1935.

snippets: Ramsey numbers were introduced by Ramsey [Ram[30] in 1930, and the problem of estimating their value has been one of the central questions in extremal combinatorics ever since, with particular attention paid to the diagonal Ramsey numbers R(k, k). Erdős and Szekeres [ES[35] proved that R(k, k) ≤ 4 k in 1935. Despite a series of important improvements [Con09,Sah23,Tho[88] throughout the years, based on the quasirandomness properties of colorings close to the upper bound, the first exponential improvement of the Erdős-Szekeres bound was obtained only very recently in a breakthrough result by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [CGMS[23]. They proved that that there exists ε > 0 such that R(k, k) ≤ (4 − ε) k for sufficiently large k ∈ N
they show that (1) is satisfied with ε = 2 −7. For the off-diagonal Ramsey numbers, Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [CGMS[23] establish

snippets: Ramsey's theorem states that if $N$ is sufficiently large, then no matter how one colors the edges among $N$ vertices with two colors, there are always $k$ vertices spanning edges in only one color. Given this theorem, it is natural to ask ``how large is sufficiently large?'' Ramsey's original proof showed that $N=k!$ is sufficient, and five years later Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres improved this bound to $N=4^k$. And then progress stalled for almost 90 years
the recent breakthrough of Campos--Griffiths--Morris--Sahasrabudhe, who proved that $N=3.993^k$ is sufficient. In addition
the subsequent work of Balister, Bollob\'as, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba, who gave an alternative, and more conceptual, proof.
citations.title: Upper bounds on diagonal Ramsey numbers [after Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe]

snippets: Ramsey [10] proved in 1930 that R r (k) is finite for every k, r ∈ N, and a few years later his theorem was rediscovered in a famous paper of Erdős and Szekeres [6], who gave the first reasonable upper bound on the Ramsey numbers, showing that R r (k) r rk. This bound turns out to be not too far from the truth: Erdős [5] proved in 1947 that R r (k) r k/2, in one of the earliest applications of the probabilistic method

Progress on the upper bound has been much slower, except in the case r = 2, where the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres was improved by Rödl (see [7]) and Thomason [14] in the 1980s, by Conlon [2] in 2009, and by Sah [11] in 2023, leading to a bound of the form R 2 (k) e −c(log k) 2 4 k for some constant c > 0. An exponential improvement was finally obtained last year by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [1]
For each $r \geqslant 3$, this is the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres from 1935.
citations.title: Upper bounds for multicolour Ramsey numbers

snippets: The classic problem in Ramsey Theory asks for the smallest integer n such that every r-colouring of the edges of the complete graph K n contains a monochromatic copy of K k . Despite nearly a century of research, this problem remains poorly understood, even for small values of r or k. In the 2-colour case, the early work of Erdős (Erdös, 1947) and Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) in the 1940s and 1930s respectively established exponential (in k) lower and upper bounds for n. Decades of subsequent efforts only saw lower order improvements to these bounds, until the very recent breakthrough of Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [10] (further optimised by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [22]) brought the first exponential improvement on the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres. The gaps in the bounds are even wider at the other end of the spectrum, where we seek monochromatic triangles as the number of colours r grows. The best known lower bound of (321 − o(1)) r/5 comes from blowing up a 5-colouring of Exoo (Exoo, 1994), while the upper bound of er! follows from an argument of Schur [29]. Determining the correct order of growth of this multicolour Ramsey number is a famous old problem of Erdős with a $250 prize attached (Graham, 1997).
citations.title: Odd-Ramsey numbers of complete bipartite graphs

snippets: In 1930, Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) showed that every k-colouring of the edges of a very large clique contains a large monochromatic sub-clique.This classical theorem was the starting seed for Ramsey theory, and there have been numerous extensions and generalisations of it since then.One of the most important is the canonical Ramsey theorem of Erdős and Rado (Tsarpalias, 1981), which considers colourings that allow an arbitrary number of colours
Lefmann and Rödl (Lefmann et al., 1995) gave the best current bounds for this result, showing that we can take f (k) = k Ck 2 for some constant C

Lefmann, Rödl, and Thomas conjectured in 1992 that f(l, k) = l^{k - 1} and proved this for l ≥ (3 k)^{2 k}. We prove the conjecture for l ≥ k^3 (log k)^{1 + o(1)} and establish the general upper bound f(l, k) ≤ k (log k)^{1 + o(1)} · l^{k - 1}. This reduces the gap between the best lower and upper bounds from exponential to polynomial in k.
citations.title: Flashes and Rainbows in Tournaments

snippets: For a graph G, the Ramsey number r(G) is the minimum integer N such that every 2-coloring of the edges of the complete graph K N on N vertices contains a monochromatic copy of G. The existence of these numbers was famously proved by Ramsey (Ramsey, 0), while the first good quantitative bounds were proved by Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009). Since then, the field of graph Ramsey theory has flourished, and determining how r(G) depends on the graph G has become one of the most-studied questions in combinatorics

Arguably, the most important question in the field is determining the Ramsey number r(K n ) of the complete graph K n on n vertices. Here, after almost a century of only minor improvements on the standard bounds 2 n/2 ≤ r(K n ) ≤ 4 n , a significant breakthrough was recently achieved by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [5] who showed an exponentially better upper bound of (4 − ε) n for some constant ε > 0, see also [2]22]

Another prominent direction of study is to understand the Ramsey numbers of sparse graphs. In 1975, Burr and Erdős (Burr, 1973) conjectured that Ramsey numbers of graphs with bounded degeneracy are linear in their number of vertices. In 1983, Chvátal, Rödl, Szemerédi and Trotter (Chvatál et al., 1983) proved a special case of the conjecture, namely that bounded degree graphs have linear Ramsey numbers. However, proving the Burr-Erdős conjecture in full generality was very challenging, and it was only resolved by Lee in 2017 (Lee, 2015).
citations.title: Ordered Ramsey numbers of graphs with $m$ edges

snippets: A graph is $d$-degenerate if all its subgraphs have a vertex of degree at most $d$. We prove that there exists a constant $c$ such that for all natural numbers $d$ and $r$, every $d$-degenerate graph $H$ of chromatic number $r$ with $|V(H)| \ge 2^{d^22^{cr}}$ has Ramsey number at most $2^{d2^{cr}} |V(H)|$. This solves a conjecture of Burr and Erdős from 1973.
citations.title: Ramsey numbers of degenerate graphs

snippets: Ramsey theory is an area of mathematics asserting that each sufficiently large object contains a still large well-structured subobject. The foundational theorem, proved by Frank Ramsey in 1930, states that every sufficiently large graph contains a still large homogeneous subgraph, i.e. a clique or an independent set (Ramsey, 0). It is well known by a theorem of Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) and a probabilistic construction by Erdős (Erdös, 1947) that there is always a logarithmically large homogeneous set, but we cannot hope to find a larger one in general. Finding the exact base of the logarithm is one of the most difficult and important problems in Ramsey theory, which have recently witnessed a major breakthrough by the work of Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [8], which was subsequently optimized by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [20]

The celebrated Erdős-Hajnal conjecture states that for each graph H the class of H-free graphs admits the Erdős-Hajnal property (Hajnal, 1977). The conjecture is widely open in full, and was only recently resolved for all graphs on 5 vertices [25] (Chudnovsky, 2014)
Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour recently proved that graphs of bounded VC-dimensions admit the Erdős-Hajnal property [24].
citations.title: A Polynomial Ramsey Statement for Bounded VC-dimension

snippets: The Erdös–Hajnal conjecture states that for every graph H, there exists a constant δ(H)>0 such that every graph G with no induced subgraph isomorphic to H has either a clique or a stable set of size at least |V(G)|δ(H) . This article is a survey of some of the known results on this conjecture.
citations.title: The Erdös–Hajnal Conjecture—A Survey

sections.title: Current Research Directions
sections.text:
The field of structural Ramsey theory is currently experiencing significant revival and expansion, with researchers pursuing multiple interconnected directions that promise to deepen our understanding of combinatorial structures (Junge, 2022). One of the most active areas involves the sophisticated application of category theory to Ramsey problems, building on Gromov's 2015 advocacy for deeper categorical approaches and recent work by Masulovic that has created more general categorical techniques for proving Ramsey statements (Junge, 2022).

A particularly vibrant research direction focuses on big Ramsey degrees, where recent years have witnessed substantial progress in understanding infinite structures with finite big Ramsey degrees (Hubivcka et al., 2024). A remarkable pattern has emerged: in all known examples of infinite structures with finite big Ramsey degrees, there exists a single expansion called a big Ramsey structure that correctly encodes the exact big Ramsey degrees of every finite substructure simultaneously (Hubivcka et al., 2024). This observation suggests deep structural principles that researchers are actively investigating.

The connection between amalgamation and Ramsey properties continues to generate new insights, particularly through the lens of finite Ramsey degrees. Recent work has shown that for categories of finite objects with finite small Ramsey degrees, Ramsey expansions can be constructed without additional assumptions about ambient classes (Mavsulovi'c et al., 2022) (Kechris et al., 2003).

Size-Ramsey numbers represent another highly active research frontier, with considerable recent interest in improving bounds and identifying graph classes with linear size-Ramsey numbers (Allen et al., 2022). Building on the foundational result that bounded-degree graphs have linear Ramsey numbers (Liagkou et al., 2023), researchers are working to determine which graph classes achieve the optimal linear bound where the size-Ramsey number grows proportionally to the number of vertices (Allen et al., 2022).

Perhaps most ambitiously, the field is pursuing Nešetřil's program for classifying Ramsey classes, motivated by the 2005 breakthrough connecting Ramsey classes to topological dynamics (Hubivcka et al., 2025). This classification program represents a grand unifying vision that could provide systematic understanding of which classes of structures possess the Ramsey property and why (Hubivcka et al., 2025).

These research directions reflect the field's maturation into a sophisticated area that combines combinatorial, categorical, topological, and model-theoretic perspectives. The interplay between these approaches suggests that the next breakthroughs in Ramsey theory may come from unexpected connections between seemingly disparate mathematical areas.

snippets: Category theory has long been used in Ramsey theory. Leeb created a category theoretic framework for proving Ramsey statements in lecture notes that were recorded in [7] in 1973. In [3] Graham, Rothschild, and Leeb proved a Ramsey theorem for finite vector spaces with this framework. The influential Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem proved in [13], [11], [12] in the 1970's and 1980's was expressed in the language of category theory. After these results there was a shift back to the language of classes, though categorical ideas were implicit in Solecki's papers [19], [17], and [18]. In 2015 Gromov advocated for a deeper use of category theory in Ramsey theory in [5]. More recently the work of Masulovic has created more general categorical techniques to prove Ramsey statements, such as in [9]

Structural Ramsey theory was initiated by the work of Abramason-Harrington in (Abramson et al., 1978) and Nešetřil-Rödl in (Nešetřil et al., 1977), (Nešetřil et al., 1983), and (Nešetřil et al., 1989) expanded upon the Abramson and Harrington result. Recently Nešetřil and Hubička proved a version of the Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem for classes of structures with certain closure properties in (Hubička et al., 2016). This group of theorems is fundamental to structural Ramsey theory, which has seen a revival in the recent years [8], (Fox et al., 2019), (Nguyen et al., 2008), (Nešetřil, 2007), (Sokic, 2015).
citations.title: Categorical View of the Partite Lemma in Structural Ramsey Theory

snippets: In recent years, there has been much progress in the field of structural Ramsey theory, in particular in the study of big Ramsey degrees. In all known examples of infinite structures with finite big Ramsey degrees, there is in fact a single expansion of the structure, called a big Ramsey structure, which correctly encodes the exact big Ramsey degrees of every finite substructure simultaneously.
citations.title: A survey on big Ramsey structures

snippets: The intimate connection between the amalgamation property and the Ramsey property has been evident from the very beginnings of Structural Ramsey Theory in early 1970's: amalgamation lies at the heart of the partite method, one of the most powerful tools for proving the Ramsey property for a class of finite structures (see, e.g. the proof of the famous Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem (Nešetřil et al., 1977)(Nešetřil et al., 1989)). On the other hand, it is an easy by fundamental result of Nešetřil and Rödl from 1977 that every class of structures with the Ramsey property has the amalgamation property (Nešetřil et al., 1977)

In the late 1990s it was observed that many concrete classes of finite structures where a Ramsey expansion had been identified also enjoyed a weaker property of having finite Ramsey degrees [2,3,(Fouché, 1999). For Fraïssé classes, that this is not a mere coincidence was proven in one direction in (Kechris et al., 2003), who prove that classes with a Ramsey expansion have finite Ramsey degrees, and in the other by the second author in (Zucker, 2015), showing that small Ramsey degrees suffice for the existence of a Ramsey expansion. A more combinatorial proof of the same fact can be found in [11], and a reinterpretation of the latter proof in the language of category theory in (Mašulović, 2020)

In this paper we show that the assumption about the ambient class in which an ultrahomogeneous object oversees the construction is unnecessary. Imposing no additional assumptions, for each category of finite objects with finite small Ramsey degrees (the definitions are given below) we construct a Ramsey expansion.
citations.title: From Ramsey degrees to Ramsey expansions via weak amalgamation
Fraïssé Limits, Ramsey Theory, and topological dynamics of automorphism groups

snippets: Ramsey theory, an important and lively branch of combinatorics, concerns the appearance of structure in large and potentially unstructured objects. It was initiated by Ramsey's theorem, which implies that for every graph F and every number r, if N is large enough then any rcolouring of the edges of the complete graph K N on N vertices admits a monochromatic copy of F

Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp [13] combined both questions by defining the following parameter and encouraging its study. Given a graph F , the size-Ramsey number rr pF q is defined to be the minimum number of edges in a graph G such that any r-colouring of the edges EpGq of G admits a monochromatic copy of F

By a result of Chvátal, Rödl, Szemerédi and Trotter (Chvatál et al., 1983), for any fixed ∆, the Ramsey number in r colours of any n-vertex F with maximum degree at most ∆ is Opnq, and so an upper bound for these graphs is rr pF q " Opn 2 q
There has been considerable interest in improving these two bounds in recent years

Much research focused on determining graph classes for which the trivial lower bound gives the right order of magnitude for the size-Ramsey number, that is, graph classes whose graphs have size-Ramsey number linear in the number of their vertices. This was first established for paths in the 1980s by Beck [4], answering a question of Erdős.
citations.title: Partition universality for graphs of bounded degeneracy and degree

snippets: This research area was inaugurated in 1930 by Ramsey in (Ramsey, 0) in which he stated and proved the, so called, Ramsey's Theorem: for any graph H, there exists a natural number n such that for any colouring of the edges of K n (i.e. the clique on n vertices) with two colours, K n contains a monochromatic copy of H as a subgraph, not necessarily induced. The least such value n is called the Ramsey number of H and is denoted by r(H) (if H = K t , we simply write r(t))

This follows from a more general result of Chvátal, Rödl, Szemerédi and Trotter in (Chvatál et al., 1983) which states that if H is a graph on n vertices and maximum degree ∆, then the Ramsey number r(H) is bounded by c(∆)n for some constant c(∆) depending only on ∆. That is, the Ramsey number of bounded-degree graphs grows linearly in the number of vertices.
citations.title: On the existence of highly organized communities in networks of locally interacting agents

snippets: In the 1970s, structural Ramsey theory emerged as a new branch of combinatorics. This development came with the isolation of the concepts of the $\mathbf{A}$-Ramsey property and Ramsey class. Following the influential Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il-R\"odl theorem, several Ramsey classes have been identified. In the 1980s, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il, inspired by a seminar of Lachlan, discovered a crucial connection between Ramsey classes and Fra\"iss\'e classes, and, in his 1989 paper, connected the classification programme of homogeneous structures to structural Ramsey theory. In 2005, Kechris, Pestov, and Todor\v{c}evi\'c revitalized the field by connecting Ramsey classes to topological dynamics. This breakthrough motivated Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il to propose a program for classifying Ramsey classes.
citations.title: Twenty years of Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il's classification programme of Ramsey classes

question: Describe the Sunflower conjecture, progress towards a solution, and related problems.

sections.title: Introduction and Basic Definitions
sections.text:
A **sunflower** (also called a strong Δ-system) is a fundamental combinatorial structure first studied by Erdős and Rado in 1960. A sunflower with k petals is a collection of k distinct sets S₁, S₂, ..., Sₖ such that the intersection of any two sets is identical to the intersection of all sets (Mubayi et al., 2015) (Fukuyama, 2014) (Alweiss et al., 2019). This common intersection is called the **core** (denoted C), and the parts of each set that lie outside the core (Sᵢ \ C) are called the **petals**, which are pairwise disjoint (Mubayi et al., 2015) (Chao et al., 2025).

The core can be empty, meaning the sets in the sunflower are pairwise disjoint (Lagerkvist et al., 2018). An equivalent definition states that a family forms an r-sunflower if every element in the ground set appears in either no sets, exactly one set, or all r sets (Alon et al., 2020) (Chizewer, 2023).

The **Sunflower Lemma**, proved by Erdős and Rado in 1960, establishes that sunflowers must exist in sufficiently large families of sets (Alweiss et al., 2019) (Rao, 2022). Specifically, if a family contains more than k!(w-1)ᵏ sets, each of size at most k, then it must contain a sunflower with w petals (Fukuyama, 2014) (Rao, 2022) (Chao et al., 2025).

Sunflowers are closely related to **weak Δ-systems**, where only the sizes (rather than the actual contents) of pairwise intersections must be equal (Mubayi et al., 2015). Every sunflower is a weak Δ-system, but the converse is not true.

The study of sunflowers has found applications across multiple areas of theoretical computer science, including monotone circuit complexity (Fukuyama, 2014), matrix multiplication algorithms (Fukuyama, 2014) (Lovett et al., 2019), hardness of approximation, property testing (Haviv et al., 2014), and DNF compression for counting algorithms (Lovett et al., 2019).

snippets: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets such that the intersection of any two of them is the same as the common intersection C of all of them, and |C| is smaller than each of the sets

A sunflower (or strong ∆-system) with k petals is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that S i ∩ S j = C for all i = j, and S i \ C = ∅ for all i ∈ [k]. The common intersection C is called the core of the sunflower and the sets S i \ C are called the petals. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [9] proved a fundamental result regarding the existence of sunflowers in a large family of sets of uniform size, which is now referred to as the sunflower lemma. It states that if A is a family of sets of size s with |A| > s!(k − 1) s , then A contains a sunflower with k petals. Later in 1978, Erdős and Szemerédi [10] gave the following upper bound when the underlying set has n elements. Theorem 1 (Erdős, Szemerédi [10]). There exists a constant c such that if A ⊂ 2 [n] with |A| > 2 n−c √ n then A contains a sunflower with 3 petals. In the same paper, they conjectured that for n sufficiently large, the maximum number of sets in a family A ⊂ 2 [n] with no sunflowers with three petals is at most (2 − ǫ) n for some absolute constant ǫ > 0. This conjecture remains open, and is closely related to the algorithmic problem of matrix multiplication, see [1]

A longstanding conjecture due to Erdős and Szemerédi (solved recently in [7, 9]; see also [22]) was that the maximum size of a family of subsets of [n] that contains no sunflower of fixed size k > 2 is exponentially smaller than 2n as n → ∞

Similar problems have been studied for systems of sets where only the size (rather than the actual set) of pairwise intersections is fixed. A weak ∆-system of size k is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that |S i ∩ S j | = |S 1 ∩ S 2 | for all i = j. Thus, a sunflower is a weak ∆-system but not vice versa.
citations.title: Multicolour Sunflowers

snippets: A sunflower with a core Y is a family B of sets such that U ∩ U' = Y for each two different elements U and U' in B. Equivalently, B is a sunflower if U ∩ U' = ⋂V∈B V for any U, U' ∈ B such that U ≠ U'
The sunflower lemma shown by Erdös and Rado [5] states that: A family F of sets, each of cardinality at most s, includes a k-sunflower if |F| > (k-1)^s s!

Since its proof was given in 1960, it has not been known whether the sunflower bound (k − 1)^s s! can be asymptotically improved for any k and s, despite its usefulness in combinatorics and various applications [6,7]. It is conjectured that the bound can be reduced to c_k^s for a real number c_k > 0 only depending on k, which is called the sunflower conjecture

Kostochka [8] showed that the sunflower bound for k = 3 is reduced from 2^s s! to c s! log log log s / log log s s for a constant c. The case k = 3 of the sunflower conjecture is especially emphasized by Erdös [4], which other researchers also believe includes some critical difficulty
It has also been shown [9] that F of cardinality greater than k^s 1 + c^s k^-2 -s includes a k-sunflower for some c^s ∈ R+ depending only on s

With the sunflower bound (k−1)^s s!, Razborov proved an exponential lower bound on the monotone circuit complexity of the clique problem [10]. Alon and Boppana strengthened the bound [1] by relaxing the condition to be a sunflower

(Alon et al., 2012) discusses the sunflower conjecture and its variants in relation to fast matrix multiplication algorithms. Especially, it is shown in the paper that if the sunflower conjecture is true, the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture implying a faster matrix multiplication algorithm [3] does not hold.
citations.title: Asymptotic Improvement of the Sunflower Bound

snippets: A sunflower with r petals is a collection of r sets so that the intersection of each pair is equal to the intersection of all. Erdős and Rado proved the sunflower lemma: for any fixed r, any family of sets of size w, with at least about w w sets, must contain a sunflower. The famous sunflower conjecture is that the bound on the number of sets can be improved to c w for some constant c. In this paper, we improve the bound to about (logw) w.
citations.title: Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma

snippets: The Erdős-Rado sunflower lemma (Abbott et al., 1972) is a classical result in combinatorics, which states that any sufficiently large set system must contain a sunflower. A sunflower (or delta-system) is a collection of k distinct sets S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S k such that their pairwise intersections are identical, called the core. Their non-overlapping parts are the petals. The lemma gives an upper bound on the size of a set family that avoids a sunflower with k sets: |F| ď pk ´1q r r!, where r is the maximum set size. In a recent breakthrough, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang (Alweiss et al., 2019) improved the bound in the sunflower lemma significantly, and the current best-known bound was proven by Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke (Bell et al., 2020)

In recent years, significant progress has been made on several important combinatorial problems under the additional assumption of a bounded VC-dimension, such as the Erdős-Schur conjecture (Fox et al., 2019), the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture (Fox et al., 2017)[23] and the sunflower conjecture [3,(Fox et al., 2021). In particular, assuming bounded VC-dimension, Balogh, Bernshteyn, Delcourt, Ferber, and Pham [3] quantitatively strengthened the sunflower lemma.
citations.title: Uniform set systems with small VC-dimension

snippets: A sunflower (with k sets) is a collection of k sets S 1 , . . . , S k with common intersection S = S 1 ∩ . . . ∩ S k , called the core, such that for every pair i, j ∈ [k], i = j, we have S i ∩ S j = S. Note that we may have S = ∅. The sunflower conjecture (Abbott et al., 1972), in the form we will need, states that for every k there is a constant C k such that for every n, every collection of at least C n k sets of cardinality n contains a sunflower with k petals. This conjecture was the subject of the Polymath 10 collaborative mathematics project, but remains a notorious open problem. See Alon, Shpilka and Umans (Alon et al., 2012) for variations of the conjecture and connections to other problems
Furthermore, if the sunflower conjecture holds for sunflowers with k sets, then the partial k-NU language has an improved algorithm via local search

An extreme negative result, such as the conclusion that the full problem Inv(f)-SAT admits an improved algorithm only when the abstract Inv(f)problem does, would by Theorem 45 need to refute the sunflower conjecture.
citations.title: Which NP-Hard SAT and CSP Problems Admit Exponentially Improved Algorithms?

snippets:
Introduced by Erdős and Rado (Abbott et al., 1972), sunflowers (also called strong ∆-systems) have a long history of study and applications in extremal combinatorics and theoretical computer science. Recall that a family H of r distinct subsets of [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} is called a sunflower of size r if every i ∈ [n] belongs to either 0, 1 or r of the sets in H. 

Erdős and Rado famously conjectured that if F is a k-uniform family of sets (i.e., |A| = k for every A ∈ F) not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ C k , where C is a constant depending only on r. For many years, the best known upper bound was close to k! for any fixed r. A recent breakthrough due to Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [3] improved the bound to (log k) (1+o(1))k for any fixed r, but the original conjecture is still open even for r = 3. 

Seeking a bound that depends on the size n of the ground set rather than the uniformity k, Erdős and Szemerédi (Erdös et al., 1978) conjectured that if F is a family of subsets of [n] not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ c n , where c < 2 is a constant depending only on r. They showed (implicitly, made explicit by Deuber et al. (Deuber et al., 1997)) that their conjecture would follow from the Erdős-Rado conjecture. The recent solution by Ellenberg and Gijswijt (Ellenberg et al., 2017) of the cap set problem, confirmed the r = 3 case of the Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture (via a reduction due to the first author, Shpilka and Umans (Alon et al., 2012)); see also Naslund and Sawin (Naslund et al., 2016) and Hegedűs (Hegedus, 2018) for explicit bounds. But the conjecture is still open for r ≥ 4.
citations.title: Near-sunflowers and focal families

snippets: A sunflower with $r$ petals is a collection of $r$ sets over a ground set $X$ such that every element in $X$ is in no set, every set, or exactly one set. Erdős and Rado \cite{er} showed that a family of sets of size $n$ contains a sunflower if there are more than $n!(r-1)^n$ sets in the family

Erdős and Rado conjectured that a stronger bound holds than the one they proved in the initial paper. Conjecture 1.2 (Erdős and Rado [5]). Let F be an n-uniform set family. There exists some constant C = C(r) depending only on r such that F contains an r-sunflower whenever

Recently, Alweiss et al. (Alweiss et al., 2019), and subsequently Rao (Rao, 2019) and Bell et al. [2], made progress toward this bound by showing there exists some constant C such that F contains an r-sunflower whenever |F | > [Cr log(n)] n
We study the Sunflower Problem with added restrictions on the pairwise intersections
The problem of sunflowers in L-intersecting set families was first studied in (HegedHus, 2016).

snippets: A sunflower with w petals is a collection of w sets whose pairwise intersections are identical. The common intersection is called the core. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [4] proved a Ramsey theoretic result concerning sunflowers: every large collection of sets must contain a sunflower. They gave a simple inductive argument showing that every collection of more than k! · (w − 1) k sets of size at most k must contain a sunflower with w petals. There are examples with Ω(w) k sets that have no sunflowers, and they conjectured that the correct bound is O(w) k

In 2019, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang (Alweiss et al., 2019) made significant progress towards proving the sunflower conjecture. Subsequent refining by myself [13], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park [7] and Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke [3] led to the result that every collection of O(w log k) k sets of size at most k must contain a sunflower with w petals
The ideas used to prove the sunflower lemma are ultimately useful to prove the threshold vs expectation threshold conjecture, as well as the threshold vs fractional expectation threshold conjecture.
citations.title: Sunflowers: from soil to oil

snippets:
The sunflower conjecture is one of the most well-known open problems in combinatorics. An r-sunflower is a family of r sets S 1 , . . . , S r where all pairwise intersections are the same. A w-set system is a collection of sets where each set has size at most w. Erdős and Rado [ER[60] asked how large can a w-set system be, without containing an r-sunflower. They proved an upper bound of w!(r − 1) w , and conjectured that the bound can be improved.

Conjecture 1.1 (Sunflower conjecture, [ER[60]). Let r ≥ 3. There is a constant c r such that any w-set system F of size |F | ≥ c w r contains an r-sunflower. 60 years later, only lower order improvements have been achieved, and the best bounds are still of the order of magnitude of about w w for any fixed r, same as in the original theorem of Erdős and Rado. A good survey on the current bounds is [Kos[00].

Sunflowers have been useful in various areas in theoretical computer science. Some examples include monotone circuit lower bounds [Raz85,Ros[10], barriers for improved algorithms for matrix multiplication [ASU[13] and faster deterministic counting algorithms via DNF compression [GMR[13].
citations.title: From DNF compression to sunflower theorems via regularity

snippets:
A k-sunflower is a collection of k sets that have the same pairwise intersections. This notion was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado [17], and besides being of great interest in combinatorics, it found applications in several areas of computer science, e.g., circuit complexity [30,2], hardness of approximation [14], and property testing [4]. The main question regarding k-sunflowers is how large a collection of sets containing no k-sunflowers can be. It was shown in [17] that the size of any collection of subsets of size s of some universe U with no k-sunflowers is at most s! • (k − 1)^s. The classical sunflower conjecture of Erdős and Rado asserts the following.

Conjecture 1.1 (Classical Sunflower Conjecture [17]). For every k > 0 there exists a constant c_k, such that every collection of at least c_k^s subsets of size s of some universe U contains a k-sunflower.

The above conjecture is still open even for the special case of k = 3. For this case, Kostochka showed an improved upper bound of c • s! • 30^(ln ln ln s / ln ln s) for some constant c > 0 [25]

.following their definition, we say that k vectors v_1, . . . , v_k in Z_D^n form a k-sunflower if for every i ∈ [n] it holds that the ith entries (v_1)_i, . . . , (v_k)_i of the vectors are either all equal or all distinct

.It was shown in [5] that Conjecture 1.2 can be equivalently formulated in terms of sunflowers of vectors as follows.

Conjecture 1.3 (Sunflower Conjecture in Z_D^n [5]). There exist ε > 0, D_0 and n_0, such that for every D ≥ D_0 and n ≥ n_0, every collection F of vectors in Z_D^n of size |F| ≥ D^(1−ε)n contains a 3-sunflower

.Conjecture 1.4 (Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_D [5]). There exist ε > 0 and n_0, such that for every n ≥ n_0, every collection

Of special importance is the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_3, which refers to the maximum possible size of a collection of vectors in the group Z_3^n with no 3-term arithmetic progressions (or, equivalently, non-trivial triples of vectors with zero sum modulo 3). The largest known construction of such collections has cardinality c^n for c ≈ 2.217 [15]. An upper bound of 2 • 3^n/n was shown by Meshulam in [29] (see [28] for a generalization of his result), and this was recently improved by Bateman and Katz to O(3^n/n^(1+ε)) for some constant ε > 0 [6].

Given the similarity between Conjecture 1.3 and the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_D, one might guess that the latter is true for small values of D. In fact, it was observed in [5] that for every D ≥ 3, the assertion of the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_D implies Conjecture 1.3.

sections.title: The Sunflower Conjecture
sections.text:
The **Sunflower Conjecture**, formulated by Erdős and Rado in 1960, is one of the most famous open problems in combinatorics (Naslund et al., 2016) (Lovett et al., 2019). The conjecture asserts that for every fixed number of petals r ≥ 3, there exists a constant C_r such that any family of sets of size k containing at least C_r^k sets must contain an r-sunflower (Naslund et al., 2016) (Lagerkvist et al., 2018).

This conjecture is significantly stronger than the original Erdős-Rado theorem, which only guaranteed the existence of sunflowers when the family size exceeded k!(r-1)^k (Fukuyama, 2014) (Rao, 2019). The difference is exponential: the conjecture proposes a bound that grows as C^k rather than k!(k-1)^k, making it one of the most challenging problems in extremal set theory.

A related variant, the **Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture**, focuses on families of subsets of an n-element ground set. It conjectures that any 3-sunflower-free family of subsets of {1,2,...,n} has size at most c^n for some constant c < 2 (Naslund et al., 2016). The 3-sunflower case of this conjecture was resolved following the breakthrough work of Ellenberg and Gijswijt on the cap set problem (Alon et al., 2020) (Naslund et al., 2016), but the conjecture remains open for r ≥ 4 (Alon et al., 2020).

The sunflower conjecture has been the subject of intense study, including a collaborative Polymath project, yet even the case of 3-sunflowers remains unsolved (Lagerkvist et al., 2018) (Fox et al., 2021). Erdős considered this problem so important that he offered a $1000 reward for its solution (Naslund, 2022).

The conjecture also has equivalent formulations in terms of vectors over finite fields. A collection of k sets is said to form a k-sunflower, or ∆-system, if the intersection of any two sets from the collection is the same. A family of sets F is said to be k-sunflower-free if no k members form a k-sunflower, and when k = 3 we simply say that the collection F is sunflower-free. It is a longstanding conjecture that sunflower-free families must be small, and there are two natural situations in which we may ask this question. The first, and most general case, is when each set in the family has size m. Erdős and Rado made the following conjecture which is now known as the Sunflower Conjecture.

CONJECTURE 1 (Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture [5]). Let k ≥ 3, and suppose that F is a k-sunflower-free family of sets, each of size m. Then |F| ≤ Ck^m for a constant Ck > 0 depending only on k.

In their paper, Erdős and Rado [5] proved that any k-sunflower-free family of sets of size m has size at most m!(k − 1)^m, but the conjectured bound of Ck^m remains out of reach for any k ≥ 3. A k-sunflower is a collection of k sets that have the same pairwise intersections. This notion was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado [17], and besides being of great interest in combinatorics, it found applications in several areas of computer science, e.g., circuit complexity [30,2], hardness of approximation [14], and property testing [4]. The main question regarding k-sunflowers is how large a collection of sets containing no k-sunflowers can be. It was shown in [17] that the size of any collection of subsets of size s of some universe U with no k-sunflowers is at most s! • (k − 1)^s. Conjecture 1.1 (Classical Sunflower Conjecture [17]). For every k > 0 there exists a constant c_k, such that every collection of at least c_k^s subsets of size s of some universe U contains a k-sunflower.

Of special importance is the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_3, which refers to the maximum possible size of a collection of vectors in the group Z_3^n with no 3-term arithmetic progressions (or, equivalently, non-trivial triples of vectors with zero sum modulo 3). The largest known construction of such collections has cardinality c^n for c ≈ 2.217 [15]. An upper bound of 2 • 3^n/n was shown by Meshulam in [29] (see [28] for a generalization of his result), and this was recently improved by Bateman and Katz to O(3^n/n^(1+ε)) for some constant ε > 0 [6].

sections.title: Progress Towards Solutions
sections.text:
For nearly 60 years after Erdős and Rado's original 1960 result, progress on the Sunflower Conjecture was minimal (Lovett et al., 2019). The original bound of k!(r-1)^k remained essentially unchanged, with only minor improvements achieved (Fukuyama, 2014). Kostochka made some progress on the special case of 3-sunflowers, reducing the bound from 2^k k! to a slightly better expression involving logarithmic terms, but this fell far short of the conjectured C^k bound (Fukuyama, 2014).

The field experienced a major breakthrough in 2019 when Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang achieved the first substantial improvement to the sunflower bound (Alweiss et al., 2019). Their remarkable result improved the bound from approximately k^k to (log k)^k, representing an exponential improvement over the previous bounds (Alweiss et al., 2019) (Rao, 2019). Notably, they proved this result for a robust notion of sunflowers, and their bound is tight up to lower order terms (Alweiss et al., 2019).

Following this breakthrough, several researchers refined and improved upon these techniques. Rao provided a simplified proof using Shannon's entropy methods and further improvements (Rao, 2019) (Alweiss, 2020). Building on methods developed by Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan, and Park, subsequent work by Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke led to the current record bound (Buci'c et al., 2020) (Rao, 2022).

The current best known upper bound shows that every collection of O(k log r)^k sets of size at most k must contain a sunflower with r petals (Rao, 2022) (Buci'c et al., 2020). This represents the state-of-the-art progress toward the conjectured C^k bound, though the conjecture itself remains open even for the case of 3-sunflowers (Alon et al., 2020).

The techniques developed by Alweiss et al. have had remarkable applications beyond sunflowers, leading to breakthroughs in seemingly unrelated areas such as threshold phenomena and the resolution of conjectures by Talagrand and Kahn-Kalai (Park, 2023) (Park, 2023) (Frankston et al., 2019) (Pham, 2024). This unexpected connection between sunflower methods and probabilistic combinatorics demonstrates the fundamental nature of the underlying techniques (Park, 2023).

sections.title: Related Problems and Variants
sections.text:
The study of sunflowers has generated a rich collection of related problems and variants that explore different aspects of the underlying combinatorial structure:

**Weak Δ-systems and Pseudo-sunflowers**
- **Weak Δ-systems**: Collections where only the sizes (rather than actual contents) of pairwise intersections must be equal (Mubayi et al., 2015) (Naslund, 2022). Every sunflower is a weak Δ-system, but not vice versa (Mubayi et al., 2015).
- **Pseudo-sunflowers** and **near-sunflowers**: Alternative relaxations of the sunflower definition (Frankl et al., 2023).

**Sunflowers with Fixed Core Size (Turán-type problems)**
- The **Duke-Erdős problem** (1977): Finding the maximum size of a family avoiding sunflowers with a specific number of petals and fixed core size (Buci'c et al., 2020) (Bradavc et al., 2021).
- **Frankl-Füredi results**: Asymptotic bounds for sunflower-free families when the core size is fixed (Kupavskii et al., 2024) (Bradac et al., 2022).

**Sunflowers Over Finite Fields and Vector Spaces**
- **Vector sunflowers over Z_D^n**: k vectors form a sunflower if for every coordinate, the entries are either all equal or all distinct (Haviv et al., 2014).
- **Cap set connections**: The resolution of the cap set problem helped solve the 3-sunflower case of the Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture using polynomial methods (Alon et al., 2020) (Naslund et al., 2016).
- **Weak sunflower conjecture over finite fields**: Particularly important for Z_3^n in connection with 3-term arithmetic progressions (Haviv et al., 2014).

**Geometric and Structural Variants**
- **VC-dimension bounded families**: Fox et al. showed progress toward the conjecture for families with bounded Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension (Fox et al., 2021).
- **Near-sunflowers**: Families where every element belongs to either 0, 1, r-1, or r of the sets (Huang et al., 2024).
- **Sparse vector sunflowers**: Variants involving vectors with limited numbers of non-zero coordinates (Karam, 2024).

**Equivalence Results**
- Alon, Shpilka, and Umans demonstrated that the classical sunflower conjecture is equivalent to certain statements about families of vectors over finite fields (Grochow, 2018) (Alon et al., 2020) (Naslund et al., 2016).

A sunflower (or strong ∆-system) with k petals is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that S i ∩ S j = C for all i = j, and S i \ C = ∅ for all i ∈ [k]. The common intersection C is called the core of the sunflower and the sets S i \ C are called the petals. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [9] proved a fundamental result regarding the existence of sunflowers in a large family of sets of uniform size, which is now referred to as the sunflower lemma. It states that if A is a family of sets of size s with |A| > s!(k − 1) s , then A contains a sunflower with k petals. Later in 1978, Erdős and Szemerédi [10] gave the following upper bound when the underlying set has n elements. Theorem 1 (Erdős, Szemerédi [10]). There exists a constant c such that if A ⊂ 2 [n] with |A| > 2 n−c √ n then A contains a sunflower with 3 petals. In the same paper, they conjectured that for n sufficiently large, the maximum number of sets in a family A ⊂ 2 [n] with no sunflowers with three petals is at most (2 − ǫ) n for some absolute constant ǫ > 0. This conjecture remains open, and is closely related to the algorithmic problem of matrix multiplication, see [1]

A longstanding conjecture due to Erdős and Szemerédi (solved recently in [7, 9]; see also [22]) was that the maximum size of a family of subsets of [n] that contains no sunflower of fixed size k > 2 is exponentially smaller than 2n as n → ∞

Similar problems have been studied for systems of sets where only the size (rather than the actual set) of pairwise intersections is fixed. A weak ∆-system of size k is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that |S i ∩ S j | = |S 1 ∩ S 2 | for all i = j. Thus, a sunflower is a weak ∆-system but not vice versa.

A family of at least three sets is a sunflower (or a ∆-system) if every element is contained either in all of the sets, or in at most one. If a family of sets contains no sets that form a sunflower, it is called sunflower-free. This notion was introduced by Erdős and Rado [10] in 1960, and it has become one of the standard tools in extremal combinatorics [14]. Erdős and Rado conjectured that the maximum size of any sunflower-free family of k-element sets is at most c^k, for a suitable constant c > 0. This conjecture is still open; for recent progress, see [4]. 

Erdős and Szemerédi [11] studied the maximum possible size of a sunflower-free family of subsets of {1, . . ., n}. Denote this quantity by f (n) and let µ = lim f (n)^(1/n). Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that µ < 2, and this was proved by Naslund and Sawin [18], using the methods of Croot, Lev, P. Pach [6], Ellenberg and Gijswijt [8], and Tao [19]. They showed that µ < 1.89, while the best currently known lower bound, µ > 1.551, follows from a construction of Deuber et al. [7].

Erdős, Milner and Rado [9] called a family of at least three sets a weak sunflower if the intersection of any pair of them has the same size. For a survey, see Kostochka [16]. In the literature, we can also find pseudo-sunflowers [13] and near-sunflowers [3].

snippets: A family A1, . . . , Ak of distinct sets is said to be a sunflower if there exists a kernel C contained in each of the Ai such that the petals Ai \ C are disjoint. For r, k ≥ 1, let fr(k) denote the smallest natural number with the property that any family of fr(k) sets of size r contains an (r-uniform) sunflower with k petals. The celebrated Erdős-Rado theorem [15] from 1960 asserts that fr(k) is finite; in fact Erdős and Rado gave the following bounds: (k − 1) ≤ fr(k) ≤ (k − 1) r! + 1. They conjectured that for a fixed k the upper bound can be improved to fr(k) ≤ O(k)r. Despite significant efforts, a solution to this conjecture remains elusive. A recent breakthrough in this direction was obtained by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [1]. The ideas they developed to tackle this problem have found quite wide applications not only within combinatorics but also in theoretical computer science and probability theory. Their methods have since been pushed a bit further by Rao [34] (Tao [38] found a different proof of this result using Shannon entropy) and Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke [2], giving the current record of fr(k) ≤ O(k log r)r. About 45 years ago, Duke and Erdős [11] initiated the systematic investigation of a closely related problem, where one in addition fixes the size of the kernel of the sunflower. In particular, we seek the r-uniform sunflower with k petals and kernel of size t, which we will denote by S(r)t(k). Duke and Erdős asked for the minimum number of sets of size r which guarantees us to be able to find S(r)t(k). In other words, they ask for the Turán number of the sunflower S(r)t(k). Over the years this problem has been reiterated several times [7,27] including in a recent collaborative "polymath" project [33].

A k-sunflower is a collection of k sets that have the same pairwise intersections. This notion was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado [17], and besides being of great interest in combinatorics, it found applications in several areas of computer science, e.g., circuit complexity [30,2], hardness of approximation [14], and property testing [4]. The main question regarding k-sunflowers is how large a collection of sets containing no k-sunflowers can be. It was shown in [17] that the size of any collection of subsets of size s of some universe U with no k-sunflowers is at most s! • (k − 1)^s. The classical sunflower conjecture of Erdős and Rado asserts the following.

Conjecture 1.1 (Classical Sunflower Conjecture [17]). For every k > 0 there exists a constant c_k, such that every collection of at least c_k^s subsets of size s of some universe U contains a k-sunflower.

The above conjecture is still open even for the special case of k = 3. For this case, Kostochka showed an improved upper bound of c • s! • 30^(ln ln ln s / ln ln s) for some constant c > 0 [25]

snippets:
Introduced by Erdős and Rado (Abbott et al., 1972), sunflowers (also called strong ∆-systems) have a long history of study and applications in extremal combinatorics and theoretical computer science. Recall that a family H of r distinct subsets of [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} is called a sunflower of size r if every i ∈ [n] belongs to either 0, 1 or r of the sets in H. 

Erdős and Rado famously conjectured that if F is a k-uniform family of sets (i.e., |A| = k for every A ∈ F) not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ C k , where C is a constant depending only on r. For many years, the best known upper bound was close to k! for any fixed r. A recent breakthrough due to Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [3] improved the bound to (log k) (1+o(1))k for any fixed r, but the original conjecture is still open even for r = 3. 

Seeking a bound that depends on the size n of the ground set rather than the uniformity k, Erdős and Szemerédi (Erdös et al., 1978) conjectured that if F is a family of subsets of [n] not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ c n , where c < 2 is a constant depending only on r. They showed (implicitly, made explicit by Deuber et al. (Deuber et al., 1997)) that their conjecture would follow from the Erdős-Rado conjecture. The recent solution by Ellenberg and Gijswijt (Ellenberg et al., 2017) of the cap set problem, confirmed the r = 3 case of the Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture (via a reduction due to the first author, Shpilka and Umans (Alon et al., 2012)); see also Naslund and Sawin (Naslund et al., 2016) and Hegedűs (Hegedus, 2018) for explicit bounds. But the conjecture is still open for r ≥ 4.

A collection of k sets is said to form a k-sunflower, or ∆-system, if the intersection of any two sets from the collection is the same. A family of sets F is said to be k-sunflower-free if no k members form a k-sunflower, and when k = 3 we simply say that the collection F is sunflower-free. It is a longstanding conjecture that sunflower-free families must be small, and there are two natural situations in which we may ask this question. The first, and most general case, is when each set in the family has size m. Erdős and Rado made the following conjecture which is now known as the Sunflower Conjecture.

CONJECTURE 1 (Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture [5]). Let k ≥ 3, and suppose that F is a k-sunflower-free family of sets, each of size m. Then |F| ≤ Ck^m for a constant Ck > 0 depending only on k.

In their paper, Erdős and Rado [5] proved that any k-sunflower-free family of sets of size m has size at most m!(k − 1)^m, but the conjectured bound of Ck^m remains out of reach for any k ≥ 3. The second setting for upper bounds for k-sunflower-free sets concerns the case where each member of F is a subset of the same n-element set. There can be at most 2^n such subsets, and the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture states that this trivial upper bound can be improved by an exponential factor. CONJECTURE 2 (Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture [6]). Let S be a k-sunflower-free collection of subsets of {1, 2, . . . , n}. Then |S| < ck^n for some constant ck < 2 depending only on k.

In Erdős and Szemerédi's paper [6], they prove that Conjecture 2 follows from Conjecture 1 (see also [1,Theorem 2.[3]), and so it is a weaker variant of the sunflower problem

sections.title: Applications and Connections
sections.text:
The study of sunflowers has generated a rich array of applications across multiple domains of theoretical computer science and mathematics. In **circuit complexity**, sunflowers have been instrumental in proving lower bounds, with Razborov using the sunflower lemma to establish exponential lower bounds on the monotone circuit complexity of the clique problem (Fukuyama, 2014). These techniques were later strengthened by Alon and Boppana through relaxed sunflower conditions (Fukuyama, 2014).

The sunflower conjecture has deep connections to **matrix multiplication algorithms**. Research has shown that if the sunflower conjecture is true, then the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture for faster matrix multiplication algorithms does not hold (Fukuyama, 2014) (Mubayi et al., 2015). This creates a fundamental barrier where progress on sunflowers directly impacts the possibility of certain algorithmic improvements (Grochow, 2018).

In **computational complexity theory**, sunflowers have found applications in hardness of approximation, property testing, and DNF compression for counting algorithms (Haviv et al., 2014) (Lovett et al., 2019). Recent work has also connected sunflower improvements to better algorithms for constraint satisfaction problems, where refuting the sunflower conjecture would lead to improved algorithms for certain NP problems (Lagerkvist et al., 2018).

Perhaps most remarkably, the techniques developed by Alweiss et al. in their 2019 sunflower breakthrough have led to unexpected connections with **probabilistic combinatorics**. These methods were adapted by Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan, and Park to prove a fractional version of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture, which had been conjectured by Talagrand (Park, 2023) (Frankston et al., 2019). This connection is particularly striking because threshold phenomena seemingly have no relation to sunflower problems (Park, 2023).

The sunflower techniques have since been instrumental in resolving the full **Kahn-Kalai conjecture**, one of the most important problems in probabilistic combinatorics (Pham, 2024) (Park et al., 2022). Additionally, these methods contributed to resolving **Talagrand's selector process conjecture** (Pham, 2024) (Park et al._1, 2022). Recent improvements to the sunflower lemma have also enabled near-linear size bounds for certain communication complexity problems (Beame et al., 2022).

The breadth of these applications demonstrates that sunflowers represent a fundamental combinatorial structure whose understanding has far-reaching implications across theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics (Lovett et al., 2019) (Grochow, 2018).

snippets: A sunflower with a core Y is a family B of sets such that U ∩ U' = Y for each two different elements U and U' in B. Equivalently, B is a sunflower if U ∩ U' = ⋂V∈B V for any U, U' ∈ B such that U ≠ U'
The sunflower lemma shown by Erdös and Rado [5] states that: A family F of sets, each of cardinality at most s, includes a k-sunflower if |F| > (k-1)^s s!

Since its proof was given in 1960, it has not been known whether the sunflower bound (k − 1)^s s! can be asymptotically improved for any k and s, despite its usefulness in combinatorics and various applications [6,7]. It is conjectured that the bound can be reduced to c_k^s for a real number c_k > 0 only depending on k, which is called the sunflower conjecture

Kostochka [8] showed that the sunflower bound for k = 3 is reduced from 2^s s! to c s! log log log s / log log s s for a constant c. The case k = 3 of the sunflower conjecture is especially emphasized by Erdös [4], which other researchers also believe includes some critical difficulty
It has also been shown [9] that F of cardinality greater than k^s 1 + c^s k^-2 -s includes a k-sunflower for some c^s ∈ R+ depending only on s

With the sunflower bound (k−1)^s s!, Razborov proved an exponential lower bound on the monotone circuit complexity of the clique problem [10]. Alon and Boppana strengthened the bound [1] by relaxing the condition to be a sunflower
