sections.title: Recent Promising Methods and Approaches
sections.text:
To address the fundamental limitations of generative models in medical imaging, researchers have developed several promising approaches that combine the strengths of different architectures while mitigating their individual weaknesses. **Hybrid VAE-GAN models** have emerged as a compelling solution that leverages the capacity of VAEs to acquire condensed feature representations and the ability of GANs to generate high-quality synthetic images (Rguibi et al., 2023). These hybrid approaches can learn complex and structured generative models of medical imaging data while addressing challenges such as mode collapse and training instability through improved optimization algorithms and regularization techniques (Rguibi et al., 2023) (Xiao et al., 2021).

**Diffusion model optimizations** represent another major advancement, with researchers actively exploring methods to reduce the prohibitive computational costs that have limited clinical adoption. Progressive distillation, FastDPM, and DDIM variants are being developed to significantly decrease sampling time while maintaining image quality (Kebaili et al., 2023). Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) follow a two-stage process where a Variational Auto-Encoder first maps high-dimensional image data into a lower-dimensional latent space, enabling more efficient diffusion model training (Stojanovski et al., 2024) (Rombach et al., 2021). These efficiency improvements have made diffusion models more practical for medical imaging applications, with DDIM variants reframing the stochastic process as an ordinary differential equation to reduce inference steps significantly (Yazdani et al., 2025) (Song et al., 2020).

**Standardized development platforms** have addressed the complexity and reproducibility challenges that have hindered progress in medical generative modeling. The MONAI Generative Models platform extends the MONAI framework to ease development and deployment of generative models in a standardized way, reproducing state-of-the-art studies involving different architectures such as diffusion models, autoregressive transformers, and GANs (Pinaya et al., 2023).

**Advanced architectural innovations** have focused on generating high-resolution 3D medical images while preserving anatomical accuracy. Hierarchical schemes using modified UNet architectures start by synthesizing low-resolution images conditioned on text, serving as a foundation for subsequent generators to produce complete volumetric data (Xu et al., 2023). To ensure anatomical plausibility, these models provide additional guidance by generating vascular, airway, and lobular segmentation masks in conjunction with CT images (Xu et al., 2023). Memory-efficient approaches like MedLoRD use Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder Generative Adversarial Networks with 3D U-Net denoising in latent space, enabling synthesis of high-fidelity 3D volumes up to 512×512×256 resolution on 24GB GPUs without post-processing (Seyfarth et al., 2025).

**Controllable generation methods** have emerged to address the lack of spatial control in medical image synthesis. Models like XReal incorporate Anatomy and Pathology Controllers to introduce precise spatial control over anatomy and pathology location in pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models without fine-tuning (Hashmi et al., 2024). LeFusion, a lesion-focused diffusion model, redesigns diffusion learning objectives to focus on lesion areas while preserving high-fidelity backgrounds by integrating forward-diffused background contexts into the reverse diffusion process (Zhang et al., 2024).

**Specialized medical applications** have demonstrated significant clinical utility. brainSPADE3D enables 3D generative modeling for brain MRI with associated segmentations, allowing users to condition on specific pathological phenotypes and contrasts (Fernandez et al., 2023). GenerateCT represents the first approach to generating 3D medical imaging conditioned on free-form medical text prompts, demonstrating an 11% improvement in classification tasks when training on combined real and generated volumes (Liu et al._1, 2023) (Hamamci et al., 2023).

**Transfer learning and federated approaches** offer viable pathways to overcome limited medical data availability. Pre-trained generative models can be adapted to specific requirements of medical imaging through transfer learning, leveraging knowledge from existing datasets for more precise characterization (Islam et al., 2025). Multi-center studies and federated learning provide additional solutions for addressing data scarcity while maintaining privacy requirements (Islam et al., 2025).

Recent developments have also emphasized **utility-aware evaluation**, recognizing that synthetic image quality cannot be measured without performing downstream tasks. Researchers now advocate for utility-aware and explainable models for medical image synthesis that can address the shortcomings of current deep generative models and improve the applicability of synthetic images for medical classification tasks (Xing et al., 2023).

Our approach leverages the capacity of VAEs to acquire condensed feature representations, and the ability of GANs to generate high-quality synthetic images to learn an embedding that keeps high-level abstract visual qualities

VAE-GAN models are a promising approach for generating synthetic images and for performing unsupervised learning tasks in the domain of medical imaging. By combining the strengths of VAEs and GANs, VAE-GAN models are able to learn complex and structured generative models of medical imaging data, which can be used for a wide range of applications.

snippets: Face recognition is greatly improved by deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Recently, these face recognition models have been used for identity authentication in security sensitive applications. However, deep CNNs are vulnerable to adversarial patches, which are physically realizable and stealthy, raising new security concerns on the real-world applications of these models. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of face recognition models using adversarial patches based on transferability, where the attacker has limited accessibility to the target models. First, we extend the existing transfer-based attack techniques to generate transferable adversarial patches. However, we observe that the transferability is sensitive to initialization and degrades when the perturbation magnitude is large, indicating the overfitting to the substitute models. Second, we propose to regularize the adversarial patches on the low dimensional data manifold. The manifold is represented by generative models pre-trained on legitimate human face images. Using face-like features as adversarial perturbations through optimization on the manifold, we show that the gaps between the responses of substitute models and the target models dramatically decrease, exhibiting a better transferability. Extensive digital world experiments are conducted to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in the black-box setting. We apply the proposed method in the physical world as well.
citations.title: Improving Transferability of Adversarial Patches on Face Recognition with Generative Models

snippets: GANs also have their drawbacks, such as learning instability, difficulty in converging, and suffering from mode collapse (Mescheder et al., 2018), which is a state where the generator produces only a few samples. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) [18] are another type of deep generative model that has received less attention in data augmentation. VAEs outperform GANs in terms of output diversity and are free of mode collapse. However, the major problem is their tendency to often produce blurry and hazy output images. This undesirable effect is due to the regularization term in the loss function
One of the drawbacks of DMs is their high computational cost and huge sampling time

the complex structures of medical images, which encompass anatomical variation and irregular tumor shapes, may render these basic operations unsuitable, resulting in the production of irrelevant images that disrupt the logical image structure (Chlap et al., 2021), and additionally, can lead to image deformations and the generation of aberrant data that can adversely impact the model performance. One basic data augmentation operator that is not well suited for medical images is flipping images, which can sometimes cause anatomical inconsistencies [121]

VAEs may produce fuzzy images that lack important details, which can be especially problematic in medical imaging. To address this limitation, improved VAE variants have been developed, such as vector quantized VAE, which uses powerful priors to generate synthetic samples with higher coherence and fidelity. Another approach involves combining VAEs with adversarial learning to improve the level of detail in the generated images. Alternatively, GANs have been found to generate high-quality images with fine details, and can be memory-efficient due to their upsampling-only architecture. However, GANs can be difficult to train and may suffer from mode collapse. Techniques such as WGAN and minibatch discrimination can help stabilize GAN training, and increasing the size of the training set can also be effective. Diffusion models have also been shown to generate high-quality images with increased sharpness and fine details, better than previous generative models, but they require significant computational resources to train and may be less interpretable. Researchers are currently exploring ways to reduce the sampling time of diffusion models, such as with progressive distillation, FastDPM, and DDIM variants.
citations.title: Deep Learning Approaches for Data Augmentation in Medical Imaging: A Review

snippets: DDPMs still face limitations; primarily, training and generating datasets using DDPMs has a prohibitive computational expense compared to GANs for many applications and users [26]. Recent research has focused on mitigating these costs, for instance by generating images with fewer diffusion steps by more advanced Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) solvers (Song et al., 2020), architectural innovations to improve convergence rates (Jabri et al., 2022), and knowledge distillation methods to compress large diffusion models into more compact and efficient versions [29]. The most popular efficiency strategy for SOTA models is to train a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) (Rombach et al., 2021). LDMs follow a two-stage process in which a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) is first trained to map highdimensional image data into a lower-dimensional, Gaussiandistributed latent space. When the VAE has been trained, it then encodes full-resolution images into a low-resolution latent space on which the diffusion model can be trained.
citations.title: Efficient Semantic Diffusion Architectures for Model Training on Synthetic Echocardiograms

snippets: By decomposing the image formation process into a sequential application of denoising autoencoders, diffusion models (DMs) achieve state-of-the-art synthesis results on image data and beyond. Additionally, their formulation allows for a guiding mechanism to control the image generation process without retraining. However, since these models typically operate directly in pixel space, optimization of powerful DMs often consumes hundreds of GPU days and inference is expensive due to sequential evaluations. To enable DM training on limited computational resources while retaining their quality and flexibility, we apply them in the latent space of powerful pretrained autoencoders. In contrast to previous work, training diffusion models on such a representation allows for the first time to reach a near-optimal point between complexity reduction and detail preservation, greatly boosting visual fidelity. By introducing cross-attention layers into the model architecture, we turn diffusion models into powerful and flexible generators for general conditioning inputs such as text or bounding boxes and high-resolution synthesis becomes possible in a convolutional manner. Our latent diffusion models (LDMs) achieve new state of the art scores for image inpainting and class-conditional image synthesis and highly competitive performance on various tasks, including unconditional image generation, text-to-image synthesis, and super-resolution, while significantly reducing computational requirements compared to pixel-based DMs.
citations.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

snippets: Deep generative models have shown promising results in various medical applications, enabling more robust training for machine learning models. Early generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Treat et al., 2018) have been widely used for medical image synthesis across modalities, including echocardiographic imaging (Tiago et al., 2024)

Despite generating high-quality images, GANs often lack diversity and suffer from training instability and mode collapse without careful tuning (Nichol et al., 2021). To address these limitations, diffusion models, particularly Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) (Ho et al., 2020), have emerged as a powerful alternative
their practical adoption is hindered by long inference times

Diffusion models incorporate various conditioning mechanisms for enhanced control. Prompt-based conditioning, like Latent Diffusion Models (LDM) (Rombach et al., 2021), has been applied to Breast MRI and head CT synthesis (Song et al., 2023), while mask-or image-based conditioning, as in ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023), has been used for colon polyp synthesis, showcasing their flexibility in medical imaging. Building on these advancements, diffusion models have also been optimized for efficiency. Deterministic variants like DDIM [23] reframe the stochastic process as an ordinary differential equation (ODE), significantly reducing inference steps while maintaining performance.
citations.title: Flow Matching for Medical Image Synthesis: Bridging the Gap Between Speed and Quality

snippets: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) have achieved high quality image generation without adversarial training, yet they require simulating a Markov chain for many steps to produce a sample. To accelerate sampling, we present denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIMs), a more efficient class of iterative implicit probabilistic models with the same training procedure as DDPMs. In DDPMs, the generative process is defined as the reverse of a Markovian diffusion process. We construct a class of non-Markovian diffusion processes that lead to the same training objective, but whose reverse process can be much faster to sample from. We empirically demonstrate that DDIMs can produce high quality samples $10 \times$ to $50 \times$ faster in terms of wall-clock time compared to DDPMs, allow us to trade off computation for sample quality, and can perform semantically meaningful image interpolation directly in the latent space.
citations.title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models

snippets: However, due to the complexity of these models, their implementation and reproducibility can be difficult. This complexity can hinder progress, act as a use barrier, and dissuade the comparison of new methods with existing works

The rising popularity of medical generative models has sparked a surge in new terms, concepts, techniques, architectures, and metrics (Chen et al., 2022)[25]. However, this field is accompanied by challenges, including the use of various quality evaluation metrics and the complexity of the models. These issues can hinder progress and the implementation of these models

Our platform reproduces state-of-art studies in a standardised way involving different architectures (such as diffusion models, autoregressive transformers, and GANs), and provides pre-trained models for the community.

snippets: While diffusion-based generative models are increasingly used in medical imaging, current state-of-the-art approaches are limited to low-resolution outputs and underutilize radiology reports' abundant information
expanding text-guided generation to high-resolution 3D images poses significant memory and anatomical detail-preserving challenges

To enhance the image resolution for generative models, increasing the voxel count within a fixed field of view is memory-intensive (Sun et al., 2020). Synthesizing 3D volumetric images at high resolutions (e.g., 256 × 256 × 256) demands substantial memory since the neural network must store intermediate activations for backpropagation

Although GANs (Sun et al., 2020)- [9] and conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (cDPMs) [10]- [12] have set benchmarks in volumetric medical imaging synthesis, each has its limitations. GANs, despite their inference efficiency, can compromise sample diversity and sometimes produce anatomically implausible artifacts. Conversely, diffusion models, built to boost sample diversity through iterative denoising, grapple with memory constraints, primarily due to their resource-intensive 3D attention UNet. The iterative denoising coupled with the sequential sub-volume generation in cDPMs makes them timeintensive at the inference stage. As a result, many diffusion models are relegated to 2D or low-resolution volumetric applications

Addressing the memory issue, we introduce a hierarchical scheme that uses a modified UNet architecture. We start by synthesizing low-resolution images conditioned on the text, serving as a foundation for subsequent generators for complete volumetric data. To ensure the anatomical plausibility of the generated samples, we provide further guidance by generating vascular, airway, and lobular segmentation masks in conjunction with the CT images.
citations.title: MedSyn: Text-Guided Anatomy-Aware Synthesis of High-Fidelity 3-D CT Images

snippets: Medical imaging data is high-dimensional, making it difficult for generative models to operate efficiently with limited GPU resources. Some approaches downsample data to capture global structures (Peng et al., 2022)(Dorjsembe et al., 2023) but risk losing fine-grained details critical for diagnosis, while others apply post-processing techniques (Guo et al., 2024) that may introduce artifacts. Additionally, many studies rely on high-end GPUs that are often unavailable in clinical environments, creating a gap between research and practical implementation (Guo et al., 2024)(Xu et al., 2023)

current state-of-the-art methods are often impractical for computational resource-constrained healthcare environments. These models rely on data sub-sampling, raising doubts about their feasibility and real-world applicability. Furthermore, many of these models are evaluated on quantitative metrics that alone can be misleading in assessing the image quality and clinical meaningfulness of the generated images

MedLoRD uses Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder Generative Adversial Networks (VQ-VAE GANs) for encoding and a 3D U-Net for image denoising in the latent space. Leveraging a streamlined VQ-VAE design, memory-efficient attention mechanisms, and a lightweight conditioning module, MedLoRD can be trained effectively on small datasets and synthesizes high-fidelity 3D volumes up to 512×512×256 in resolution on 24GB GPUs, without requiring post-processing.
citations.title: MedLoRD: A Medical Low-Resource Diffusion Model for High-Resolution 3D CT Image Synthesis

snippets: However, they continue to grapple with hallucination challenges and the generation of anatomically inaccurate outputs. These limitations are mainly due to the reliance on textual inputs and lack of spatial control over the generated images, hindering the potential usefulness of such models in real-life settings

XReal, a novel controllable diffusion model for generating realistic chest X-ray images through precise anatomy and pathology location control. Our lightweight method comprises an Anatomy Controller and a Pathology Controller to introduce spatial control over anatomy and pathology in a pre-trained Text-to-Image Diffusion Model, respectively, without fine-tuning the model.
citations.title: XReal: Realistic Anatomy and Pathology-Aware X-ray Generation via Controllable Diffusion Model

snippets: However, a persistent challenge for these methods is preserving anatomically accurate backgrounds alongside the lesions. In medical imaging, the background must respect the anatomical structure of the human body, which makes generating realistic backgrounds significantly more difficult than synthesizing isolated lesions, particularly in large-scale 3D images. While recent studies (Hamamci et al., 2024;Peng et al., 2024) have begun to address large-scale 3D medical image generation, these methods often require significant computational resources and extensive data. Another limitation of current methods is the lack of explicit control when generating image-mask pairs. Typically, both the lesion and its corresponding mask are generated simultaneously, without explicit constraints linking the two. This results in limited control over key lesion properties, such as texture, size, location, and alignment between the image and mask. The absence of high-quality background preservation and fine control over these properties hinders the scalability and effectiveness, negatively impacting the performance of downstream tasks such as segmentation

Inspired by diffusion-based image inpainting, we propose LeFusion, a lesion-focused diffusion model. By redesigning the diffusion learning objectives to focus on lesion areas, we simplify the learning process and improve control over the output while preserving high-fidelity backgrounds by integrating forward-diffused background contexts into the reverse diffusion process.
citations.title: LeFusion: Controllable Pathology Synthesis via Lesion-Focused Diffusion Models

Moreover, many of the proposed generative MRI models lack the ability to generate arbitrary modalities due to the absence of explicit contrast conditioning. These limitations prevent the user from adjusting the contrast and content of the images and obtaining more generalisable data for training task-specific models

In recent years, there has been an increased interest in using these models for data augmentation and synthetic data sharing, using architectures such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) or diffusion models (DMs)

we propose brainSPADE3D, a 3D generative model for brain MRI and associated segmentations, where the user can condition on specific pathological phenotypes and contrasts. The proposed joint imaging-segmentation generative model is shown to generate high-fidelity synthetic images and associated segmentations, with the ability to combine pathologies.

snippets: However, these approaches are limited, as these generative architectures are typically restricted to synthesizing imaging data in a specific modality, anatomy, and/or pathology. Furthermore, the generated imaging data may lack semantic segmentation, which could provide further downstream utility

A promising paradigm that has emerged is the use of generative adversarial networks (GANs) (11) to create synthetic medical images for the training of machine learning models (Schütte et al., 2020)(13)(Frid-Adar et al., 2018)(Guo et al., 2023)(Skandarani et al., 2021)(Gonzales et al., 2023)

Gao et al. developed SyntheX, a framework for developing generalizable AI algorithms from annotated computed tomography (CT), to generate synthetic X-ray images for model training and achieved comparable or better performance than CycleGAN (18) and other models trained directly on real data in three downstream clinical tasks (hip imaging segmentation, surgical robotic tool detection, and COVID-19 lesion segmentation) (19). Guo et al. proposed MedGAN, a GAN architecture using Wasserstein loss as a convergence metric, which was used to generate medical images for few-shot learning models on various disease classification and lesion localization datasets (Guo et al., 2023). Gheorghiță et al. used a GauGAN model (20) to generate synthetic short-axis cardiac Cine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans for convolutional neural network (CNN) pretraining, which significantly improved cardiac function quantification (21).
citations.title: RadImageGAN - A Multi-modal Dataset-Scale Generative AI for Medical Imaging

snippets: GenerateCT, the first approach to generating 3D medical imaging conditioned on free-form medical text prompts, incorporates a text encoder and three key components: a novel causal vision transformer for encoding 3D CT volumes, a text-image transformer for aligning CT and text tokens, and a text-conditional super-resolution diffusion model. Without directly comparable methods in 3D medical imaging, we benchmarked GenerateCT against cutting-edge methods, demonstrating its superiority across all key metrics. Importantly, we evaluated GenerateCT's clinical applications in a multi-abnormality classification task. First, we established a baseline by training a multi-abnormality classifier on our real dataset. To further assess the model's generalization to external data and performance with unseen prompts in a zero-shot scenario, we employed an external set to train the classifier, setting an additional benchmark. We conducted two experiments in which we doubled the training datasets by synthesizing an equal number of volumes for each set using GenerateCT. The first experiment demonstrated an 11% improvement in the AP score when training the classifier jointly on real and generated volumes. The second experiment showed a 7% improvement when training on both real and generated volumes based on unseen prompts. Moreover, GenerateCT enables the scaling of synthetic training datasets to arbitrary sizes. As an example, we generated 100,000 3D CTs, fivefold the number in our real set, and trained the classifier exclusively on these synthetic CTs. Impressively, this classifier surpassed the performance of the one trained on all available real data by a margin of 8%. Last, domain experts evaluated the generated volumes, confirming a high degree of alignment with the text prompt. Access our code, model weights, training data, and generated data at https://github.com/ibrahimethemhamamci/GenerateCT
citations.title: GenerateCT: Text-Conditional Generation of 3D Chest CT Volumes

snippets: Some of those challenges are the very wide dynamic range of lesion uptake, benign uptake in organs that may be adjacent to sites of disease, insufficient large datasets for training AI models, as well as artifacts in the images

To address training instabilities, commonly associated with GAN and VAE, stabilization techniques such as spectral normalization or the application of Wasserstein loss have shown promise [68,82]. These methods can help reduce issues like mode collapse and improve the diversity of synthetic images, as demonstrated in advanced GAN variants outlined in Table 1

By leveraging knowledge from existing datasets, these models can be fine-tuned to achieve more precise characterization of individual lesions, thereby supporting personalized treatment decisions. Multi-center studies and federated learning offer two other viable pathways to overcome the challenges associated with limited PSMA-PET image data availability [80]81]

the development of hybrid models that combine the strengths of different generative AI architectures, such as integrating GANs with VAEs or incorporating attention mechanisms, can enhance model performance by focusing on clinically critical regions of interest within the images (Zhao et al., 2022).

snippets: Additionally, diffusion models required a large amount of GPU resources for training and optimization, and their inference time increased dramatically with image resolution. While our work demonstrated a high utility of diffusion model synthesized medical images, the lack of fidelity and high computational costs raise questions about their real-world application in medical image synthesis for data augmentation in high-resolution medical image classification tasks
Furthermore, we found that metrics used to evaluate the quality of synthetic images were questionable, as images with high-quality scores may have low utility for downstream tasks

Our study demonstrates that synthetic image utility cannot be measured without performing downstream tasks. Rather than blindly using synthesized images from deep generative models, we propose the development of utility-aware and explainable models for medical image synthesis. question: What are the key challenges in designing lightweight computer vision models for real-time object detection on resource-constrained IoT devices?

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: The rapid growth of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has created strong demand for computer vision models that can run directly on edge devices with limited computational resources <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Unlike traditional computer vision systems that rely on powerful cloud servers or desktop GPUs, IoT devices such as smart cameras, drones, and embedded sensors must perform object detection using minimal processing power, memory, and battery life <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This shift toward edge computing brings unique technical challenges that require fundamental changes in how we design and optimize neural networks <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The core difficulty lies in maintaining acceptable detection accuracy while meeting strict constraints on model size, inference speed, and energy consumption <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. These requirements often conflict with each other, as more accurate models typically need more parameters and computations, leading to slower performance and higher power usage <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Successfully addressing these challenges is critical for enabling widespread deployment of intelligent vision systems in real-world IoT applications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Hardware and Resource Constraints
sections.text:
The fundamental hardware limitations of IoT devices create the most significant barriers to deploying object detection models at the edge. Microcontrollers typically have extremely limited on-chip memory ranging from 100-320 KB SRAM and flash storage between 256 KB-1 MB, requiring the entire neural network model with its weight parameters and code to fit within these small memory budgets (Chowdhery et al., 2019). Beyond storage constraints, the temporary memory buffer required to store input and output activations during computation must not exceed the available SRAM (Chowdhery et al., 2019).

Processing power represents another critical bottleneck, as edge devices have significantly fewer computational resources compared to server systems. Modern server-grade CPUs feature 32 cores while the latest edge devices have only 6 cores with substantially lower base clock speeds (Kim et al., 2025). This computational gap becomes particularly problematic when considering that traditional object detection networks like YOLO and R-CNN have extensive weight parameters - for example, processing a 416×416 image with YOLOv4 involves managing over 60 million parameters during inference (Setyanto et al., 2024) (Redmon et al., 2015).

Power consumption adds another layer of complexity, as many edge devices operate on restricted electricity sources such as batteries rather than wall power (Kim et al., 2025) (Sah et al., 2024). The combination of limited battery life and the need for continuous operation creates strict energy budgets that further constrain the computational complexity of deployable models (Chowdhery et al., 2019) (Lazarevich et al., 2023). These hardware realities necessitate the development of specialized object detection models that can achieve optimal trade-offs between accuracy and resource utilization (Lazarevich et al., 2023) (Boyle et al., 2023).

snippets: The two key challenges in deploying neural networks on microcontrollers are the low memory footprint and the limited battery life

Typical microcontrollers have extremely limited on-chip memory (100-320 KB SRAM) and flash storage (256 KB-1 MB). The entire neural network model with its weight parameters and code has to fit within the small memory budget of flash storage. Further, the temporary memory buffer required to store the input and output activations during computation must not exceed the SRAM. Thus, we need to design tiny vision models that achieve high accuracy on the typical microcontroller vision use-cases and fit within these constraints.

snippets: We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance. Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared to state-of-the-art detection systems, YOLO makes more localization errors but is less likely to predict false positives on background. Finally, YOLO learns very general representations of objects. It outperforms other detection methods, including DPM and R-CNN, when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork.

sections.title: Model Size and Computational Complexity
sections.text:
Traditional object detection networks create significant deployment barriers due to their massive parameter counts and computational requirements. Models like YOLOv4 with CSPDarknet53 backbone involve managing over 60 million parameters during inference when processing a 416×416 image, far exceeding the memory and processing capabilities of typical edge devices (Setyanto et al., 2024). These extensive weight parameters in networks such as Regional Convolutional Neural Network (RCNN) and You Only Look Once (YOLO) lead to high demands on memory and computing resources that edge devices simply cannot support (Setyanto et al., 2024) (Li et al., 2021).

The computational intensity of deep neural networks makes direct application to resource-constrained devices extremely difficult (Kang et al., 2022). Even state-of-the-art models that achieve high detection accuracy typically require extensive computational resources, posing major challenges for real-world deployment on resource-constrained edge devices (Nguyen et al., 2024) (Chen et al., 2025). The complexity extends beyond just parameter count - current object detection algorithm models are becoming increasingly complex, with networks requiring large amounts of data and multiple GPUs for training, creating significant resource waste and deployment difficulties (You, 2022).

Existing approaches to address these challenges have significant limitations. Direct deployment of complex models like YOLOv8 on IoT embedded devices presents major challenges, especially for real-time detection tasks (Chen et al., 2025). Lightweight object detectors that use architectures like MobileNet or ShuffleNet pre-trained on classification datasets result in poor network structure flexibility and are not suitable for specific scenarios (Li et al., 2021). Even miniaturized algorithms designed to cope with computationally demanding models still need further optimization to fit edge device deployment environments, and both lightweight networks and pruning approaches encounter the persistent challenge of accuracy loss after optimization (Hua et al., 2024).

The deployment process itself adds complexity, as well-designed networks that work in laboratory environments require extensive testing and tuning to ensure effectiveness on edge devices (More et al., 2025). Parameters and networks must be compiled and quantified before deployment, and certain innovative modules or network layers often cannot be developed due to hardware devices' limited instruction sets and basic operators, reducing network adaptability (More et al., 2025).

sections.title: Accuracy vs Efficiency Trade-offs
sections.text:
The fundamental trade-off between accuracy and efficiency represents one of the most persistent challenges in deploying object detection models on resource-constrained devices. Contemporary lightweight algorithms like NanoDet and YOLOX-Nano have been specifically designed for resource-limited devices, but their performance demonstrates the severity of this trade-off (Su et al., 2023). While these models can achieve real-time performance of 30fps+ on high-end mobile chipsets, their frame rates drop significantly to around 10fps on low-cost hardware platforms like Raspberry Pi, falling short of ideal real-time performance requirements (Su et al., 2023).

The accuracy penalty for achieving computational efficiency is substantial and measurable across benchmark datasets. For instance, YOLOX-M achieves an average precision of 46.4 on the COCO object detection dataset, while its lightweight counterpart YOLOX-Nano achieves only 25.3 average precision - representing an approximately 1.8x performance gap (Su et al., 2023). This pattern is consistent across different approaches to model compression, where both lightweight networks and pruning methods encounter persistent challenges of accuracy loss after optimization (Hua et al., 2024).

The challenge extends beyond simple parameter reduction, as existing lightweight object detectors that use architectures like MobileNet or ShuffleNet pre-trained on classification datasets result in poor network structure flexibility and are not suitable for specific scenarios (Li et al., 2021). Even when researchers attempt to address speed and efficiency requirements through architectures like SSD and YOLOv3-tiny, they must compromise some accuracy for faster processing (Alsharabi, 2023). The core difficulty lies in designing lightweight neural architectures that can achieve both fast inference and high performance simultaneously (Ye et al., 2023).

This trade-off is further complicated by the fact that resource constraints in embedded systems commonly require object detection models with lighter computational footprints, which can result in occasional but significant reductions in accuracy (Qiu et al., 2024). Efforts to reduce parameters and computational burden often fail to achieve a balance between precision and efficiency, either sacrificing detection accuracy or failing to significantly improve computational efficiency without losing accuracy (Fang et al., 2024). Additionally, lightweight model designs frequently compromise feature extraction capabilities, reducing overall robustness particularly in complex scenes with background noise, varying lighting conditions, and occlusions (Yang et al., 2025).

sections.title: Real-time Performance Requirements
sections.text:
The growing demand for real-time object detection capabilities on resource-constrained IoT devices creates significant performance challenges that extend beyond simple model optimization (Saidani, 2023). Unlike traditional applications where detection can be performed offline, IoT applications require algorithms that can process images and video streams in real-time while operating within strict resource limitations (You, 2022). This requirement becomes particularly challenging because the position and size of objects in real-time environments are constantly changing, significantly increasing computational complexity (You, 2022).

Current lightweight algorithms demonstrate the substantial gap between theoretical capabilities and practical performance on resource-constrained hardware. While contemporary algorithms like NanoDet and YOLOX-Nano achieve real-time performance of 30+ fps on high-end mobile chipsets, their frame rates drop dramatically to around 10fps on low-cost platforms like Raspberry Pi, falling significantly short of ideal real-time requirements (Su et al., 2023). This performance degradation highlights how hardware limitations directly impact the ability to maintain consistent real-time processing speeds across different deployment scenarios.

The computational intensity of deep learning methodologies poses fundamental challenges for achieving real-time functionality, as swift frame processing is essential but conflicts with the resource demands of accurate detection models (Alsharabi, 2023). To address speed requirements, researchers have developed architectures like SSD and YOLOv3-tiny, but these solutions compromise detection accuracy for faster processing (Alsharabi, 2023). The challenge is further complicated by memory limitations and power consumption constraints, as edge devices must balance real-time performance requirements with battery life and processing capabilities (Toan et al., 2024).

Small object detection adds another layer of complexity to real-time requirements, as detection heads must scan numerous positions on image feature maps, creating extremely demanding computational requirements for lightweight detectors (Chen et al., 2023). To reduce computational costs, many systems downscale input images and perform detection on small feature maps, but this approach sacrifices detection performance for small objects, creating a fundamental tension between real-time processing speed and detection capability (Chen et al., 2023). Successfully balancing accuracy, processing speed, and energy consumption remains a critical challenge that researchers and industries must address when selecting appropriate models and edge devices for deployment (Alqahtani et al., 2024).

sections.title: Small Object Detection Challenges
sections.text:
Small object detection represents one of the most challenging aspects of computer vision on IoT devices due to fundamental limitations in how these objects appear in images and how neural networks process them. Small objects are only covered by very few pixels, making it difficult to generate distinctive features necessary for accurate identification (Boyle et al., 2023). This limited pixel coverage significantly inhibits the ability of object detectors to extract meaningful information, creating a substantial signal-to-noise ratio problem (Boyle et al., 2024).

The architectural design of convolutional neural networks creates additional barriers for small object detection on resource-constrained devices. Striding operations in CNNs can result in small objects disappearing completely in the feature maps, effectively removing them from the detection pipeline (Boyle et al., 2023) (Boyle et al., 2024). This problem is compounded by the computational requirements, as small object detection requires the detection head to scan a large number of positions on image feature maps, which is extremely hard for computation- and energy-efficient lightweight generic detectors (Chen et al., 2023).

The trade-offs required for IoT deployment further worsen small object detection performance. To reduce computation cost, lightweight detectors usually downscale the input image by a large ratio and perform object detection on small feature maps (Chen et al., 2023). While this approach helps reduce computational demands, small feature maps have no detailed information and poor positional resolution, causing previous lightweight detectors to have very limited ability to detect small objects (Chen et al., 2023). The detectors sacrifice the detection performance of small objects for high efficiency, creating a fundamental tension between resource constraints and detection capability.

Memory limitations add another layer of complexity to small object detection on IoT devices. High-resolution images that could improve small object detection exceed the typical 1 MB of flash memory available on low power microcontrollers - for example, RGB images with 8-bit color depth and 577×577 pixel resolution already surpass this memory limit (Boyle et al., 2024) (Lin et al., 2021). The limited computational budget on embedded processors results in high execution latency of multiple seconds for processing even a single image (Boyle et al., 2024) (Lin et al., 2021), making real-time small object detection extremely challenging. Additionally, most publicly available datasets display a bias towards large objects, which adversely affects the usefulness of transfer learning - an important tool for developing models for specific use cases with limited datasets (Boyle et al., 2023).

snippets: Small object detection requires the detection head to scan a large number of positions on image feature maps, which is extremely hard for computation- and energy-efficient lightweight generic detectors
the inference procedure of advanced detection models costs massive computational resources, which makes them hard to be applied on resource-constrained mobile or edge devices
To reduce the computation cost, they usually downscale the input image by a large ratio and perform object detection on small feature maps

Performing object detection with small input images and on small feature maps is helpful to reducing computation cost. However, small feature maps have no detailed information and poor positional resolution. Previous lightweight detectors have very limited ability to detect small objects. They sacrifice the detection performance of small objects for high efficiency
HR feature maps significantly improve the small object detection ability but also bring much more computation cost.

snippets: Tiny deep learning on microcontroller units (MCUs) is challenging due to the limited memory size. We find that the memory bottleneck is due to the imbalanced memory distribution in convolutional neural network (CNN) designs: the first several blocks have an order of magnitude larger memory usage than the rest of the network. To alleviate this issue, we propose a generic patch-by-patch inference scheduling, which operates only on a small spatial region of the feature map and significantly cuts down the peak memory. However, naive implementation brings overlapping patches and computation overhead. We further propose network redistribution to shift the receptive field and FLOPs to the later stage and reduce the computation overhead. Manually redistributing the receptive field is difficult. We automate the process with neural architecture search to jointly optimize the neural architecture and inference scheduling, leading to MCUNetV2. Patch-based inference effectively reduces the peak memory usage of existing networks by 4-8x. Co-designed with neural networks, MCUNetV2 sets a record ImageNet accuracy on MCU (71.8%), and achieves>90% accuracy on the visual wake words dataset under only 32kB SRAM. MCUNetV2 also unblocks object detection on tiny devices, achieving 16.9% higher mAP on Pascal VOC compared to the state-of-the-art result. Our study largely addressed the memory bottleneck in tinyML and paved the way for various vision applications beyond image classification.
citations.title: MCUNetV2: Memory-Efficient Patch-based Inference for Tiny Deep Learning

sections.title: Deployment and Optimization Challenges
sections.text:
The deployment of object detection models on resource-constrained IoT devices requires sophisticated optimization strategies that address multiple competing requirements simultaneously. Creating efficient systems that are computationally efficient, consume lower power, and counter hardware limitations without compromising computer vision quality represents one of the greatest challenges in this field (Walambe et al., 2021). Researchers have proposed various optimization methods including compression of deep learning models, reducing computational complexity, knowledge distillation, quantization, network pruning, and efficient network design (Walambe et al., 2021) (Plastiras et al., 2020).

A fundamental challenge lies in achieving the dual requirements of low computational costs and high accuracy rates, particularly given that many IoT devices have limited processing power and memory (Ni, 2023) (Fang et al., 2020). Current optimization approaches face persistent limitations where efforts to reduce parameters and computational burden often sacrifice detection accuracy or fail to significantly improve computational efficiency without losing accuracy (Fang et al., 2024). This creates a fundamental tension where existing models are often not fully optimized for specific terminal devices, limiting their deployment capabilities on resource-constrained systems (Fang et al., 2024).

The deployment process itself introduces substantial technical barriers beyond model optimization. Well-designed networks that function effectively in laboratory environments require extensive testing and tuning to ensure effectiveness on edge devices (More et al., 2025). Parameters and networks must be compiled and quantified before deployment, but hardware devices' limited instruction sets and basic operators often prevent the development of certain innovative modules or network layers, reducing network adaptability and making deployment more difficult (More et al., 2025).

The complexity extends to balancing multiple design aspects that include appropriate algorithm design, architecture simplification techniques, power efficiency optimization, and edge-specific metrics such as cost and model size versus resource availability (Hozhabr et al., 2025). Traditional CNNs with their complicated structures and large parameter counts are frequently overly resource-intensive, leading to long inference times and excessive energy usage that reduces their practical utility in applications requiring real-time processing and low-latency responses (More et al., 2025). Successfully addressing these deployment challenges requires efficient model compression techniques such as network pruning and quantization to maintain accuracy while reducing computational demand (Hozhabr et al., 2025).

snippets: Creating efficient systems that are computationally efficient, consume lower power, and counter the limitations of hardware without compromising the quality of the computer vision results is one of the greatest challenges faced while designing self-driving cars. Researchers have proposed optimizing object detection through different methods, with the compression of deep learning models, reducing the computational complexity of models, and knowledge distillation among these numerous methods. Creating lightweight CNN architectures has been the focus of many works, including some state-of-the-art detectors like AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and hybrid approaches that achieve efficiency by combining feature extractors with neural networks (Girshick, 2015). Quantization [50], network pruning [51], compression [52], and efficient network design [53] were proposed for computer vision tasks on resource-constrained devices (Plastiras et al., 2020).
citations.title: Lightweight Object Detection Ensemble Framework for Autonomous Vehicles in Challenging Weather Conditions

snippets: Embedded visual AI is a growing trend in applications requiring low latency, real-time decision support, increased robustness and security. Visual object detection, a key task in visual data analytics, has enjoyed significant improvements in terms of capabilities and accuracy due to the emergence of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). However, such complex paradigms require heavy computational resources that prevent their deployment on resource-constrained devices, and in particular, impose significant constraints in possible hardware accelerators geared towards such applications. In this work therefore, we investigate how a combination of techniques can lead to efficient visual AI pipelines for resource-constrained object detection. In particular we leverage an efficient search strategy based on a combination of pre-processing mechanisms, that reduce the processing demands of deep network as a counter measure for potential accuracy reduction caused by quantization. The proposed approach enables the detection of objects in higher resolution frames using quantized models, while maintaining the accuracy of full-precision CNN-based object detectors. We illustrate the impact on the accuracy and average processing time using quantization techniques and different tiling approaches on efficient object detection architectures; as a case study, we focus on Unmanned-Aerial- Vehicles (UAVs). Through the proposed methodology, hardware accelerator demands are thereby reduced, leading to both performance benefits and associated power savings.
citations.title: Efficient Embedded Deep Neural-Network-based Object Detection Via Joint Quantization and Tiling

snippets: One major challenge is the requirement for low computational costs and high accuracy rates (Fang et al., 2020)(Wang et al., 2021). Many IoT devices have limited processing power and memory, making it necessary to develop lightweight deep-learning algorithms that can achieve high accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, the lack of publicly available datasets specifically designed for IoT Smart Shop Surveillance Systems poses another challenge for researchers.

snippets: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown prominent performance in the field of object detection. However, DNNs usually run on powerful devices with high computational ability and sufficient memory, which have greatly limited their deployment for constrained environments such as embedded devices. YOLO is one of the state-of-the-art DNN-based object detection approaches with good performance both on speed and accuracy and Tiny-YOLO-V3 is its latest variant with a small model that can run on embedded devices. In this paper, Tinier-YOLO, which is originated from Tiny-YOLO-V3, is proposed to further shrink the model size while achieving improved detection accuracy and real-time performance. In Tinier-YOLO, the fire module in SqueezeNet is appointed by investigating the number of fire modules as well as their positions in the model in order to reduce the number of model parameters and then reduce the model size. For further improving the proposed Tinier-YOLO in terms of detection accuracy and real-time performance, the connectivity style between fire modules in Tinier-YOLO differs from SqueezeNet in that dense connection is introduced and fine designed to strengthen the feature propagation and ensure the maximum information flow in the network. The object detection performance is enhanced in Tinier-YOLO by using the passthrough layer that merges feature maps from the front layers to get fine-grained features, which can counter the negative effect of reducing the model size. The resulting Tinier-YOLO yields a model size of 8.9MB (almost $4\times $ smaller than Tiny-YOLO-V3) while achieving 25 FPS real-time performance on Jetson TX1 and an mAP of 65.7% on PASCAL VOC and 34.0% on COCO. Tinier-YOLO alse posses comparable results in mAP and faster runtime speed with smaller model size and BFLOP/s value compared with other lightweight models like SqueezeNet SSD and MobileNet SSD.

sections.title: Environmental and Data Quality Issues
sections.text:
The significant mismatch between training data quality and real-world deployment conditions creates substantial challenges for object detection on IoT devices. Most computer vision applications that use deep learning on constrained devices come from IoT or robotics fields where low-quality cameras are used to capture input images in real time, while most pretrained models typically undergo training on high-quality image datasets (Kamath et al., 2024). This fundamental disconnect means that low-quality, noisy, or blurry images captured with resource-constrained devices could possibly have a negative impact on the models' performance (Kamath et al., 2024).

The problem stems from multiple sources in existing training datasets. Images in public datasets are often taken using high-resolution cameras, which differ significantly from the low-resolution noisy images adopted in real-time constrained device applications, and the processed and improved images that were used to train these models are usually unavailable (Kamath et al., 2024). Additionally, due to the enormous volume of large-scale datasets, crowd-sourcing data annotations often prove to be the only possible option, which can cause several types of issues with annotation consistency and accuracy that could be a primary reason why these models struggle to achieve acceptable accuracy on constrained deployments (Kamath et al., 2024).

Real-world environmental conditions add another layer of complexity beyond image quality issues. Robust detection in complex scenes with background noise, varying lighting conditions, and occlusions is difficult to achieve (Yang et al., 2025). These challenging conditions are particularly problematic for lightweight models, as their designs frequently compromise feature extraction capabilities, reducing overall robustness (Yang et al., 2025). The combination of poor image quality from low-cost sensors and harsh environmental conditions creates a compound effect that significantly impacts detection performance on IoT devices compared to controlled laboratory settings.

question: What are the primary sources of data leakage in machine learning model development, and how can preventive strategies implemented before and during model training minimize its impact while preserving model accuracy and generalizability?

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.text: Data leakage represents one of the most critical yet often overlooked challenges in machine learning model development <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. At its core, data leakage occurs when information that would not be available during real-world model deployment inadvertently influences the training process, creating artificially inflated performance metrics that fail to reflect true model capabilities <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This phenomenon can manifest in subtle ways that are difficult to detect, making it particularly dangerous for practitioners who may unknowingly deploy compromised models to production environments <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The consequences extend beyond mere performance degradation—leaked models can lead to overconfident predictions, poor business decisions, and significant financial losses when the model encounters genuinely unseen data <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Understanding and preventing data leakage is therefore essential for building robust, generalizable machine learning systems that maintain their performance in real-world applications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Primary Sources of Data Leakage
sections.text:
Data leakage can be systematically categorized into several primary sources that occur at different stages of the machine learning pipeline (Kapoor et al., 2022) (Kapoor et al., 2023). The most fundamental source is the **lack of clean separation between training and test datasets**, which manifests in multiple ways including having no separate test set, applying preprocessing to the entire dataset before splitting, and performing feature selection on combined train-test data (Kapoor et al., 2023) (Andrades et al., 2021).

**Preprocessing-related leakage** represents one of the most common yet subtle forms of data leakage. This occurs when normalization, standardization, imputation, or oversampling techniques are applied to the complete dataset before partitioning into train and test sets (Andrades et al., 2021) (Lones, 2021) (Drobnjakovi'c et al., 2022). For time series data, additional preprocessing issues arise when smoothing, decomposition, or feature extraction operations use information from the entire series rather than just the training portion (Hewamalage et al., 2022) (Lubba et al., 2019).

**Illegitimate features** constitute another major source of leakage, occurring when models use features that are proxies for the outcome variable or contain information that would not be legitimately available during real-world prediction (Kapoor et al., 2022) (Filho et al., 2021). In financial analytics, increasingly complex features can mask underlying temporal dependencies that create leakage (Muralidhar et al., 2021). This category also includes cases where features are modified or generated after the target outcome has been achieved (Zhang et al., 2022).

**Temporal and structural leakage** occurs when the independence assumptions between training and test data are violated. Temporal leakage happens when training data includes information from future events that should be predicted, particularly problematic in time series where random splits can easily introduce future information into training (Lones, 2021) (Kapoor et al., 2022) (Cerqua et al., 2024). Non-independence between samples can also create leakage when duplicate or highly similar samples appear across train and test sets (Munappy et al., 2022) (Babu et al., 2024).

**Multi-test leakage** represents a more subtle form that occurs when the same test data is used repeatedly for model evaluation, algorithm selection, or hyperparameter tuning, effectively turning test data into validation data (Yang et al., 2022) (Lones, 2021). This problem is particularly insidious because it can lead to implicit optimization on test performance even when practitioners believe they are maintaining proper separation (Mazanov et al., 2025) (Alturayeif et al., 2025) (Suboti'c et al., 2021).

The complexity of modern machine learning pipelines has made data leakage increasingly difficult to detect, as it often occurs through indirect relationships that are not immediately obvious at the code level (Drobnjakovi'c et al., 2022) (Hahn et al., 2022). This challenge is compounded by the growing use of automated machine learning tools by non-experts across various scientific fields, leading to widespread reproducibility failures affecting hundreds of papers (Semmelrock et al., 2023) (Kapoor et al., 2022).

snippets: Data leakage is indeed a widespread problem and has led to severe reproducibility failures

through a survey of literature in research communities that adopted ML methods, we find 17 fields where errors have been found, collectively affecting 329 papers and in some cases leading to wildly overoptimistic conclusions
our taxonomy addresses data leakage arising during the data collection, pre-processing, modeling and evaluation steps

[L[2] Model uses features that are not legitimate. If the model has access to features that should not be legitimately available for use in the modeling exercise, this could result in leakage. One instance when this can happen is if a feature is a proxy for the outcome variable (Kaufman et al., 2011). For example, (Filho et al., 2021) find that a recent study included the use of anti-hypertensive drugs as a feature for predicting hypertension. Such a feature could lead to leakage because the model would not have access to this information when predicting the health outcome for a new patient

[L[3] Test set is not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest. The distribution of data on which the performance of an ML model is evaluated differs from the distribution of data about which the scientific claims are made. The performance of the model on the test set does not correspond to its performance on data drawn from the distribution of scientific interest. [L3.[1] Temporal leakage. When an ML model is used to make predictions about a future outcome of interest, the test set should not contain any data from a date before the training set. If the test set contains data from before the training set, the model is built using data "from the future" that it should not have access to during training, and can cause leakage. [L3.[2] Nonindependence between train and test samples
we propose model info sheets for reporting scientific claims based on ML models that would address all types of leakage identified in our survey.
citations.title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science

snippets:
Data leakage is a spurious relationship between the independent variables and the target variable that arises as an artifact of the data collection, sampling, or pre-processing strategy. Because the spurious relationship will not be present in the distribution about which scientific claims are made, leakage usually leads to inflated estimates of model performance.

Our taxonomy addresses data leakage arising during the data collection, pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps

[L[1] Lack of clean separation of training and test dataset. If the training dataset is not separated from the test dataset during all pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps, the model has access to information in the test set before its performance is evaluated. Because the model has access to information from the test set at training time, the model learns relationships between the predictors and the outcome that would not be available in additional data drawn from the distribution of interest

This can happen in several ways, such as: [L1.[1] No test set. Using the same dataset for training and testing the model is a textbook example of overfitting, which leads to overoptimistic performance estimates. [L1.[2] Pre-processing on training and test set. Using the entire dataset for any pre-processing steps, such as imputation or over/under sampling, results in leakage. For instance, using oversampling before splitting the data into training and test sets leads to an imperfect separation between the training and test sets because data generated using oversampling from the training set will also be present in the test set. [L1.[3] Feature selection on training and test set. Feature selection on the entire dataset results in using information about which feature performs well on the test set to make a decision about which features should be included in the model.
citations.title: Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science

snippets: Data leakage happens when information from the test set is accidentally used to develop the model, which may happen in subtle ways. For instance, pre-processing the complete dataset with normalization, standardization, or data imputation techniques before data partitioning (e.g., holdout or k-fold cross-validation) cause data points from test set to influence in the train set. Similarly, performing feature selection in the complete dataset that will further be divided into independent partitions for model training and validation produces the same unintentional effect. Even under the use of crossvalidation, data leakage may occur if the same test fold used to optimize the model with hyperparameter tuning or feature selection, for instance, is also applied for model evaluation and selection

Taking steps to prevent data leakage is imperative to guarantee better generalization of models. Data preparation pipelines should be modeled based on training data only and then applied to all partitions (e.g., train, test, and validation set). Nested cross-validation is a promising alternative for comparing and selecting ML models with sizelimited datasets, reducing the bias in the error estimate when both hyperparameter tuning and evaluation are carried out (Varma et al., 2006)(Vabalas et al., 2019). Moreover, FS protocols for high-dimensional data have been proposed to minimize optimistic performance estimates (Kuncheva et al., 2018), especially under low-sample-size as it is the case for some cancer types.
citations.title: Machine learning methods for prediction of cancer driver genes: a survey paper

snippets: A common problem is allowing information about this data to leak into the configuration, training or selection of models

There are a number of ways that information can leak from a test set. Some of these seem quite innocuous. For instance, during data preparation, using information about the means and ranges of variables within the whole data set to carry out variable scaling or imputation -in order to prevent information leakage, these statistics should be calculated using only the training data. Other common examples of information leakage are carrying out feature selection before partitioning the data
using the same test data to evaluate the generality of multiple models
and applying data augmentation before splitting off the test data

The best thing you can do to prevent these issues is to partition off a subset of your data right at the start of your project, and only use this independent test set once to measure the generality of a single model at the end of the project

There are also forms of data leakage which are specific to certain types of data. Time series data is particularly problematic, since the order of samples is significant, and random splits can easily cause leakage and overfitting
Even for non-time series data, the experimental conditions used to generate data sets may lead to temporal dependencies, or other problematic conditions such as duplicated or similar samples
In order to prevent leakage, these kinds of issues need to be identified and taken into account when splitting data

This occurs when you train multiple models in succession, using knowledge gained about each model's performance to guide the configuration of the next one, and you use the same test set to evaluate each model
the problem lies in using the test set throughout this process, since using the test set to choose between models means that information about the test set implicitly leaks into the training process

The solution is to either use a validation set (i.e. a separate set of samples that are not directly used in training, but which are used to guide training) or use a holdout data set to test the final model.
citations.title: Avoiding common machine learning pitfalls

snippets: Data leakages arise when dependent data is used to train and test a model. This can come in the form of overlapping data sets or, more insidiously, by library transformations that create indirect data dependencies

a data leakage is introduced because line 2 performs a normalization, before line 3 and 4 split into train and test data. This implicitly uses the mean over the entire dataset to perform the data transformation and, as a result, the train and test data are implicitly dependent on each other

Mainstream methods rely on detecting data leakages retroactively (Kaufman et al., 2011)[17]. Given a suspicious result, e.g., an overly accurate model, data analysis methods are used to identify data dependencies. However, a reasonable result may avoid suspicion from a data scientist until the model is already deployed
it is advantageous to detect data leakages as early as possible in the development life cycle.
citations.title: Abstract Interpretation-Based Data Leakage Static Analysis

snippets: Data leakage refers to the inadvertent use of data from the test set, or more generally data not available during inference, while training a model

in forecasting, data leakage can happen by performing smoothing, decomposition (mode decomposition), normalisation etc. over the whole series before partitioning for training and testing. Data leakage can happen even when extracting features such as tsfeatures (Hyndman et al., 2019), catch22 (Lubba et al., 2019)) that are not constant over time, to feed as inputs to the model. Thus, features can be extracted only from the training set data, and may need to be re-calculated either periodically or over the specific input windows.
citations.title: Forecast evaluation for data scientists: common pitfalls and best practices

snippets: Capturing the dynamical properties of time series concisely as interpretable feature vectors can enable efficient clustering and classification for time-series applications across science and industry. Selecting an appropriate feature-based representation of time series for a given application can be achieved through systematic comparison across a comprehensive time-series feature library, such as those in the hctsa toolbox. However, this approach is computationally expensive and involves evaluating many similar features, limiting the widespread adoption of feature-based representations of time series for real-world applications. In this work, we introduce a method to infer small sets of time-series features that (i) exhibit strong classification performance across a given collection of time-series problems, and (ii) are minimally redundant. Applying our method to a set of 93 time-series classification datasets (containing over 147,000 time series) and using a filtered version of the hctsa feature library (4791 features), we introduce a set of 22 CAnonical Time-series CHaracteristics, catch22, tailored to the dynamics typically encountered in time-series data-mining tasks. This dimensionality reduction, from 4791 to 22, is associated with an approximately 1000-fold reduction in computation time and near linear scaling with time-series length, despite an average reduction in classification accuracy of just 7%. catch22 captures a diverse and interpretable signature of time series in terms of their properties, including linear and non-linear autocorrelation, successive differences, value distributions and outliers, and fluctuation scaling properties. We provide an efficient implementation of catch22, accessible from many programming environments, that facilitates feature-based time-series analysis for scientific, industrial, financial and medical applications using a common language of interpretable time-series properties.
citations.title: catch22: CAnonical Time-series CHaracteristics

snippets: Data leakage refers broadly to scenarios wherein a model makes use of information that it is not supposed to have or would not have available in production. Data leakage leads to overly optimistic model performance estimates and poses serious downstream problems upon model deployment (specifically in high risk applications). Leakage can happen sometimes unintentionally when feature selection is driven by model validation or test performance or due to the presence of (typically unavailable) features highly correlated with the label

In our domain of financial analytics, increasingly complex features are constantly developed such that their complexity masks underlying temporal dependencies which are often the primary causes of leakage.
