snippets: We extend Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes to perform posterior inference for the weights of Stick-Breaking processes. This development allows us to define a Stick-Breaking Variational Autoencoder (SB-VAE), a Bayesian nonparametric version of the variational autoencoder that has a latent representation with stochastic dimensionality. We experimentally demonstrate that the SB-VAE, and a semi-supervised variant, learn highly discriminative latent representations that often outperform the Gaussian VAE's.
citations.title: Stick-Breaking Variational Autoencoders

sections.title: Automatic Topic Number Discovery
sections.text:
One of the persistent challenges in topic modeling is determining the optimal number of topics, an issue that affects both classical and neural approaches differently. Classical probabilistic models generally require manual specification of topic numbers, with LDA having several reported limitations including the necessity for data cleaning and pre-processing, the selection of model parameters such as the number of topics, and challenges related to interpretability and validation of generated topics (Ramon-Gonen et al., 2023). However, some classical models address this limitation through Bayesian nonparametric approaches, with Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes (HDP) being a notable example that automatically infers the number of topics or mixture components from the data (Zhang et al., 2024).

Neural topic models show mixed capabilities in automatic topic discovery. Many neural approaches still face the same limitations as classical models, with experimental evidence showing that while models like ETM demonstrate high coherence and rather good stability for large datasets, the question of the number of topics remains unsolved for this model (Koltcov et al., 2024). Some neural models like GLDAW have shown promise, as it is possible to determine the optimal number of topics in datasets for the GLDAW model, while the ETM model is unable for that (Koltcov et al., 2024).

Modern neural approaches like BERTopic and Top2Vec offer a different solution to automatic topic discovery through their clustering-based pipelines. Two notable advanced neural models that offer automated pipelines for neural topic modeling are Top2Vec and BERTopic, where both methods begin with input texts, create document embeddings, reduce embedding vector dimensions, and apply HDBSCAN clustering to automatically determine topics (Ramon-Gonen et al., 2023). BERTopic represents an unsupervised method that does not require the number of topics to be specified a priori (Austin et al., 2024).

However, this automatic topic determination in clustering-based neural models creates evaluation challenges. Since the Top2Vec model, BERTopic and the HDP model inevitably determine the number of topics during their inference procedure, it is difficult to directly compare those models with others, as the number of topics is a very central hyperparameter directly impacting performance measures (Reuter et al., 2024). This fundamental difference in how topic numbers are determined makes fair comparisons between classical and neural approaches particularly complex when evaluating their relative performance.

snippets: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) stands out as the most widely used algorithm for topic modelling based on statistical analysis and has been used in most healthcare applications. LDA is an unsupervised, probabilistic method built upon the concept that documents can be modeled as a mixture of latent topics, where each topic is a distribution over words. There are multiple variations of LDA, one of the widely used is LDA with Gibbs sampling, which is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique used for approximate inference in probabilistic models and is effective in handling high dimensional probabilistic models such as LDA. However, LDA has several reported limitations. These include the necessity for data cleaning and pre-processing, the selection of model parameters, such as the number of topics, and challenges related to the interpretability and validation of the generated topics. To tackle these limitations, in recent years, more advanced algorithms have been invented as an alternative technique for topic modeling, such as cluster analysis of document embeddings. Two notable advanced neural models techniques that offer automated pipelines for neural topic modeling are Top2Vec and BERTopic. In their general pipelines, both methods begin with a collection of input texts. They then create document embeddings, followed by reducing the size of the embedding vectors through a dimensionality reduction algorithm. Subsequently, HDBSCAN is applied to cluster the reduced vectors and at the end they generate topic representations.

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics and Performance
sections.text:
The evaluation landscape for topic models reveals significant performance advantages for neural approaches across multiple metrics. Neural topic models demonstrate substantial improvements in traditional evaluation measures, with some models like RETM showing remarkable gains that vastly improve by more than 15 times in training data and between 10% and 90% better performance based on test dataset values for perplexity compared to classical approaches (Vargas et al., 2023). Similarly, other research shows that neural models can outperform standard LDA in terms of topic grouping, model perplexity, classification and comment generation (Fang et al., 2022).

Comparative evaluations across different neural architectures reveal nuanced performance patterns. Among neural topic models, experiments demonstrate that the ETM model achieves the best performance in terms of coherence for two of three datasets, while the GLDAW model takes second place for those datasets and first place for the third dataset, with GLDAW showing higher stability than ETM and demonstrating the smallest computational cost among considered models (Koltcov et al., 2024). Additionally, proposed models like ITAR have been shown to perform better than other popular topic models including LDA, ARTM, and BERTopic, producing diverse topics with moderate perplexity (Gorbulev et al., 2024).

However, the evaluation of topic models faces important methodological challenges that complicate direct comparisons. Neural topic models have gained prominence by besting classical probabilistic topic models on automatic evaluation metrics such as coherence, but automated evaluation metrics have been called into question as they do not necessarily correlate with human ratings on topic model outputs (Li et al., 2024). This discrepancy highlights the importance of task-centered evaluations and human-in-the-loop studies.

User studies provide valuable insights into practical performance differences between classical and neural approaches. Research shows that the choice of Contextualized Topic Model helps users create higher quality label sets than using classical LDA, as measured by both cluster metrics and user ratings, though LDA remains competitive or better when compared with two other popular neural topic models (Li et al., 2024). In domain-specific evaluations, BERTopic outperforms LDA and Top2Vec in topic clustering, achieving at least 34.2% better performance in Chinese and English datasets, with superior topic separation, clearer semantics, and a deeper understanding of text structure and content (Raman et al., 2025) (Egger et al., 2022) (Alamsyah et al., 2023) (Raman et al., 2024).

sections.title: Scenarios Where Classical Models Are Preferred
sections.text:
Despite the advances of neural topic models, classical approaches like LDA maintain distinct advantages in specific use cases and continue to be recommended for certain applications. Research has identified LDA as the most stable traditional model, with recent studies showing that neural topic models fail to outperform it in some contexts, leading to recommendations for its continued use in content analysis (Li et al., 2025). Human evaluation studies provide strong evidence for classical model competitiveness, as research shows that Gibbs LDA is still hard to beat with respect to human evaluation (Rahimi et al., 2023) (Hoyle et al., 2021).

The interpretability advantage of classical models represents a fundamental strength that neural approaches struggle to match. LDA is a generation model that provides a clear explanation of the document generation process, with each topic represented by a distribution of words, facilitating easier interpretation of topics (Cheng et al., 2024). This interpretability becomes crucial when users need to understand not just what topics exist, but how they are generated and why certain words belong together.

Practical implementation considerations favor classical models in many applied research contexts. Neural approaches face significant barriers for practitioners, as the number of hyperparameters, complicated training process, and need for special hardware make this type of model unsuitable for applied researchers seeking a tool for corpus exploration (Austin et al., 2024). In contrast, traditional models like LDA remain effective for exploration but are less user-friendly, yet still provide accessible solutions for researchers without extensive computational resources (Li et al., 2025).

Domain-specific applications present another scenario where classical models excel. BERTopic and other neural approaches may not perform as well on domain-specific or low-resource datasets where pre-training may be limited (Austin et al., 2024). Additionally, while neural methods generate more human-readable topics for general exploration, they produce overly generic topics for domain-specific datasets that do not easily allow users to learn much about the documents (Li et al., 2025).

The scalability and robustness of classical models provide additional advantages for certain use cases. LDA is capable of handling large text corpora and can be trained on extensive document collections, making it a powerful tool for processing massive text datasets (Cheng et al., 2024). Furthermore, despite ongoing advancements in neural topic modeling, the interpretability of these newer models has been gradually diminishing, which reinforces the continued significance and efficacy of traditional methods like LDA (Cheng et al., 2024).

snippets: Topic model evaluation, like evaluation of other unsupervised methods, can be contentious. However, the field has coalesced around automated estimates of topic coherence, which rely on the frequency of word co-occurrences in a reference corpus. At the same time, topic model evaluation suffers from a validation gap: automated coherence, developed for classical models, has not been validated using human experimentation for neural models. In addition, a meta-analysis of topic modeling literature reveals a substantial standardization gap in automated topic modeling benchmarks. To address the validation gap, we compare automated coherence with the two most widely accepted human judgment tasks: topic rating and word intrusion. To address the standardization gap, we systematically evaluate a dominant classical model and two state-of-the-art neural models on two commonly used datasets. question: Are there any recent theoretical works to understand active learning applied to deep learning? It should specifically address the observation that usually a random sampling works as good as more sophisticated sampling strategies.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.text: Active learning is a machine learning paradigm designed to minimize the amount of labeled data needed to train effective models by strategically selecting which unlabeled examples should be annotated <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The core idea is that an intelligent sampling strategy can identify the most informative data points, leading to better model performance with fewer labeled examples compared to random sampling <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This approach is particularly appealing in deep learning applications where obtaining large amounts of labeled data is expensive and time-consuming <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. However, empirical studies have consistently shown a puzzling phenomenon: sophisticated active learning strategies that work well in traditional machine learning settings often fail to outperform simple random sampling when applied to deep neural networks <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This observation has created a significant gap between the theoretical promise of active learning and its practical performance in modern deep learning systems, prompting researchers to investigate the underlying causes and develop new theoretical frameworks to understand these limitations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Theoretical Gaps in Deep Active Learning
sections.text:
The disconnect between active learning theory and deep learning practice stems from fundamental limitations in how existing theoretical frameworks apply to complex neural architectures. The theoretical foundations of active learning algorithms have been extensively studied and provide strong statistical guarantees, but these guarantees are often not directly applicable to deep neural networks (Sun et al., 2025) (Beygelzimer et al., 2008). Due to these limitations, practical active learning applications often rely on heuristic approaches to select examples for labeling (Sun et al., 2025).

Deep learning presents unique challenges that traditional active learning theory struggles to address. Deep neural networks tend to produce rare uncertainty during inference and require relatively large amounts of training data to function effectively (Kanclerz et al., 2023). While Bayesian deep learning approaches using dropout, batch normalization, and ensembles have shown promise in reducing prediction uncertainty (Kanclerz et al., 2023) (Wang et al., 2017) (Tan et al., 2021) (Ren et al., 2020), these methods still operate without strong theoretical guarantees about their effectiveness compared to random sampling.

The emergence of deep active learning as a field reflects the recognition that traditional machine learning's relatively modest data requirements made active learning less critical in the past, but the data-hungry nature of deep learning has renewed interest in reducing annotation costs (Ren et al., 2020). However, this renewed interest has not yet been accompanied by corresponding theoretical advances that can explain why sophisticated sampling strategies fail to consistently outperform random selection in deep learning contexts.

snippets: Recent successes in learning-based image classification, however, heavily rely on the large number of annotated training samples, which may require considerable human effort. In this paper, we propose a novel active learning (AL) framework, which is capable of building a competitive classifier with optimal feature representation via a limited amount of labeled training instances in an incremental learning manner. Our approach advances the existing AL methods in two aspects. First, we incorporate deep convolutional neural networks into AL. Through the properly designed framework, the feature representation and the classifier can be simultaneously updated with progressively annotated informative samples. Second, we present a cost-effective sample selection strategy to improve the classification performance with less manual annotations. Unlike traditional methods focusing on only the uncertain samples of low prediction confidence, we especially discover the large amount of high-confidence samples from the unlabeled set for feature learning. Specifically, these high-confidence samples are automatically selected and iteratively assigned pseudolabels. We thus call our framework cost-effective AL (CEAL) standing for the two advantages. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed CEAL framework can achieve promising results on two challenging image classification data sets, i.e., face recognition on the cross-age celebrity face recognition data set database and object categorization on Caltech-256.
citations.title: Cost-Effective Active Learning for Deep Image Classification

snippets: We study acquisition functions for active learning (AL) for text classification. The Expected Loss Reduction (ELR) method focuses on a Bayesian estimate of the reduction in classification error, recently updated with Mean Objective Cost of Uncertainty (MOCU). We convert the ELR framework to estimate the increase in (strictly proper) scores like log probability or negative mean square error, which we call Bayesian Estimate of Mean Proper Scores (BEMPS). We also prove convergence results borrowing techniques used with MOCU. In order to allow better experimentation with the new acquisition functions, we develop a complementary batch AL algorithm, which encourages diversity in the vector of expected changes in scores for unlabelled data. To allow high performance text classifiers, we combine ensembling and dynamic validation set construction on pretrained language models. Extensive experimental evaluation then explores how these different acquisition functions perform. The results show that the use of mean square error and log probability with BEMPS yields robust acquisition functions, which consistently outperform the others tested.
citations.title: Diversity Enhanced Active Learning with Strictly Proper Scoring Rules

snippets: Active learning (AL) attempts to maximize a model’s performance gain while annotating the fewest samples possible. Deep learning (DL) is greedy for data and requires a large amount of data supply to optimize a massive number of parameters if the model is to learn how to extract high-quality features. In recent years, due to the rapid development of internet technology, we have entered an era of information abundance characterized by massive amounts of available data. As a result, DL has attracted significant attention from researchers and has been rapidly developed. Compared with DL, however, researchers have a relatively low interest in AL. This is mainly because before the rise of DL, traditional machine learning requires relatively few labeled samples, meaning that early AL is rarely according the value it deserves. Although DL has made breakthroughs in various fields, most of this success is due to a large number of publicly available annotated datasets. However, the acquisition of a large number of high-quality annotated datasets consumes a lot of manpower, making it unfeasible in fields that require high levels of expertise (such as speech recognition, information extraction, medical images, etc.). Therefore, AL is gradually coming to receive the attention it is due. It is therefore natural to investigate whether AL can be used to reduce the cost of sample annotation while retaining the powerful learning capabilities of DL. As a result of such investigations, deep active learning (DeepAL) has emerged. Although research on this topic is quite abundant, there has not yet been a comprehensive survey of DeepAL-related works; accordingly, this article aims to fill this gap. We provide a formal classification method for the existing work, along with a comprehensive and systematic overview. In addition, we also analyze and summarize the development of DeepAL from an application perspective. Finally, we discuss the confusion and problems associated with DeepAL and provide some possible development directions.
citations.title: A Survey of Deep Active Learning

sections.title: Empirical Evidence for Random Sampling Performance
sections.text:
Large-scale empirical investigations have provided concrete evidence for the underwhelming performance of sophisticated active learning methods in deep learning contexts. A comprehensive study involving 11 existing acquisition functions and 15,105 trained deep neural networks revealed that when evaluating adversarial robustness, random sampling actually achieves better robustness than existing sophisticated functions, though it fails on accuracy metrics (Guo et al., 2022). This finding highlights a fundamental trade-off where acquisition functions that perform well on standard accuracy measures can perform worse than random sampling when evaluated on other important criteria like model robustness.

The inconsistency of active learning performance has become a recognized characteristic of modern approaches. Despite continuous developments in active learning strategies, it has been observed that modern AL strategies can vary wildly in performance depending on data setting and that there is no single strategy that consistently performs best (Bakker et al., 2023). This variability underscores the empirical reality that sophisticated sampling methods fail to deliver the consistent improvements over random sampling that theory would predict, further motivating the need for better theoretical understanding of why these methods struggle in deep learning environments.

sections.title: Challenges with Sophisticated Sampling Strategies
sections.text:
The fundamental problems with sophisticated sampling strategies in deep learning stem from their reliance on heuristic approaches without solid theoretical foundations. Many active learning methods lack groundedness and are basically heuristics, which contributes to their inconsistent performance compared to random sampling (Deschamps et al., 2022). This theoretical weakness means that practitioners cannot predict when these methods will succeed or fail, making random sampling a more reliable baseline.

A critical issue with uncertainty-based sampling strategies is their tendency to create sampling bias through redundant selection. Focusing only on uncertainty leads to a sampling bias where selected samples are highly similar to each other (Wu et al., 2023). This problem becomes particularly acute in batch-based convolutional neural networks, where using only uncertainty may result in redundant sampling that leads to worse performance compared to random samples (Deschamps et al., 2022). The pathological scenario of selecting highly similar samples creates problems especially in noisy and redundant real-world datasets (Wu et al., 2023).

The multi-objective nature of model performance creates additional challenges for sophisticated sampling strategies. Research has shown that acquisition functions optimized for accuracy can perform worse than random sampling on other important metrics like adversarial robustness (Guo et al., 2022). This finding reveals that sophisticated strategies may optimize for narrow objectives while inadvertently harming other aspects of model performance, suggesting that the apparent simplicity of random sampling may actually represent a more balanced approach across multiple evaluation criteria.

question: Compare weakly supervised learning vs self supervised learning applied to computer vision, specifically in video activity recognition or classification.

sections.title: Background and Introduction
sections.text:
The field of computer vision, particularly video activity recognition, has traditionally relied on fully supervised learning approaches that require extensive manual annotation of training data. However, this approach faces significant scalability challenges due to the time-consuming and expensive nature of manual labeling (Singh et al., 2022). This limitation has driven researchers to explore alternative learning paradigms that can leverage large-scale data without requiring exhaustive human annotation.

Weakly supervised learning represents a middle ground between fully supervised and unsupervised approaches, utilizing readily available but noisy supervision signals. In the context of video activity recognition, weakly supervised methods have been developed to generate pseudo ground-truth annotations from weakly labeled data. For example, researchers have proposed methods that transfer tracked object boxes from weakly-labeled videos to weakly-labeled images to automatically generate training annotations (Osep et al., 2017) (Singh et al., 2016). These approaches often leverage "free" annotations available on the internet, such as image-text pairs, hashtags, or other metadata that can be processed to produce pseudo labels (Singh et al., 2022) (Mahajan et al., 2018).

Self-supervised learning takes a different approach by learning representations without any external supervision, instead deriving supervisory signals from the data itself. These methods can use various forms of self-generated supervision, including spatial context prediction, temporal relationships in video sequences, or multi-modal signals (Osep et al., 2017) (Doersch et al., 2015) (Pathak et al., 2016). Notable self-supervised approaches have demonstrated competitive performance by learning to predict spatial relationships between image patches, performing contrastive learning, or using student-teacher architectures (Singh et al., 2022) (He et al., 2019).

The key advantage of both approaches lies in their scalability - self-supervised methods can easily scale to billions of training examples, while weakly supervised methods can leverage the vast amounts of weakly labeled data available online (Singh et al., 2022). Recent work has shown that combining these approaches through "pre-pretraining" strategies can further improve performance across various visual recognition tasks, including video recognition (Singh et al., 2023).

A key advantage of self-supervised pre-training is that is can easily be scaled to billions of training images: several studies have shown that scaling self-supervised learning can lead to substantial performance improvements [27]31].

snippets: The status quo approach to training object detectors requires expensive bounding box annotations. Our framework takes a markedly different direction: we transfer tracked object boxes from weakly-labeled videos to weakly-labeled images to automatically generate pseudo ground-truth boxes, which replace manually annotated bounding boxes. We first mine discriminative regions in the weakly-labeled image collection that frequently/rarely appear in the positive/ negative images. We then match those regions to videos and retrieve the corresponding tracked object boxes. Finally, we design a hough transform algorithm to vote for the best box to serve as the pseudo GT for each image, and use them to train an object detector. Together, these lead to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised detection results on the PASCAL 2007 and 2010 datasets.

snippets: State-of-the-art visual perception models for a wide range of tasks rely on supervised pretraining. ImageNet classification is the de facto pretraining task for these models. Yet, ImageNet is now nearly ten years old and is by modern standards "small". Even so, relatively little is known about the behavior of pretraining with datasets that are multiple orders of magnitude larger. The reasons are obvious: such datasets are difficult to collect and annotate. In this paper, we present a unique study of transfer learning with large convolutional networks trained to predict hashtags on billions of social media images. Our experiments demonstrate that training for large-scale hashtag prediction leads to excellent results. We show improvements on several image classification and object detection tasks, and report the highest ImageNet-1k single-crop, top-1 accuracy to date: 85.4% (97.6% top-5). We also perform extensive experiments that provide novel empirical data on the relationship between large-scale pretraining and transfer learning performance.
citations.title: Exploring the Limits of Weakly Supervised Pretraining

snippets: This work explores the use of spatial context as a source of free and plentiful supervisory signal for training a rich visual representation. Given only a large, unlabeled image collection, we extract random pairs of patches from each image and train a convolutional neural net to predict the position of the second patch relative to the first. We argue that doing well on this task requires the model to learn to recognize objects and their parts. We demonstrate that the feature representation learned using this within-image context indeed captures visual similarity across images. For example, this representation allows us to perform unsupervised visual discovery of objects like cats, people, and even birds from the Pascal VOC 2011 detection dataset. Furthermore, we show that the learned ConvNet can be used in the R-CNN framework [19] and provides a significant boost over a randomly-initialized ConvNet, resulting in state-of-the-art performance among algorithms which use only Pascal-provided training set annotations.
citations.title: Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning by Context Prediction

snippets: Very recently, there has been significant interest in learning meaningful representations using weakly-supervised and self-supervised learning. One useful source of supervision is to use the temporal information contained in videos. Consistency across temporal frames has been used as supervision to learn embeddings which perform well on a number of tasks (Goroshin et al., 2014)(Ramanathan et al., 2015). Another way to use consistency is to track patches in frames of video containing task-relevant attributes and use the coherence of tracked patches to guide the training (Srivastava, 2015).
citations.title: Context Encoders: Feature Learning by Inpainting

snippets: We present Momentum Contrast (MoCo) for unsupervised visual representation learning. From a perspective on contrastive learning as dictionary look-up, we build a dynamic dictionary with a queue and a moving-averaged encoder. This enables building a large and consistent dictionary on-the-fly that facilitates contrastive unsupervised learning. MoCo provides competitive results under the common linear protocol on ImageNet classification. More importantly, the representations learned by MoCo transfer well to downstream tasks. MoCo can outperform its supervised pre-training counterpart in 7 detection/segmentation tasks on PASCAL VOC, COCO, and other datasets, sometimes surpassing it by large margins. This suggests that the gap between unsupervised and supervised representation learning has been largely closed in many vision tasks.

sections.title: Definitional Comparison of Approaches
sections.text:
The fundamental distinction between weakly supervised and self-supervised learning lies in their source of supervisory signals. Weakly supervised learning relies on readily available but noisy external annotations, such as hashtags, image-text pairs, or other metadata that can be processed to produce pseudo labels (Singh et al., 2023) (Mahajan et al., 2018). In contrast, self-supervised learning derives supervisory signals entirely from the data itself without any external supervision, using techniques such as spatial context prediction, temporal relationships, or multi-modal signals (Osep et al., 2017) (Pathak et al., 2016) (Doersch et al., 2015).

The approaches exhibit distinct trade-offs in terms of semantic information and scalability. Weakly supervised pretraining provides a moderate semantic learning signal for each training example but can be obtained at large scale with relative ease, representing a middle ground between fully supervised and self-supervised approaches (Singh et al., 2022). Self-supervised methods receive minimal semantic information during training but can easily scale to billions of training examples, with recent approaches using contrastive learning, cluster prediction, or student-teacher architectures (Singh et al., 2022) (He et al., 2019).

In video activity recognition specifically, these definitional differences manifest in distinct methodological approaches. Weakly supervised methods often generate pseudo ground-truth annotations from video-level labels or transfer tracked object boxes between videos and images (Osep et al., 2017) (Singh et al., 2016). Self-supervised approaches for video tasks typically focus on pretext tasks like masked feature reconstruction, clip-order prediction, or temporal consistency constraints to learn meaningful video representations (Vahdani et al., 2021) (Wang et al., 2021) (Jain et al., 2020).

The nature of supervisory signals also affects the types of features learned by each approach. Language-supervised weakly supervised models excel at high-level semantic understanding but often underperform on dense, localized prediction tasks, as they learn what objects are present but not where they are located (Baharoon et al., 2024). Self-supervised methods have demonstrated the ability to learn more granular, localized representations that complement high-level semantic features, making them particularly valuable for tasks requiring spatial understanding (Baharoon et al., 2024).

snippets: Self-supervised learning refers to training with pseudo labels where pseudo labels are automatically generated for a pre-defined pretext task without involving any human annotations. Actionbytes (Jain et al., 2020) adopted a self-supervised iterative approach for training boundary-aware models by decomposing trimmed videos into ActionBytes. SSTAP (Wang et al., 2021) designed two pretext tasks, i.e., masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction, to learn the relation of temporal clues and achieved the state-of-the-art results on ActivityNet-1.3 among semisupervised methods. Gong et al. (Gong et al., 2021) proposed a self-supervised equivariant transform consistency constraint and attained the state-of-the-art results on ActivityNet-1.2 among weakly-supervised methods.
citations.title: Deep Learning-Based Action Detection in Untrimmed Videos: A Survey

snippets: Self-supervised learning presents a remarkable performance to utilize unlabeled data for various video tasks. In this paper, we focus on applying the power of self-supervised methods to improve semi-supervised action proposal generation. Particularly, we design an effective Self-supervised Semi-supervised Temporal Action Proposal (SSTAP) framework. The SSTAP contains two crucial branches, i.e., temporal-aware semi-supervised branch and relation-aware self-supervised branch. The semi-supervised branch improves the proposal model by introducing two temporal perturbations, i.e., temporal feature shift and temporal feature flip, in the mean teacher framework. The self-supervised branch defines two pretext tasks, including masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction, to learn the relation of temporal clues. By this means, SSTAP can better explore unlabeled videos, and improve the discriminative abilities of learned action features. We extensively evaluate the proposed SSTAP on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3 datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that SSTAP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods and even matches fully-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wangxiang1230/SSTAP.
citations.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Semi-Supervised Temporal Action Proposal

snippets: This paper tackles the problem of localizing actions in long untrimmed videos. Different from existing works, which all use annotated untrimmed videos during training, we learn only from short trimmed videos. This enables learning from large-scale datasets originally designed for action classification. We propose a method to train an action localization network that segments a video into interpretable fragments, we call ActionBytes. Our method jointly learns to cluster ActionBytes and trains the localization network using the cluster assignments as pseudo-labels. By doing so, we train on short trimmed videos that become untrimmed for ActionBytes. In isolation, or when merged, the ActionBytes also serve as effective action proposals. Experiments demonstrate that our boundary-guided training generalizes to unknown action classes and localizes actions in long videos of Thumos14, MultiThumos, and ActivityNet1.2. Furthermore, we show the advantage of ActionBytes for zero-shot localization as well as traditional weakly supervised localization, that train on long videos, to achieve state-of-the-art results.
citations.title: ActionBytes: Learning From Trimmed Videos to Localize Actions

snippets: Weakly-supervised learning, specifically language-guided or language-supervised learning, was popularized by CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and learns visual and textual representations using contrastive loss by maximizing the similarity between image-captions pairs and minimizing the similarity of non-paired imagecaptions (Radford et al., 2021;Cherti et al., 2022). Because this approach relies on semantic captions as a supervisory signal, language-supervised models are strong at high-level tasks like image classification, but significantly underperform on dense, low-level prediction tasks that require localized features (Radford et al., 2021;Wang et al., 2024;2022). In other words, these paradigms are good at learning what objects are present in a visual input, but not where they are
On the other hand, self-supervised learning methods have shown the ability to learn granular representations, complementing the high-level features in vision-language training

due to the nature of the supervisory signal in these paradigms, they lack the ability to learn localized features, leading to degraded performance on dense prediction tasks such as segmentation and detection. On the other hand, self-supervised learning methods have shown the ability to learn granular representations, complementing the high-level features in vision-language training.

sections.title: Applications in Video Activity Recognition
sections.text:
Self-supervised learning has found rich applications in video activity recognition by exploiting the temporal structure inherent in video sequences. Early work established that temporal consistency across video frames provides a powerful supervisory signal, with methods using coherence of tracked patches and temporal embeddings to learn meaningful representations (Pathak et al., 2016) (Ramanathan et al., 2015) (Goroshin et al., 2014). More recent advances have developed sophisticated pretext tasks specifically for video understanding, including masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction, which have achieved notable performance on challenging datasets like ActivityNet (Vahdani et al., 2021) (Wang et al., 2021).

A particularly successful application area has been temporal action localization, where self-supervised methods learn to decompose videos into interpretable segments called ActionBytes using cluster assignments as pseudo-labels (Vahdani et al., 2021) (Jain et al., 2020). These approaches have demonstrated the ability to generalize to unknown action classes and achieve competitive results on standard benchmarks like THUMOS14 and ActivityNet without requiring temporal boundary annotations during training.

Weakly supervised approaches in video activity recognition typically leverage video-level action labels while avoiding the need for expensive frame-level annotations. Recent work has developed frameworks that use dynamic time warping to find corresponding frames between videos with the same action labels, creating paired contrastive losses that improve temporal understanding (Chen et al., 2022). These methods have shown the ability to achieve strong performance in video alignment and fine-grained frame retrieval tasks, demonstrating that video-level supervision can be effectively used to learn detailed temporal correspondences.

Both approaches have found specialized applications in domain-specific video analysis. In surgical workflow analysis, self-supervised methods using remaining surgery duration prediction have been developed to reduce reliance on expensive manual annotations (Ramesh et al., 2023) (Yengera et al., 2018) (Funke et al., 2018). Similarly, robotic imitation learning has benefited from self-supervised video representations that capture viewpoint-invariant relationships between end-effectors and environments (Walmer et al., 2023) (Sermanet et al., 2017).

The field has also seen integration of both paradigms, with some methods combining self-supervised pretext tasks with weakly supervised temporal action localization to achieve improved performance (Zhang et al., 2021). Large-scale weakly supervised pre-training using hashtag-based supervision has demonstrated competitive performance with self-supervised methods in video action recognition tasks, showing the continued relevance of weakly supervised approaches (Chen et al., 2024).

snippets: In this paper, we propose to learn temporal embeddings of video frames for complex video analysis. Large quantities of unlabeled video data can be easily obtained from the Internet. These videos possess the implicit weak label that they are sequences of temporally and semantically coherent images. We leverage this information to learn temporal embeddings for video frames by associating frames with the temporal context that they appear in. To do this, we propose a scheme for incorporating temporal context based on past and future frames in videos, and compare this to other contextual representations. In addition, we show how data augmentation using multi-resolution samples and hard negatives helps to significantly improve the quality of the learned embeddings. We evaluate various design decisions for learning temporal embeddings, and show that our embeddings can improve performance for multiple video tasks such as retrieval, classification, and temporal order recovery in unconstrained Internet video.
citations.title: Learning Temporal Embeddings for Complex Video Analysis

snippets: Current state-of-the-art classification and detection algorithms train deep convolutional networks using labeled data. In this work we study unsupervised feature learning with convolutional networks in the context of temporally coherent unlabeled data. We focus on feature learning from unlabeled video data, using the assumption that adjacent video frames contain semantically similar information. This assumption is exploited to train a convolutional pooling auto-encoder regularized by slowness and sparsity priors. We establish a connection between slow feature learning and metric learning. Using this connection we define "temporal coherence" -- a criterion which can be used to set hyper-parameters in a principled and automated manner. In a transfer learning experiment, we show that the resulting encoder can be used to define a more semantically coherent metric without the use of labels.
citations.title: Unsupervised Learning of Spatiotemporally Coherent Metrics

snippets: Self-supervised learning refers to training with pseudo labels where pseudo labels are automatically generated for a pre-defined pretext task without involving any human annotations. Actionbytes (Jain et al., 2020) adopted a self-supervised iterative approach for training boundary-aware models by decomposing trimmed videos into ActionBytes. SSTAP (Wang et al., 2021) designed two pretext tasks, i.e., masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction, to learn the relation of temporal clues and achieved the state-of-the-art results on ActivityNet-1.3 among semisupervised methods. Gong et al. (Gong et al., 2021) proposed a self-supervised equivariant transform consistency constraint and attained the state-of-the-art results on ActivityNet-1.2 among weakly-supervised methods.
citations.title: Deep Learning-Based Action Detection in Untrimmed Videos: A Survey

snippets: Self-supervised learning presents a remarkable performance to utilize unlabeled data for various video tasks. In this paper, we focus on applying the power of self-supervised methods to improve semi-supervised action proposal generation. Particularly, we design an effective Self-supervised Semi-supervised Temporal Action Proposal (SSTAP) framework. The SSTAP contains two crucial branches, i.e., temporal-aware semi-supervised branch and relation-aware self-supervised branch. The semi-supervised branch improves the proposal model by introducing two temporal perturbations, i.e., temporal feature shift and temporal feature flip, in the mean teacher framework. The self-supervised branch defines two pretext tasks, including masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction, to learn the relation of temporal clues. By this means, SSTAP can better explore unlabeled videos, and improve the discriminative abilities of learned action features. We extensively evaluate the proposed SSTAP on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3 datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that SSTAP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods and even matches fully-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wangxiang1230/SSTAP.
citations.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Semi-Supervised Temporal Action Proposal

snippets: This paper tackles the problem of localizing actions in long untrimmed videos. Different from existing works, which all use annotated untrimmed videos during training, we learn only from short trimmed videos. This enables learning from large-scale datasets originally designed for action classification. We propose a method to train an action localization network that segments a video into interpretable fragments, we call ActionBytes. Our method jointly learns to cluster ActionBytes and trains the localization network using the cluster assignments as pseudo-labels. By doing so, we train on short trimmed videos that become untrimmed for ActionBytes. In isolation, or when merged, the ActionBytes also serve as effective action proposals. Experiments demonstrate that our boundary-guided training generalizes to unknown action classes and localizes actions in long videos of Thumos14, MultiThumos, and ActivityNet1.2. Furthermore, we show the advantage of ActionBytes for zero-shot localization as well as traditional weakly supervised localization, that train on long videos, to achieve state-of-the-art results.
citations.title: ActionBytes: Learning From Trimmed Videos to Localize Actions

snippets: Real-time algorithms for automatically recognizing surgical phases are needed to develop systems that can provide assistance to surgeons, enable better management of operating room (OR) resources and consequently improve safety within the OR. State-of-the-art surgical phase recognition algorithms using laparoscopic videos are based on fully supervised training. This limits their potential for widespread application, since creation of manual annotations is an expensive process considering the numerous types of existing surgeries and the vast amount of laparoscopic videos available. In this work, we propose a new self-supervised pre-training approach based on the prediction of remaining surgery duration (RSD) from laparoscopic videos. The RSD prediction task is used to pre-train a convolutional neural network (CNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) network in an end-to-end manner. Our proposed approach utilizes all available data and reduces the reliance on annotated data, thereby facilitating the scaling up of surgical phase recognition algorithms to different kinds of surgeries. Additionally, we present EndoN2N, an end-to-end trained CNN-LSTM model for surgical phase recognition and evaluate the performance of our approach on a dataset of 120 Cholecystectomy laparoscopic videos (Cholec120). This work also presents the first systematic study of self-supervised pre-training approaches to understand the amount of annotations required for surgical phase recognition. Interestingly, the proposed RSD pre-training approach leads to performance improvement even when all the training data is manually annotated and outperforms the single pre-training approach for surgical phase recognition presently published in the literature. It is also observed that end-to-end training of CNN-LSTM networks boosts surgical phase recognition performance.
citations.title: Less is More: Surgical Phase Recognition with Less Annotations through Self-Supervised Pre-training of CNN-LSTM Networks

snippets: In order to provide the right type of assistance at the right time, computer-assisted surgery systems need context awareness. To achieve this, methods for surgical workflow analysis are crucial. Currently, convolutional neural networks provide the best performance for video-based workflow analysis tasks. For training such networks, large amounts of annotated data are necessary. However, collecting a sufficient amount of data is often costly, time-consuming, and not always feasible. In this paper, we address this problem by presenting and comparing different approaches for self-supervised pretraining of neural networks on unlabeled laparoscopic videos using temporal coherence. We evaluate our pretrained networks on Cholec80, a publicly available dataset for surgical phase segmentation, on which a maximum F1 score of 84.6 was reached. Furthermore, we were able to achieve an increase of the F1 score of up to 10 points when compared to a non-pretrained neural network.
citations.title: Temporal coherence-based self-supervised learning for laparoscopic workflow analysis

snippets: We propose a self-supervised approach for learning representations and robotic behaviors entirely from unlabeled videos recorded from multiple viewpoints, and study how this representation can be used in two robotic imitation settings: imitating object interactions from videos of humans, and imitating human poses. Imitation of human behavior requires a viewpoint-invariant representation that captures the relationships between end-effectors (hands or robot grippers) and the environment, object attributes, and body pose. We train our representations using a triplet loss, where multiple simultaneous viewpoints of the same observation are attracted in the embedding space, while being repelled from temporal neighbors which are often visually similar but functionally different. This signal causes our model to discover attributes that do not change across viewpoint, but do change across time, while ignoring nuisance variables such as occlusions, motion blur, lighting and background. We demonstrate that this representation can be used by a robot to directly mimic human poses without an explicit correspondence, and that it can be used as a reward function within a reinforcement learning algorithm. While representations are learned from an unlabeled collection of task-related videos, robot behaviors such as pouring are learned by watching a single 3rd-person demonstration by a human. Reward functions obtained by following the human demonstrations under the learned representation enable efficient reinforcement learning that is practical for real-world robotic systems. Video results, open-source code and dataset are available at sermanet.github.io/imitate

sections.title: Performance Comparison and Trade-offs
sections.text:
Recent comparative studies have revealed nuanced performance differences between weakly supervised and self-supervised approaches in video activity recognition. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that weakly supervised methods often achieve superior performance, with some studies showing that weakly supervised models substantially outperform their self-supervised counterparts across various settings (Singh et al., 2022). This performance advantage stems from the moderate but meaningful semantic signals provided by weak supervision, which falls between the strong signals of fully supervised learning and the minimal semantic information available in self-supervised approaches.

The fundamental trade-offs between these approaches reflect their different learning paradigms. Weakly supervised pretraining benefits from noisy semantic learning signals that can be obtained at large scale with relative ease, while self-supervised pretraining receives minimal semantic information but can easily scale to billions of training examples (Singh et al., 2022) (Mahajan et al., 2018). This scalability advantage of self-supervised methods has led to substantial performance improvements as dataset sizes increase, with notable approaches using contrastive learning and student-teacher architectures achieving competitive results (He et al., 2019).

In specific video analysis tasks, self-supervised techniques have demonstrated the ability to outperform both image-level scene representations and weakly supervised classifiers trained on image labels, showing statistical significance in retaining representative power of video-level scene representations (Peri et al., 2022). However, the relative performance depends heavily on the availability of complementary supervision signals, with weakly supervised approaches showing further improvements when video-level labels are available (Chen et al., 2022).

The choice between approaches also involves practical considerations beyond raw performance metrics. Weakly supervised learning has become particularly prevalent in domains where frame-level annotations are extremely difficult to obtain, such as anomaly detection, where the balance between performance, speed, and resource usage becomes critical (Tan et al., 2022). Self-supervised methods, while requiring more computational resources for large-scale pretraining, offer the advantage of not requiring any external annotation efforts, making them attractive for applications with strict labeling constraints.

snippets: There are trade-offs between these three types of pretraining. Fully supervised pre-training benefits from a strong semantic learning signal for each training example, but does not scale well because manual labeling of training data is time-consuming. By contrast, self-supervised pretraining receives hardly any semantic information on the training examples, but can be scaled to billions of training examples relatively easily [27,(He et al., 2019). Weakly-supervised approaches fall somewhere in between: for example, hashtags or other text associated with visual data generally provide a noisy semantic learning signal but can be obtained at large scale with relative ease (Mahajan et al., 2018)[57]
Throughout our experiments, we find the weakly-supervised approach to be very competitive: our best models perform on par with the state-of-the-art on a range

We also compare our models with those obtained via large-scale self-supervised learning. We find our weakly-supervised models to be very competitive across all settings, and find they substantially outperform their self-supervised counterparts

Whereas early self-supervised learners such as RotNet [26] or DeepCluster [10] substantially lagged their supervised counterparts in vision pre-training, more recent approaches have become quite competitive. These approaches learn to predict clusters [11], use contrastive learning [13,31,51], or use student-teacher architectures in which the teacher is an exponentially moving average of the student [12,14,29]. A key advantage of self-supervised pre-training is that is can easily be scaled to billions of training images: several studies have shown that scaling self-supervised learning can lead to substantial performance improvements [27]31].
citations.title: Revisiting Weakly Supervised Pre-Training of Visual Perception Models

snippets: State-of-the-art visual perception models for a wide range of tasks rely on supervised pretraining. ImageNet classification is the de facto pretraining task for these models. Yet, ImageNet is now nearly ten years old and is by modern standards "small". Even so, relatively little is known about the behavior of pretraining with datasets that are multiple orders of magnitude larger. The reasons are obvious: such datasets are difficult to collect and annotate. In this paper, we present a unique study of transfer learning with large convolutional networks trained to predict hashtags on billions of social media images. Our experiments demonstrate that training for large-scale hashtag prediction leads to excellent results. We show improvements on several image classification and object detection tasks, and report the highest ImageNet-1k single-crop, top-1 accuracy to date: 85.4% (97.6% top-5). We also perform extensive experiments that provide novel empirical data on the relationship between large-scale pretraining and transfer learning performance.
citations.title: Exploring the Limits of Weakly Supervised Pretraining

snippets: We present Momentum Contrast (MoCo) for unsupervised visual representation learning. From a perspective on contrastive learning as dictionary look-up, we build a dynamic dictionary with a queue and a moving-averaged encoder. This enables building a large and consistent dictionary on-the-fly that facilitates contrastive unsupervised learning. MoCo provides competitive results under the common linear protocol on ImageNet classification. More importantly, the representations learned by MoCo transfer well to downstream tasks. MoCo can outperform its supervised pre-training counterpart in 7 detection/segmentation tasks on PASCAL VOC, COCO, and other datasets, sometimes surpassing it by large margins. This suggests that the gap between unsupervised and supervised representation learning has been largely closed in many vision tasks.
citations.title: Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning

sections.title: Hybrid and Combined Approaches
sections.text:
The natural complementarity between weakly supervised and self-supervised learning has led researchers to develop hybrid approaches that combine both paradigms for enhanced video activity recognition performance. These methods seek to leverage the semantic guidance of weak supervision while maintaining the scalability and robustness of self-supervised learning. A notable example is "weakly-guided self-supervision," which leverages weak labels during pretraining while designing pretext tasks based on augmentations similar to self-supervised methods (Kahatapitiya et al., 2021).

One promising direction involves "pre-pretraining" strategies that sequentially combine weakly supervised and self-supervised approaches. These methods first perform weakly supervised pretraining using readily available noisy supervision signals, followed by self-supervised pretraining to further refine the learned representations (Singh et al., 2023). Large-scale empirical studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of this combined approach across various visual recognition tasks, including video recognition, showing that the sequential application of both paradigms can outperform either approach used in isolation.

The integration of these approaches has been facilitated by advances in contrastive learning frameworks that can accommodate both supervised and self-supervised signals. Extending contrastive learning to hybrid settings has proven straightforward, with methods like PSC proposing hybrid networks that jointly perform self-supervised learning and prototypical supervised contrastive learning in a cumulative learning manner (Tan et al._1, 2022) (Wang et al._1, 2021). These frameworks unify different learning objectives, including consistency regularization and entropy minimization, to mitigate issues like confirmation bias in pseudo-label-based learning.

Progressive learning strategies have emerged as a key technique in hybrid approaches, where the learning process transitions from feature learning using self-supervised objectives to classifier learning using weak supervision. This embodies the principle that better features lead to better classifiers, allowing the combined system to benefit from both the robust feature representations learned through self-supervision and the semantic guidance provided by weak labels (Tan et al._1, 2022) (Wang et al._2, 2021).

snippets: The paper proposes a weakly-guided self-supervised pretraining method for activity detection, using large-scale classification data with no extra annotations. We augment pretraining data to capture fine-grained details and use detection as the pretraining (or pretext) task -a step closer to bridging the gap with downstream detection

Our method leverages weak labels during pretraining, having downstream settings unchanged. Also, we design a pretext task based on augmentations similar to the work in selfsupervision. Considering the traits of both domains, we term our work as weakly-guided self-supervision.
citations.title: Weakly-Guided Self-Supervised Pretraining for Temporal Activity Detection

snippets: Weakly supervised pretraining (WSP) is a middle-ground between supervised and self-supervised pretraining. Instead of ignoring annotations completely as in self-supervised pretraining, or requiring exhaustive labels as in supervised pretraining, WSP relies on the large quantity of "free" annotation available on the internet. These annotations occur as image-text pairs [59]65], where the text can additionally be processed to produce pseudo labels
Self-supervised pretraining is a promising alternative to learn these representation without relying on large welllabeled datasets
Given the lack of supervision during pretraining, these representations often require significant finetuning to align to downstream tasks

Our method combines two common pretraining tasks in vision: (1) weakly supervised pretraining that uses weak, often noisy, signals such as text or image hashtags as supervision, and (2) self-supervised pretraining that only uses the data without additional supervision. Both forms of pretraining start training with a randomly initialized model and have proven effective at learning general purpose vision models

We perform a large-scale empirical study to measure the effectiveness of pre-pretraining on 10 different visual recognition tasks spanning image classification, video recognition, object detection, low-shot classification and zero-shot recognition.

snippets: Extending contrastive learning to semi-supervised learning or weakly-supervised learning is straightforward

Self-Tuning (Wang et al., 2021) explores group contrastive learning and tackles confirmation bias and model shift issues in an efficient onestage framework towards data-efficient transfer learning and semi-supervised learning. CoMatch [43] unifies contrastive learning, consistency regularization, entropy minimization and graph-based SSL to mitigate confirmation bias in pseudo-label-based semi-supervised learning. PSC (Wang et al., 2021) proposes a hybrid network that jointly performs both selfsupervised learning and prototypical supervised contrastive learning in a cumulative learning manner. BalFeat (Kang et al., 2021) combines strengths of supervised methods and contrastive methods to learn representations that are both discriminative and balanced. MoPro [44] simultaneously optimizes classical supervised loss and prototypical contrastive loss using momentum prototypes and tries to achieve robust weakly-supervised learning.
citations.title: Hyperspherical Consistency Regularization

snippets: Learning discriminative image representations plays a vital role in long-tailed image classification because it can ease the classifier learning in imbalanced cases. Given the promising performance contrastive learning has shown recently in representation learning, in this work, we explore effective supervised contrastive learning strategies and tailor them to learn better image representations from imbalanced data in order to boost the classification accuracy thereon. Specifically, we propose a novel hybrid network structure being composed of a supervised contrastive loss to learn image representations and a cross-entropy loss to learn classifiers, where the learning is progressively transited from feature learning to the classifier learning to embody the idea that better features make better classifiers. We explore two variants of contrastive loss for feature learning, which vary in the forms but share a common idea of pulling the samples from the same class together in the normalized embedding space and pushing the samples from different classes apart. One of them is the recently proposed supervised contrastive (SC) loss, which is designed on top of the state-of-the-art unsupervised contrastive loss by incorporating positive samples from the same class. The other is a prototypical supervised contrastive (PSC) learning strategy which addresses the intensive memory consumption in standard SC loss and thus shows more promise under limited memory budget. Extensive experiments on three long-tailed classification datasets demonstrate the advantage of the proposed contrastive learning based hybrid networks in long-tailed classification.
citations.title: Contrastive Learning based Hybrid Networks for Long-Tailed Image Classification

snippets: Deep learning has made revolutionary advances to diverse applications in the presence of large-scale labeled datasets. However, it is prohibitively time-costly and labor-expensive to collect sufficient labeled data in most realistic scenarios. To mitigate the requirement for labeled data, semi-supervised learning (SSL) focuses on simultaneously exploring both labeled and unlabeled data, while transfer learning (TL) popularizes a favorable practice of fine-tuning a pre-trained model to the target data. A dilemma is thus encountered: Without a decent pre-trained model to provide an implicit regularization, SSL through self-training from scratch will be easily misled by inaccurate pseudo-labels, especially in large-sized label space; Without exploring the intrinsic structure of unlabeled data, TL through fine-tuning from limited labeled data is at risk of under-transfer caused by model shift. To escape from this dilemma, we present Self-Tuning to enable data-efficient deep learning by unifying the exploration of labeled and unlabeled data and the transfer of a pre-trained model, as well as a Pseudo Group Contrast (PGC) mechanism to mitigate the reliance on pseudo-labels and boost the tolerance to false labels. Self-Tuning outperforms its SSL and TL counterparts on five tasks by sharp margins, e.g. it doubles the accuracy of fine-tuning on Cars with 15% labels.
citations.title: Self-Tuning for Data-Efficient Deep Learning

question: What are some promising works in domain adaptation applied to video summarization? Let's say we want to finetune general models for higher performance on narrow domains such as summarizing sport videos.

sections.title: Background
sections.text: Video summarization aims to create concise representations of long videos by selecting the most important frames or segments <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Traditional approaches train models on general datasets that contain diverse video types, but these models often struggle when applied to specific domains due to significant differences in visual patterns, temporal structures, and content characteristics <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. For example, sports videos have unique features like repeated actions, specific camera angles, and domain-specific events that differ greatly from general video content <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Domain adaptation addresses this challenge by using techniques that can transfer knowledge learned from source domains (general videos) to target domains (specific applications like sports) while accounting for the distribution shift between domains <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This approach is particularly valuable because collecting large amounts of labeled data for each specific domain is expensive and time-consuming, making it practical to start with pre-trained general models and adapt them to specialized tasks <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.

sections.title: Cross-Domain Video Summarization Approaches
sections.text:
Several notable approaches have emerged to address cross-domain challenges in video summarization. Early work by Zhang et al. demonstrated that domain adaptation techniques can improve summarization performance by reducing statistical discrepancies across heterogeneous video datasets, showing that combining diverse video datasets with different contents and visual styles can benefit model training when proper domain adaptation methods are applied (Zhang et al., 2016). More recent work has focused on specific cross-domain scenarios, such as transferring knowledge from third-person to first-person videos. Ho et al. proposed a semi-supervised framework that performs cross-domain feature embedding by jointly training on fully annotated third-person videos, unlabeled first-person videos, and a small number of annotated first-person examples, effectively reducing the semantic gap between different video perspectives (Ho et al., 2017). 

For highlight detection specifically, researchers have explored unsupervised domain adaptation approaches that learn different types of knowledge about highlight moments and integrate them for target video categories (Xu et al., 2021). Additionally, some methods have bridged the gap between different video formats, such as transferring knowledge learned from movie trailers to full movie analysis, where visual and temporal analysis modules can be trained separately on trailers and movies respectively (Gan et al., 2023). These approaches demonstrate the potential for adapting models trained on one video domain to perform well on entirely different types of video content, which is particularly relevant for applications like sports video summarization where domain-specific patterns need to be captured.

sections.title: Dataset Adaptation and Multi-Dataset Training
sections.text:
A major challenge in domain-specific video summarization is the lack of large annotated datasets for training robust models. Dataset adaptation emerges as a practical solution by including heterogeneous videos from different datasets into a common format, allowing models to benefit from diverse training data (K. et al., 2019). This approach is particularly valuable because it can adapt existing datasets from other computer vision tasks to meet video summarization requirements, significantly reducing the effort needed to prepare datasets from scratch (K. et al., 2019).

The key to successful multi-dataset training lies in applying domain adaptation techniques that minimize the statistical differences between diverse video collections. Research has shown that domain adaptation methods like CORAL (Correlation Alignment) can effectively reduce domain shift by aligning the statistical properties of source and target distributions (Zhang et al., 2016) (Sun et al., 2015). When properly applied, these techniques enable the combination of video datasets that are heterogeneous in both content and visual styles, leading to improved model performance compared to training on individual datasets alone (Zhang et al., 2016).

This multi-dataset training approach is especially relevant for sports video summarization, where domain-specific datasets may be limited. By leveraging adaptation techniques, researchers can combine general video datasets with smaller sports-specific collections, creating more robust models that can generalize better to the target sports domain while maintaining the benefits of large-scale training data.

snippets: Unlike human learning, machine learning often fails to handle changes between training (source) and test (target) input distributions. Such domain shifts, common in practical scenarios, severely damage the performance of conventional machine learning methods. Supervised domain adaptation methods have been proposed for the case when the target data have labels, including some that perform very well despite being ``frustratingly easy'' to implement. However, in practice, the target domain is often unlabeled, requiring unsupervised adaptation. We propose a simple, effective, and efficient method for unsupervised domain adaptation called CORrelation ALignment (CORAL). CORAL minimizes domain shift by aligning the second-order statistics of source and target distributions, without requiring any target labels. Even though it is extraordinarily simple--it can be implemented in four lines of Matlab code--CORAL performs remarkably well in extensive evaluations on standard benchmark datasets.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Applications and Extensions
sections.text:
• **Sports Video Applications**: Early video summarization work focused specifically on sports videos for event detection and highlight video compilation (Pang et al., 2024). Recent research has developed cross-category video highlight detection methods that use unsupervised domain adaptation to transfer knowledge between different sports and video categories (Xu et al., 2021).

• **Multi-Modal Domain Knowledge Integration**: Advanced approaches link web videos with domain-specific knowledge to analyze content and generate summaries. These methods use tag localization and key-shot mining to estimate relevance scores for video shots with respect to specific events or queries (Zhu et al., 2019).

• **Cross-Domain Extensions**: The field has expanded from domain-specific sports videos to general applications including social media videos, news, first-person videos, and vlogs (Gan et al., 2023). Some approaches bridge different video formats, such as transferring knowledge learned from movie trailers to full movie analysis, where visual and temporal modules can be trained separately on different video types (Gan et al., 2023).

• **Query-Based Highlight Detection**: Recent work includes query-based video highlight datasets that cover diverse topics from lifestyle vlogs to news videos, enabling the development of systems that can detect relevant moments and highlights based on natural language queries (Gan et al., 2023) (Lei et al., 2021).

snippets: Detecting customized moments and highlights from videos given natural language (NL) user queries is an important but under-studied topic. One of the challenges in pursuing this direction is the lack of annotated data. To address this issue, we present the Query-based Video Highlights (QVHIGHLIGHTS) dataset. It consists of over 10,000 YouTube videos, covering a wide range of topics, from everyday activities and travel in lifestyle vlog videos to social and political activities in news videos. Each video in the dataset is annotated with: (1) a human-written free-form NL query, (2) relevant moments in the video w.r.t. the query, and (3) five-point scale saliency scores for all query-relevant clips. This comprehensive annotation enables us to develop and evaluate systems that detect relevant moments as well as salient highlights for diverse, flexible user queries. We also present a strong baseline for this task, Moment-DETR, a transformer encoder-decoder model that views moment retrieval as a direct set prediction problem, taking extracted video and query representations as inputs and predicting moment coordinates and saliency scores end-to-end. While our model does not utilize any human prior, we show that it performs competitively when compared to well-engineered architectures. With weakly supervised pretraining using ASR captions, MomentDETR substantially outperforms previous methods. Lastly, we present several ablations and visualizations of Moment-DETR. Data and code is publicly available at https://github.com/jayleicn/moment_detr

sections.title: Technical Methods and Frameworks
sections.text:
The technical foundation for cross-domain video summarization relies heavily on unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algorithms that can transfer knowledge between different video categories without requiring labeled data in the target domain. Recent work has explored cross-category video highlight detection through learning two types of knowledge about highlight moments and integrating them on target video categories, with methods that outperform typical UDA algorithms on various cross-category highlight detection tasks (Xu et al., 2021) (Gan et al., 2023).

For cross-modal applications, researchers have developed unsupervised domain adaptation methods specifically for text-video retrieval tasks that can generalize to new data sources without requiring corresponding text annotations (Cai et al., 2024) (Chen et al., 2021) (Liu et al., 2021). These methods include frameworks like Concept-Aware-Pseudo-Query (CAPQ) that learn discriminative and transferable features to bridge cross-domain discrepancies, and Adaptive Cross-Modal Prototypes that minimize both uni-modal and cross-modal distribution shift across source and target domains (Chen et al., 2021) (Liu et al., 2021).

Semi-supervised approaches have proven effective for domain adaptation in video summarization, particularly when limited labeled data is available in the target domain. These frameworks perform cross-domain feature embedding by jointly training on fully annotated source domain videos, unlabeled target domain videos, and small amounts of annotated target examples, effectively reducing semantic gaps between different video domains while alleviating overfitting issues (Ho et al., 2017). Modern transformer-based architectures like Moment-DETR treat highlight detection as a direct set prediction problem, taking video and query representations as inputs and predicting moment coordinates and saliency scores end-to-end, demonstrating competitive performance without requiring human priors (Gan et al., 2023) (Lei et al., 2021).

snippets:
When can we expect a text-video retrieval system to work effectively on datasets that differ from its training domain? In this work, we investigate this question through the lens of unsupervised domain adaptation in which the objective is to match natural language queries and video content in the presence of domain shift at query-time. Such systems have significant practical applications since they are capable generalising to new data sources without requiring corresponding text annotations. We make the following contributions: (1) We propose the UDAVR (Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Video Retrieval) benchmark and employ it to study the performance of text-video retrieval in the presence of domain
shift. (2) We propose Concept-Aware-Pseudo-Query (CAPQ), a method for learning discriminative and transferable features that bridge these cross-domain discrepancies to enable effective target domain retrieval using source domain supervision. (3) We show that CAPQ outperforms alternative domain adaptation strategies on UDAVR.
